Technical Appendices

Core GlossaryAppendix A

I. The Task and Positioning of This Appendix

This appendix provides systematic definitions and explanations of the core terms used throughout The Normative Foundations of Interstellar Civilization. As a foundational work of Interstellar Civilization Studies, this book proposes a large number of original concepts that constitute the conceptual basis of the New Three Views framework and of Cosmic Responsibility Ethics. The task of this appendix is to provide precise definitions of these concepts so that readers can accurately understand and apply the theoretical framework of this work.

VI. Boundary Statement

In accordance with the "first-generation rough-model positioning" of Chapter Zero §0.6, the term definitions in this appendix are in a state of continuous revision. As Interstellar Civilization Studies develops, the definitions of some terms may need adjustment. We welcome suggestions from the academic community for improving the term definitions.

A.1 Ontological Terms

This section collects core terms related to ontology. These terms derive mainly from the New Cosmological View (NC) and the New View of Life (NL), and describe the essential features of the universe, life, and existence.

A.1.1 Relational Reality

【Relational Reality】(Relational Reality)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{RelationalReality} \triangleq \forall e \in \mathcal{E}: \text{Identity}(e) = f(\{r_{ij}\}_{j \in \mathcal{N}(e)})$$

Where:

  • $\mathcal{E}$ is the set of beings
  • $e$ is any being
  • $\mathcal{N}(e)$ is the set of other beings associated with $e$
  • $r_{ij}$ is the relation between beings $i$ and $j$
  • $\text{Identity}(e)$ is the identity of being $e$

II. Natural-Language Definition

Relational reality refers to an ontological position that holds that the essence of a being lies not in its intrinsic properties but in the network of relations it has with other beings. On this view, "relations precede entities"—any entity is a node in a relational network, and its identity is constituted by the relations in which it participates.

III. Core Features

FeatureContentOpposite
Relational priorityRelations are ontologically prior to entitiesEntity priority
External constitutionIdentity is constituted by external relationsIntrinsic essentialism
Network structureBeings constitute a relational networkAtomism
DynamismRelations change dynamicallyStatic essence

Positive Examples

  1. Quantum entanglement: the states of entangled particles cannot be described independently, but only through the relations between them
  2. Ecosystem: the "essence" of a species depends on its position and function in the ecological network
  3. Social identity: an individual's social identity (such as "father," "citizen") is relational

Negative Examples

  1. Atomism: holds that there exist indivisible basic entities with intrinsic essences
  2. Substantial essentialism: holds that the essence of a thing is intrinsic and independent of relations
  3. Reductionism: holds that wholes can be fully reduced to parts

IV. Relations to Related Concepts

Related conceptRelationExplanation
→Processuality (A.1.2)ComplementaryRelations unfold in process
→Participatory Nature (A.1.3)ComplementaryThe observer participates in reality through relations
→Emergence (A.1.4)EntailmentEmergence is a result of relational networks
Substance ontologyOppositionRelational ontology vs. substance ontology

V. Theoretical Anchoring

Relational reality is the ontological basis of NC-1 (relations precede entities), a core proposition of the New Cosmological View (NC). It provides a conceptual framework for understanding the universe as a relational network.

$$\text{NC-1} \Leftarrow \text{RelationalReality}$$

First appearance

Volume One, Chapter One, §1.1.1

References

  1. Rovelli, C. (2021). Helgoland: Making Sense of the Quantum Revolution. Riverhead Books.
  2. Barad, K. (2007). Meeting the Universe Halfway: Quantum Physics and the Entanglement of Matter and Meaning. Duke University Press.
  3. Whitehead, A. N. (1929). Process and Reality. Macmillan.

A.1.2 Processuality

【Processuality】(Processuality)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{Processuality} \triangleq \forall e \in \mathcal{E}: e = \lim_{t \to \infty} \int_{0}^{t} \dot{e}(\tau) d\tau$$

Where:

  • $e$ is any being
  • $\dot{e}(\tau)$ is the rate of change of the being at time $\tau$
  • A being is defined as the integral of its process of change

Or, in a more intuitive formulation:

$$\text{Being} = \text{Becoming}$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

Processuality refers to an ontological position that holds that the essence of existence is process rather than static state. On this view, "process precedes state"—any apparently static state is a cross-section of a process, and the process itself is the more fundamental reality.

III. Core Features

FeatureContentOpposite
Process priorityProcesses are ontologically prior to statesState priority
Dynamic essenceThe essence of a being is dynamicStatic essence
TemporalityTime is a constitutive dimension of existenceTimeless eternity
GenerativityBeings constantly become and transformFixed immutability

Positive Examples

  1. River: a river is not a fixed entity but a process of water flowing
  2. Life: life is not a static structure but a process of metabolism
  3. Consciousness: consciousness is not a fixed state but a continuous stream of experience

Negative Examples

  1. Platonic Forms: an eternally unchanging world of Forms
  2. Newtonian particle: a point mass with determinate position and momentum
  3. Logical atom: an unanalyzable basic proposition

IV. Relations to Related Concepts

Related conceptRelationExplanation
→Relational Reality (A.1.1)ComplementaryRelations unfold in process
→Participatory Nature (A.1.3)ComplementaryParticipation is a process
→Emergence (A.1.4)EntailmentEmergence is a result of dynamic processes
Substance ontologyOppositionProcess ontology vs. substance ontology

V. Theoretical Anchoring

Processuality is the ontological basis of NC-2 (process precedes state), a core proposition of the New Cosmological View (NC). It provides a conceptual framework for understanding the universe as a dynamic process.

$$\text{NC-2} \Leftarrow \text{Processuality}$$

First appearance

Volume One, Chapter One, §1.1.2

References

  1. Whitehead, A. N. (1929). Process and Reality. Macmillan.
  2. Rescher, N. (1996). Process Metaphysics: An Introduction to Process Philosophy. SUNY Press.
  3. Bergson, H. (1911). Creative Evolution. Henry Holt and Company.

A.1.3 Participatory Nature

【Participatory Nature】(Participatory Nature)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{ParticipatoryNature} \triangleq \forall o \in \mathcal{O}, \forall s \in \mathcal{S}: \text{State}(s | o) \neq \text{State}(s | \neg o)$$

Where:

  • $\mathcal{O}$ is the set of observers
  • $\mathcal{S}$ is the set of systems
  • $\text{State}(s | o)$ is the state of system $s$ under observation by observer $o$
  • The state of the system depends on the observer's participation

A stronger formulation:

$$\text{Reality} = f(\text{Observer}, \text{Observed}, \text{Observation})$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

Participatory nature refers to an ontological position that holds that the observer is not a spectator external to the observed system, but a participant who constitutes the system's state through the act of observation. On this view, "participation precedes spectatorship"—there is a constitutive relation between the epistemic subject and the epistemic object.

III. Core Features

FeatureContentOpposite
Observer dependenceSystem states depend on the observerObserver independence
Constitutive relationThe observer participates in constituting realityReflective relation
Subject-object intertwiningSubject and object are inseparableSubject-object dichotomy
InterventionalityObservation is interventionPassive reflection

Positive Examples

  1. Quantum measurement: the act of measurement "collapses" the quantum state, and the observer participates in determining the measurement result
  2. Anthropological fieldwork: the presence of the researcher changes the behavior of the group being studied
  3. Financial markets: investors' expectations affect market prices, producing self-fulfilling prophecies

Negative Examples

  1. Classical physics: assumes that an observer can observe a system without disturbing it
  2. God's-eye view: assumes the existence of an omniscient observer transcending the system
  3. Objectivism: assumes the existence of an objective reality independent of the observer

IV. Relations to Related Concepts

Related conceptRelationExplanation
→Relational Reality (A.1.1)EntailmentThere is a relation between observer and observed
→Processuality (A.1.2)ComplementaryParticipation is a process
→Participatory Cognition (A.2.1)CorrespondenceParticipatory nature is the ontological basis of participatory cognition
ObjectivismOppositionParticipatory nature vs. objectivism

V. Theoretical Anchoring

Participatory nature is the ontological basis of NC-3 (participation precedes spectatorship), a core proposition of the New Cosmological View (NC), and also the ontological basis of NK-1 (cognition is intervention), a core proposition of the New View of Cognition (NK).

$$\text{NC-3} \Leftarrow \text{ParticipatoryNature}$$ $$\text{NK-1} \Leftarrow \text{ParticipatoryNature}$$

First appearance

Volume One, Chapter One, §1.1.3

References

  1. Wheeler, J. A. (1990). "Information, Physics, Quantum: The Search for Links." In Complexity, Entropy, and the Physics of Information. Addison-Wesley.
  2. Barad, K. (2007). Meeting the Universe Halfway. Duke University Press.
  3. Fuchs, C. A. (2017). "On Participatory Realism." In Information and Interaction. Springer.

A.1.4 Emergence

【Emergence】(Emergence)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{Emergence} \triangleq \exists P_{\text{whole}}: P_{\text{whole}} \neq f(\{P_{\text{part}_i}\}_{i=1}^{n})$$

Where:

  • $P_{\text{whole}}$ is a property at the level of the whole
  • $P_{\text{part}_i}$ is a property at the level of the parts
  • The properties of the whole cannot be derived from the properties of the parts by any function

A more precise formulation distinguishes strong emergence from weak emergence:

$$\text{WeakEmergence}: P_{\text{whole}} = f(\{P_{\text{part}_i}\}, \{R_{ij}\})$$

$$\text{StrongEmergence}: P_{\text{whole}} \neq f(\{P_{\text{part}_i}\}, \{R_{ij}\}, \text{Laws})$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

Emergence refers to the phenomenon in which new properties or new behaviors appear at the level of the whole that are not possessed at the level of the parts. Weak emergence means that these new properties can in principle be derived from the parts and their relations, but are difficult to predict in practice; strong emergence means that these new properties cannot in principle be derived from the parts.

III. Core Features

FeatureContentExplanation
LevelsEmergence occurs between different levelsMicro → macro
NoveltyEmergent properties are newNon-additivity
IrreducibilityEmergent properties cannot be fully reducedAnti-reductionism
Downward causationEmergent properties may affect the partsCausal efficacy

Positive Examples

  1. Consciousness: consciousness may emerge from neuronal activity but cannot be reduced to neurons
  2. Life: life emerges from chemical reactions but possesses properties that chemical reactions do not have
  3. Social institutions: institutions emerge from individual behavior but possess causal power that individuals do not have

Negative Examples

  1. Additive properties: mass is additive, and the mass of the whole equals the sum of the masses of the parts
  2. Reducible properties: temperature can be reduced to the average kinetic energy of molecules
  3. Combinatorial properties: the number of elements of a set is determined by the number of elements of its subsets

IV. Relations to Related Concepts

Related conceptRelationExplanation
→Relational Reality (A.1.1)BasisEmergence derives from relations
→Complexity (A.1.5)ConditionEmergence is more likely in complex systems
→Self-organization (A.1.6)MechanismSelf-organization is a mechanism of emergence
ReductionismOppositionEmergentism vs. reductionism

V. Theoretical Anchoring

Emergence is an important concept of the New Cosmological View (NC), supporting NC-1 (relations precede entities) and NC-2 (process precedes state). Emergence is also an important concept of the New View of Life (NL), supporting NL-1 (the continuum of life).

$$\text{Emergence} \rightarrow \text{NC-1}, \text{NC-2}, \text{NL-1}$$

First appearance

Volume One, Chapter One, §1.2.1

References

  1. Bedau, M. A., & Humphreys, P. (Eds.). (2008). Emergence: Contemporary Readings in Philosophy and Science. MIT Press.
  2. Holland, J. H. (1998). Emergence: From Chaos to Order. Addison-Wesley.
  3. Kim, J. (1999). "Making Sense of Emergence." Philosophical Studies, 95(1-2), 3-36.

A.1.5 Complexity

【Complexity】(Complexity)

I. Formal Definition

Complexity can be defined from several angles. This work adopts the following composite definition:

$$\text{Complexity}(S) = \alpha \cdot H(S) + \beta \cdot I(S) + \gamma \cdot E(S)$$

Where:

  • $H(S)$ is the structural complexity of system $S$ (such as Kolmogorov complexity)
  • $I(S)$ is the degree of information integration of system $S$ (such as the Φ value)
  • $E(S)$ is the emergenceness of system $S$ (such as the number and strength of emergent properties)
  • $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are weight coefficients

II. Natural-Language Definition

Complexity refers to a system's having multiple interacting components among which nonlinear relations hold, with the whole exhibiting emergent behavior and the system's behavior being difficult to predict simply from the behavior of the parts. Complex systems lie at the "edge" between order and chaos.

III. Core Features

FeatureContentOpposite
Multiple componentsThe system consists of multiple interacting componentsSimple system
NonlinearityNonlinear relations hold among componentsLinear system
EmergentnessThe system exhibits emergent behaviorAdditivity
AdaptivityThe system can adapt to environmental changeRigid system

Positive Examples

  1. Organism: composed of trillions of cells, exhibiting the phenomenon of life
  2. Ecosystem: composed of many species and abiotic factors, exhibiting self-regulation
  3. Human society: composed of billions of people, exhibiting social institutions and culture

Negative Examples

  1. Ideal gas: no interactions among molecules
  2. Crystal: highly ordered structure, fully predictable
  3. Random system: completely random, with no structure

IV. Relations to Related Concepts

Related conceptRelationExplanation
→Emergence (A.1.4)EntailmentComplex systems exhibit emergence
→Self-organization (A.1.6)MechanismSelf-organization produces complexity
→Negentropy (A.1.8)CorrelationComplex systems maintain negentropy
SimplicityOppositionComplexity vs. simplicity

V. Theoretical Anchoring

Complexity is a core concept of the New View of Life (NL), supporting NL-2 (negentropic organization). Life is understood as a kind of complex negentropic organization.

$$\text{Complexity} \rightarrow \text{NL-2}$$

First appearance

Volume One, Chapter One, §1.2.2

References

  1. Mitchell, M. (2009). Complexity: A Guided Tour. Oxford University Press.
  2. Kauffman, S. A. (1993). The Origins of Order. Oxford University Press.
  3. Cilliers, P. (1998). Complexity and Postmodernism. Routledge.

A.1.6 Self-organization

【Self-organization】(Self-organization)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{SelfOrganization} \triangleq \exists S: \frac{\partial O(S)}{\partial t} > 0 \land \neg \exists A_{\text{ext}}: A_{\text{ext}} \rightarrow \frac{\partial O(S)}{\partial t}$$

Where:

  • $S$ is a system
  • $O(S)$ is the degree of order of the system (such as negentropy)
  • $A_{\text{ext}}$ is an external agent
  • The degree of order of the system increases, and this increase is not caused by an external agent

II. Natural-Language Definition

Self-organization refers to the process by which a system, without external control, spontaneously forms globally ordered structures or patterns through local interactions among its components. Self-organizing systems generate order from within rather than having order imposed from without.

III. Core Features

FeatureContentOpposite
SpontaneityOrder arises spontaneouslyExternal imposition
DistributedControl is distributed throughout the systemCentralized control
Local interactionBased on local rulesGlobal rules
Non-equilibriumRequires flows of energy/matterEquilibrium state

Positive Examples

  1. Bénard convection: a liquid spontaneously forms convection patterns under a temperature gradient
  2. Flocking of birds: a flock spontaneously forms ordered flight patterns
  3. Crystal growth: molecules spontaneously arrange themselves into a crystal structure

Negative Examples

  1. Mechanical assembly: assembled by an external agent according to a design
  2. Command hierarchy: an organization controlled by orders from superiors
  3. Program execution: an algorithm designed by a programmer

IV. Relations to Related Concepts

Related conceptRelationExplanation
→Complexity (A.1.5)ResultSelf-organization produces complexity
→Emergence (A.1.4)MechanismSelf-organization is a mechanism of emergence
→Negentropy (A.1.8)CorrelationSelf-organization produces negentropy
Hetero-organizationOppositionSelf-organization vs. hetero-organization

V. Theoretical Anchoring

Self-organization is an important concept of the New Cosmological View (NC) and the New View of Life (NL). It explains how the universe moves from simplicity to complexity, and how life arises from non-living matter.

$$\text{SelfOrganization} \rightarrow \text{NC-2}, \text{NL-2}$$

First appearance

Volume One, Chapter One, §1.2.3

References

  1. Kauffman, S. A. (1993). The Origins of Order. Oxford University Press.
  2. Prigogine, I., & Stengers, I. (1984). Order Out of Chaos. Bantam Books.
  3. Haken, H. (1983). Synergetics: Introduction and Advanced Topics. Springer.

A.1.7 Other Ontological Terms

This section collects other important ontological terms.

A.1.7.1 Dissipative Structure

【Dissipative Structure】(Dissipative Structure)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{DissipativeStructure} \triangleq S: \frac{dS_{\text{int}}}{dt} > 0 \land \frac{dS_{\text{tot}}}{dt} \leq 0$$

Where:

  • $S_{\text{int}}$ is the entropy internal to the system
  • $S_{\text{tot}}$ is the total entropy of the system and its environment
  • The internal entropy production of the system is positive, but the system maintains order through exchange with its environment

II. Natural-Language Definition

A dissipative structure refers to an open system far from equilibrium that, through exchanging energy and matter with its environment, maintains or produces ordered structures in the course of dissipating energy.

III. Core Features

FeatureContent
Far from equilibriumThe system is in a non-equilibrium state
OpennessExchanges energy and matter with the environment
OrderMaintains or produces ordered structures
DissipativityRequires continuous dissipation of energy

Positive examples: organisms, hurricanes, cities

Negative examples: crystals, equilibrium systems

Theoretical anchoring: NL-2 (negentropic organization)

First appearance: Volume One, Chapter Two, §2.2.1

A.1.7.2 Negentropy

【Negentropy】(Negentropy)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{Negentropy} \triangleq J = -S = k_B \ln W^{-1}$$

Where:

  • $S$ is entropy
  • $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant
  • $W$ is the number of microstates

Or, more generally:

$$J = S_{\max} - S$$

Where $S_{\max}$ is the maximum possible entropy.

II. Natural-Language Definition

Negentropy is the inverse concept of entropy, denoting the degree of order or information content of a system. Schrödinger defined life as a system that "feeds on negentropy." Negentropy is one of the core concepts of this work.

III. Core Features

FeatureContent
Measure of orderMeasures the degree of order of a system
Information-relatedPositively correlated with information content
Thermodynamic basisDerives from the second law of thermodynamics
Feature of lifeLife maintains negentropy

Positive examples: organisms, crystals, ordered information

Negative examples: thermal equilibrium state, maximum-entropy state

Theoretical anchoring: NL-2 (negentropic organization), →Negentropy Responsibility (A.3.3)

First appearance: Volume One, Chapter Two, §2.2.2

A.1.7.3 Possibility Space

【Possibility Space】(Possibility Space)

I. Formal Definition

$$\mathcal{P}(S, t) \triangleq \{s' \in \mathcal{S} : \exists \text{path}(s(t), s') \land \text{Prob}(\text{path}) > 0\}$$

Where:

  • $S$ is a system (or subject)
  • $t$ is time
  • $\mathcal{S}$ is the state space
  • $s(t)$ is the current state
  • $s'$ is a possible future state
  • $\text{path}(s(t), s')$ is a path from the current state to a future state

II. Natural-Language Definition

The possibility space refers to the set of all states that the system may reach in the future, starting from its current state. It represents the system's "degrees of freedom" or "space of choice."

III. Core Features

FeatureContent
Future-orientedPoints to possible futures
Set of statesIs a set of states
Path-dependentDepends on the current state
MeasurabilityIts size can be measured

Positive examples: an individual's space of career choices, a civilization's space of development paths

Negative examples: past events that have already occurred

Theoretical anchoring: →Recursive Freedom (A.3.1), →RFD (A.4.2)

First appearance: Volume One, Chapter Three, §3.3.1

A.1.7.4 Agency Status

【Agency Status】(Agency Status)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{AgencyStatus}(E) = g(\text{UCS}(E), \text{Autonomy}(E), \text{Interests}(E))$$

Where:

  • $E$ is an entity
  • $\text{UCS}(E)$ is the entity's Universal Consciousness Scale value
  • $\text{Autonomy}(E)$ is the entity's degree of autonomy
  • $\text{Interests}(E)$ is whether the entity has identifiable interests
  • $g$ is an aggregation function

II. Natural-Language Definition

Agency status refers to the status of whether an entity should be regarded as a moral agent (with rights and duties) or a moral patient (whose interests should be considered). This work adopts a functionalist stance, holding that agency status is a matter of degree and is functional.

III. Core Features

FeatureContent
GradednessAgency status is a matter of degree
FunctionalityBased on function rather than substrate
MultidimensionalityInvolves multiple dimensions
VariabilityMay change over time

Positive examples: humans, higher animals, (possible) advanced AI

Negative examples: stones, simple programs

Theoretical anchoring: NL-3 (functionality of agency status)

First appearance: Volume One, Chapter Two, §2.3.1

A.1.7.5 Cross-Substrate

【Cross-Substrate】(Cross-Substrate)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{CrossSubstrate}(P) \triangleq \exists S_1, S_2 \in \text{Substrates}: P(S_1) \land P(S_2) \land S_1 \neq S_2$$

Where:

  • $P$ is a property or function
  • $S_1, S_2$ are distinct material substrates
  • The same property can be realized on different substrates

II. Natural-Language Definition

Cross-substrate means that a property or function does not depend on a specific material substrate and can be realized on a variety of different material carriers. This is the core claim of functionalism.

III. Core Features

FeatureContent
Substrate independenceDoes not depend on a specific substrate
Multiple realizabilityCan be realized on multiple substrates
Functional equivalenceFunctional equivalence rather than material identity
OpennessOpen to new substrates

Positive examples: computation can be realized on many kinds of hardware; life may be realized on different chemical bases

Negative examples: a specific chemical reaction depends on specific molecules

Theoretical anchoring: NL-1 (the continuum of life), NL-3 (functionality of agency status)

First appearance: Volume One, Chapter Two, §2.1.3

A.1.7.6 Deep Time

【Deep Time】(Deep Time)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{DeepTime} \triangleq T: T \gg T_{\text{human}} \land T \sim T_{\text{geological/cosmological}}$$

Where:

  • $T$ is a timescale
  • $T_{\text{human}}$ is the human lifespan (~100 years)
  • $T_{\text{geological}}$ is the geological timescale (~10⁶-10⁹ years)
  • $T_{\text{cosmological}}$ is the cosmological timescale (~10¹⁰ years)

II. Natural-Language Definition

Deep time refers to a timescale far exceeding the human lifespan, typically denoting spans of hundreds of years, thousands of years, or longer. This work is concerned with normative questions on the scale of deep time.

III. Core Features

FeatureContent
Trans-human scaleFar exceeds an individual lifespan
Intergenerational spanSpans multiple generations
UncertaintyPrediction is more difficult
Extension of responsibilityResponsibility extends into the future

Positive examples: the long-term effects of climate change, the disposal of nuclear waste, the long-term development of civilization

Negative examples: everyday decisions, business cycles

Theoretical anchoring: →Intergenerational justice, →Long-range responsibility

First appearance: Introduction, §I.1.3

A.2 Epistemological Terms

This section collects core terms related to epistemology. These terms derive mainly from the New View of Cognition (NK) and describe the essential features of knowledge, cognition, and understanding.

A.2.1 Participatory Cognition

【Participatory Cognition】(Participatory Cognition)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{ParticipatoryCognition} \triangleq \forall K \in \mathcal{K}: K = f(\text{Knower}, \text{Known}, \text{KnowingProcess})$$

Where:

  • $\mathcal{K}$ is the set of knowledge
  • $K$ is any item of knowledge
  • Knowledge is a function of the knower, the known, and the process of knowing

A stronger formulation:

$$\text{Cognition} \Rightarrow \text{Intervention}$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

Participatory cognition refers to an epistemological position that holds that cognition is not the passive reflection of an objective reality independent of the knower, but an active process of interaction between the knower and the object of cognition. Cognition is intervention—the act of cognition changes the object cognized.

III. Core Features

FeatureContentOpposite
ActivityCognition is an active processPassive reflection
InterventionalityCognition changes the objectPure observation
InteractivityThe knower interacts with the objectOne-way transmission
ConstitutionCognition participates in constituting the objectDiscovery of a pre-existing object

Positive Examples

  1. Quantum measurement: the act of measurement changes the quantum system measured
  2. Social-science research: the researcher's intervention changes the social phenomenon studied
  3. Self-knowledge: the act of reflection changes the self reflected upon

Negative Examples

  1. Mirror theory: holds that the mind is a mirror of reality
  2. Camera model: holds that perception is a photograph of reality
  3. Computer metaphor: holds that cognition is the processing of external input

IV. Relations to Related Concepts

Related conceptRelationExplanation
→Participatory Nature (A.1.3)Ontological basisThe ontological presupposition of participatory cognition
→Social Knowledge (A.2.2)ComplementaryThe social dimension of knowledge
→Epistemic Humility (A.2.3)EntailmentParticipatory cognition entails epistemic humility
RepresentationalismOppositionParticipatory vs. representational

V. Theoretical Anchoring

Participatory cognition is the epistemological basis of NK-1 (cognition is intervention), a core proposition of the New View of Cognition (NK).

$$\text{NK-1} \Leftarrow \text{ParticipatoryCognition}$$

First appearance

Volume One, Chapter Three, §3.1.1

References

  1. Varela, F. J., Thompson, E., & Rosch, E. (1991). The Embodied Mind. MIT Press.
  2. Clark, A. (2008). Supersizing the Mind. Oxford University Press.
  3. Noë, A. (2004). Action in Perception. MIT Press.

A.2.2 Social Knowledge

【Social Knowledge】(Social Knowledge)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{SocialKnowledge} \triangleq \forall K \in \mathcal{K}: \text{Justification}(K) = h(\text{Community}(K), \text{Practices}(K))$$

Where:

  • $K$ is an item of knowledge
  • $\text{Justification}(K)$ is the justification of the knowledge
  • $\text{Community}(K)$ is the epistemic community
  • $\text{Practices}(K)$ are the cognitive practices
  • The justification of knowledge depends on community and practices

II. Natural-Language Definition

Social knowledge refers to an epistemological position that holds that knowledge is not the product of isolated individuals but a social achievement produced by social groups through shared practices, communication, and criticism. The legitimacy of knowledge derives from social recognition and collective practice.

III. Core Features

FeatureContentOpposite
SocialityKnowledge is a social productIndividualism
PracticalityKnowledge is embedded in practicePure theory
CommunicabilityKnowledge can be communicatedPrivate language
CriticizabilityKnowledge is open to criticismUnquestionability

Positive Examples

  1. Scientific knowledge: produced through the social processes of peer review and replicable experiment
  2. Legal knowledge: produced through the social processes of legislation, precedent, and jurisprudential discussion
  3. Technical knowledge: produced through the social processes of engineering practice and standard-setting

Negative Examples

  1. Cartesian doubt: assumes that knowledge can be established by an isolated individual alone
  2. Private intuition: incommunicable personal feelings
  3. Mystical revelation: unverifiable supernatural knowledge

IV. Relations to Related Concepts

Related conceptRelationExplanation
→Participatory Cognition (A.2.1)ComplementaryThe social dimension of cognition
→Negotiability (A.2.5)EntailmentSocial knowledge is negotiable
Individualist epistemologyOppositionSocial vs. individual

V. Theoretical Anchoring

Social knowledge is the epistemological basis of NK-2 (knowledge is a social achievement), a core proposition of the New View of Cognition (NK).

$$\text{NK-2} \Leftarrow \text{SocialKnowledge}$$

First appearance

Volume One, Chapter Three, §3.1.2

References

  1. Kuhn, T. S. (1962). The Structure of Scientific Revolutions. University of

Chicago Press.

  1. Longino, H. E. (1990). Science as Social Knowledge. Princeton University Press.
  2. Goldman, A. I. (1999). Knowledge in a Social World. Oxford University Press.

A.2.3 Epistemic Humility

【Epistemic Humility】(Epistemic Humility)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{EpistemicHumility} \triangleq \forall K \in \mathcal{K}: \text{Confidence}(K) \leq 1 - \epsilon, \quad \epsilon > 0$$

Where:

  • $K$ is an item of knowledge
  • $\text{Confidence}(K)$ is the degree of confidence in the knowledge
  • $\epsilon$ is the margin of uncertainty
  • A certain degree of uncertainty is maintained toward any item of knowledge

More generally:

$$\text{EpistemicHumility} \triangleq \text{Acknowledgment}(\text{Limits}(\text{Knowledge}))$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

Epistemic humility refers to acknowledging the finitude of human cognitive capacities and acknowledging that our knowledge may be incomplete, fallible, and biased. Epistemic humility is not skepticism but a clear-eyed recognition of the boundaries of knowledge.

III. Core Features

FeatureContentOpposite
Recognition of finitudeAcknowledges the finitude of cognitive capacitiesOmniscience assumption
FallibilismAcknowledges that knowledge may be erroneousInfallibilism
OpennessRemains open to revisionDogmatism
Self-reflectionReflects on one's own cognitive limitationsBlind confidence

Positive Examples

  1. Scientific method: acknowledges through falsifiability that theories may be overturned
  2. Bayesian inference: expresses uncertainty through probability
  3. Metacognition: reflects on one's own cognitive processes and limitations

Negative Examples

  1. Dogmatism: claims to possess unquestionable truth
  2. Preference for certainty: excessively pursuing certain answers
  3. Cognitive closure: refuses to consider alternative views

IV. Relations to Related Concepts

Related conceptRelationExplanation
→Deep Uncertainty (A.2.4)ResponseEpistemic humility is the attitude for responding to deep uncertainty
→Negotiability (A.2.5)EntailmentEpistemic humility entails openness to negotiation
→Reversibility (A.3.4)CorrelationEpistemic humility supports the Principle of Reversibility

Theoretical anchoring

Epistemic humility is an important concept of the New View of Cognition (NK), supporting NK-3 (rationality is ecological) and NK-4 (truth is negotiational). It is also the epistemological basis of bridge principle BP-2 (the principle of epistemic humility).

$$\text{EpistemicHumility} \rightarrow \text{NK-3}, \text{NK-4}, \text{BP-2}$$

First appearance

Volume One, Chapter Three, §3.2.1

References

  1. Sextus Empiricus. Outlines of Pyrrhonism.
  2. Kahneman, D. (2011). Thinking, Fast and Slow. Farrar, Straus and Giroux.
  3. Tetlock, P. E., & Gardner, D. (2015). Superforecasting. Crown.

A.2.4 Deep Uncertainty

【Deep Uncertainty】(Deep Uncertainty)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{DeepUncertainty} \triangleq \neg \exists P: P \in \mathcal{P}(\Omega) \land \text{Justified}(P)$$

Where:

  • $\Omega$ is the set of possible states
  • $\mathcal{P}(\Omega)$ is the set of probability distributions over $\Omega$
  • There is no justified probability distribution

A more detailed classification:

Level of uncertaintyKnownUnknown
RiskProbability distribution—
UncertaintyPossible statesProbability distribution
Deep uncertainty—Possible states, probability distribution

II. Natural-Language Definition

Deep uncertainty refers to an extreme state of uncertainty: we not only do not know the probabilities of various outcomes, but may not even know what all the possible outcomes are, do not know the causal structure of the system, and do not know the preferences of the stakeholders. Traditional probability theory and expected utility theory fail under deep uncertainty.

III. Core Features

FeatureContentDifference from risk
Probabilities unknowableCannot assign probabilitiesRisk has known probabilities
Incomplete state spacePossible states may be omittedRisk has a complete state space
Model uncertaintyDo not know the correct modelRisk has a known model
Preference uncertaintyPreferences may changeRisk has stable preferences

Positive Examples

  1. Long-term impact of AGI: cannot foresee how AGI will develop
  2. Extreme scenarios of climate change: unknown tipping points may exist
  3. Contact with extraterrestrial civilizations: cannot foresee the nature of an extraterrestrial civilization

Negative Examples

  1. Casino games: probabilities are known (risk)
  2. Insurance actuarial work: probability estimates based on historical data
  3. Weather forecasting: probabilities can be assigned in the short term

IV. Relations to Related Concepts

Related conceptRelationExplanation
→Epistemic Humility (A.2.3)AttitudeEpistemic humility is the attitude for responding to deep uncertainty
→Reversibility (A.3.4)ResponseReversibility is the strategy for responding to deep uncertainty
RiskDistinctionRisk has known probabilities
UncertaintyDistinctionUncertainty has a known state space

V. Theoretical Anchoring

Deep uncertainty is one of the core concepts of this work. It is the core concept of one of the three puzzles proposed in the Introduction (Puzzle Two: rationality under deep uncertainty), and is also the basis of legitimacy for the Principle of Reversibility (REV).

$$\text{DeepUncertainty} \rightarrow \text{Puzzle 2}, \text{REV}$$

First appearance

Introduction, §I.1.2

References

  1. Walker, W. E., et al. (2003). "Defining Uncertainty." Integrated Assessment, 4(1), 5-17.
  2. Lempert, R. J., et al. (2003). Shaping the Next One Hundred Years. RAND Corporation.
  3. Marchau, V. A., et al. (Eds.). (2019). Decision Making under Deep Uncertainty. Springer.

A.2.5 Negotiability

【Negotiability】(Negotiability)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{Negotiability}(K) \triangleq \exists \text{Process}: K \rightarrow K' \land K' \neq K \land \text{Legitimate}(\text{Process})$$

Where:

  • $K$ is an item of knowledge or a norm
  • $K'$ is the revised item of knowledge or norm
  • $\text{Process}$ is a process of negotiation
  • Through a legitimate process of negotiation, knowledge or norms can be revised

II. Natural-Language Definition

Negotiability refers to the property whereby knowledge, norms, or institutions can be revised, adjusted, or replaced through a legitimate process of negotiation. Negotiability does not imply relativism, but rather acknowledges the perfectibility of human artifacts.

III. Core Features

FeatureContentOpposite
RevisabilityCan be revisedUnchangeability
ProceduralityRequires legitimate procedureArbitrary change
Reason-orientedRevision based on reasonsBased on power
Consensus-orientedPursues consensusImposes views

Positive Examples

  1. Scientific theories: can be revised through new evidence and new arguments
  2. Legal provisions: can be revised through legislative procedure
  3. International treaties: can be revised through diplomatic negotiation

Negative Examples

  1. Mathematical theorems: cannot be changed through negotiation (though axioms can be replaced)
  2. Physical laws: cannot be changed through negotiation (they are discovered, not invented)
  3. Dogma: assertions claimed to be unquestionable

IV. Relations to Related Concepts

Related conceptRelationExplanation
→Social Knowledge (A.2.2)EntailmentSocial knowledge is negotiable
→Epistemic Humility (A.2.3)EntailmentEpistemic humility entails openness to negotiation
→Versioned Governance (A.5.5)InstitutionalizationThe institutionalized form of negotiation

V. Theoretical Anchoring

Negotiability is the epistemological basis of NK-4 (truth is negotiational), a core proposition of the New View of Cognition (NK). It is also the epistemological basis of the protocol-stack methodology.

$$\text{NK-4} \Leftarrow \text{Negotiability}$$

First appearance

Volume One, Chapter Three, §3.2.3

References

  1. Habermas, J. (1984). The Theory of Communicative Action. Beacon Press.
  2. Rawls, J. (1993). Political Liberalism. Columbia University Press.
  3. Brandom, R. (1994). Making It Explicit. Harvard University Press.

A.2.6 Other Epistemological Terms

This section collects other important epistemological terms.

A.2.6.1 Ecological Rationality

【Ecological Rationality】(Ecological Rationality)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{EcologicalRationality}(S, E) \triangleq \text{Fit}(S, E) \land \text{Adaptive}(S, E)$$

Where:

  • $S$ is a cognitive strategy
  • $E$ is an environment
  • A rational strategy is one that fits the environment

II. Natural-Language Definition

Ecological rationality refers to the view that rationality is not abstract and universal but adapted to a particular environment. A strategy that is rational in one environment may not be rational in another.

III. Core Features

FeatureContent
Environment dependenceRationality depends on the environment
AdaptivityRational strategies are adaptive
Bounded rationalityAcknowledges the finitude of cognitive resources
HeuristicsUses simple heuristics

Positive examples: fast-and-frugal heuristics, adaptive explanations of cognitive bias

Negative examples: abstract ideal rationality, unconstrained optimization

Theoretical anchoring: NK-3 (rationality is ecological)

First appearance: Volume One, Chapter Three, §3.2.2

A.2.6.2 Negotiated Truth

【Negotiated Truth】(Negotiated Truth)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{NegotiatedTruth} \triangleq T: \text{Accepted}(T, C) \land \text{Process}(T, C) = \text{Negotiation}$$

Where:

  • $T$ is a truth claim
  • $C$ is a community
  • Truth is accepted by the community through a process of negotiation

II. Natural-Language Definition

Negotiated truth refers to the view that truth is not a pre-existing fact to be discovered but is constructed through a community's process of negotiation. This is not to say that truth is arbitrary, but rather that the establishment of truth depends on legitimate cognitive practices.

III. Core Features

FeatureContent
Social constructionTruth is constructed through social processes
Procedure dependenceDepends on legitimate procedure
RevisabilityCan be revised
Consensus-orientedPursues consensus

Positive examples: scientific consensus, legal judgments, ethical norms

Negative examples: mathematical theorems (discovered rather than negotiated), physical constants (measured rather than negotiated)

Theoretical anchoring: NK-4 (truth is negotiational)

First appearance: Volume One, Chapter Three, §3.2.3

A.2.6.3 4E Cognition

【4E Cognition】(4E Cognition)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{4ECognition} \triangleq \text{Embodied} \land \text{Embedded} \land \text{Enacted} \land \text{Extended}$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

4E cognition is a research programme in contemporary cognitive science that holds that cognition is:

  • Embodied: dependent on the body
  • Embedded: embedded in an environment
  • Enacted: generated through action
  • Extended: extended into tools and the environment

III. Core Features

FeatureContent
Anti-CartesianismOpposes mind-body dualism
Anti-computationalismOpposes purely computational models
HolismCognition is a holistic process
DynamismCognition is a dynamic process

Positive examples: cognition using tools, body posture affecting judgment, environmental scaffolding

Negative examples: purely internal representation, computation in the head

Theoretical anchoring: NK-1 (cognition is intervention), NK-3 (rationality is ecological)

First appearance: Volume One, Chapter Three, §3.1.1

A.2.6.4 Minimal Argument Path

【Minimal Argument Path】(Minimal Argument Path)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{MinimalArgumentPath}(P, C) \triangleq \text{Path}(P, C): \text{Length}(\text{Path}) = \min$$

Where:

  • $P$ is a premise
  • $C$ is a conclusion
  • The minimal argument path is the shortest valid path from premise to conclusion

II. Natural-Language Definition

The minimal argument path refers to the most concise sequence of argument from basic premises to core conclusions. It is used to grasp quickly the core structure of an argument and is also the focus of critical examination.

III. Core Features

FeatureContent
ConcisenessAs brief as possible
CompletenessContains all necessary steps
TestabilityFacilitates critical examination
Pedagogical valueFacilitates teaching and understanding

Positive examples: the minimal argument paths provided in Appendix J

Negative examples: arguments containing redundant steps, arguments omitting key steps

Theoretical anchoring: methodological tool

First appearance: Volume Four, Appendix J

A.3 Normative Terms

This section collects core terms related to normativity. These terms describe the normative principles, ethical framework, and value system of this work.

A.3.1 Recursive Freedom

【Recursive Freedom】(Recursive Freedom)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{RecursiveFreedom} \triangleq \forall A \in \mathcal{A}: \mathcal{P}(A) \text{ not systematically reduced}$$

Or, more precisely:

$$\text{RFP}: \forall a \in \text{Actions}, \forall S \in \text{Subjects}: a \text{ is permissible} \Leftrightarrow \neg \exists S': \Delta \mathcal{P}(S' | a) < -\epsilon \text{ (systematic)}$$

Where:

  • $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of subjects
  • $\mathcal{P}(A)$ is the possibility space of subject $A$
  • $a$ is an action
  • $\Delta \mathcal{P}(S' | a)$ is the effect of the action on a subject's possibility space
  • An action should not systematically reduce the possibility spaces of other subjects

II. Natural-Language Definition

Recursive freedom refers to an understanding of freedom that emphasizes that freedom is not only the freedom of the individual but also includes the responsibility to protect the freedom of others. "Freedom is the guardianship of possibility"—the exercise of freedom should maintain rather than reduce the possibility spaces of others. This freedom is "recursive" because it includes the protection of the freedom of future subjects.

III. Core Features

FeatureContentDifference from the traditional concept of freedom
RecursivenessIncludes the responsibility to protect others' freedomTraditional freedom may neglect others
Possibility-orientedFocuses on the possibility spaceTraditional freedom focuses on present choices
Deep-time extensionExtends to future generationsTraditional freedom focuses on the present age
Plural subjectsIncludes non-human subjectsTraditional freedom focuses on humans

Positive Examples

  1. Environmental protection: protecting the natural environment and maintaining the ecological possibilities of future generations
  2. Education: expanding the possibility space of those educated
  3. Peace agreements: resolving conflict by peaceful means and avoiding the reduction of the other party's possibilities

Negative Examples

  1. Resource depletion: exhausting non-renewable resources and reducing the possibilities of future generations
  2. Species extinction: causing species extinction and reducing ecological possibilities
  3. Totalitarianism: systematically reducing citizens' possibility space

IV. Relations to Related Concepts

Related conceptRelationExplanation
→Possibility Space (A.1.7.3)BasisRecursive freedom protects the possibility space
→RFD (A.4.2)OperationalizationRFD is the measure of recursive freedom
→Negentropy Responsibility (A.3.3)ComplementaryNegentropy responsibility is a condition of recursive freedom
Negative libertyExtensionRecursive freedom extends negative liberty

V. Theoretical Anchoring

Recursive freedom is the core normative concept of this work. It is the conceptual basis of the Principle of Recursive Freedom (RFP) and the theoretical expression of this work's core maxim, "freedom is the guardianship of possibility."

$$\text{RFP} \Leftarrow \text{RecursiveFreedom}$$

First appearance

Volume One, Chapter Eleven, §11.1

References

  1. Berlin, I. (1969). "Two Concepts of Liberty." In Four Essays on Liberty.

Oxford University Press.

  1. Sen, A. (1999). Development as Freedom. Knopf.
  2. Pettit, P. (1997). Republicanism: A Theory of Freedom and Government. Oxford University Press.

A.3.2 Possibility Space

【Possibility Space】(Possibility Space)

Note: This term already has a basic definition in A.1.7.3; here the normative dimension is supplemented.

I. Normative Extended Definition

$$\mathcal{P}^{\text{norm}}(S, t) \triangleq \{s' \in \mathcal{P}(S, t) : \text{Valuable}(s') \lor \text{EnablingValuable}(s')\}$$

Where:

  • $\mathcal{P}(S, t)$ is the descriptive possibility space
  • $\mathcal{P}^{\text{norm}}(S, t)$ is the normative possibility space
  • $\text{Valuable}(s')$ means the state is itself valuable
  • $\text{EnablingValuable}(s')$ means the state makes valuable choices possible

II. Normative Dimensions

The possibility space is not only a descriptive concept but also a normative one:

DimensionContentNormative implication
SizeThe number of possible statesA larger possibility space is usually better
DiversityThe diversity of possible statesMore diverse choices are usually better
AccessibilityThe ease of reaching each stateChoices that are easier to reach are usually better
ReversibilityThe possibility of returning from each stateMore reversible choices are usually better

III. Relation to RFD

$$\text{RFD}(a, S) = \frac{|\mathcal{P}(S, t_1)| - |\mathcal{P}(S, t_0)|}{|\mathcal{P}(S, t_0)|}$$

Where $t_0$ is before the action and $t_1$ is after the action. RFD measures the effect of an action on the possibility space.

First appearance (normative dimension)

Volume One, Chapter Eleven, §11.2

A.3.3 Negentropy Responsibility

【Negentropy Responsibility】(Negentropy Responsibility)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{NegentropyResponsibility} \triangleq \forall S \in \mathcal{S}_{\text{neg}}: \text{Obligation}(S, \text{Maintain}(J_{\text{env}}))$$

Where:

  • $\mathcal{S}_{\text{neg}}$ is the set of negentropic organizations
  • $J_{\text{env}}$ is the negentropy of the environment
  • Negentropic organizations have an obligation to maintain the negentropy of the environment

A more general formulation:

$$\text{NRP}: \text{NegentropyCapability}(S) \Rightarrow \text{NegentropyObligation}(S)$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

Negentropy responsibility refers to the responsibility that negentropic organizations (such as life and civilization) bear for maintaining and enhancing the negentropic structures of the universe. Since the persistence of negentropic organizations depends on negentropic flows, maintaining negentropic structures is both a necessity of survival and an ethical responsibility.

III. Core Features

FeatureContentDifference from the traditional concept of responsibility
Physical basisBased on thermodynamicsTraditional responsibility is based on the social contract
Cosmic scaleConcerned with cosmic negentropyTraditional responsibility focuses on human society
ExistentialityConcerns persistenceTraditional responsibility may be violated
RecursivenessIncludes the responsibility to maintain conditionsTraditional responsibility may neglect conditions

Positive Examples

  1. Ecological protection: maintaining the complexity of ecosystems
  2. Knowledge transmission: transmitting and developing knowledge (informational negentropy)
  3. Civilization building: building and maintaining civilizational structures

Negative Examples

  1. Environmental destruction: destroying ecosystems and reducing environmental negentropy
  2. Knowledge destruction: book burning, cultural genocide
  3. Entropy-increasing behavior: wasting resources, increasing disorder

IV. Relations to Related Concepts

Related conceptRelationExplanation
→Negentropy (A.1.7.2)Ontological basisNegentropy is the object of negentropy responsibility
→Recursive Freedom (A.3.1)ComplementaryNegentropy responsibility is a condition of recursive freedom
→Reversibility (A.3.4)ComplementaryReversibility protects negentropic structures

V. Theoretical Anchoring

Negentropy responsibility is the core normative concept of this work. It is the conceptual basis of the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility (NRP) and a core component of Cosmic Responsibility Ethics.

$$\text{NRP} \Leftarrow \text{NegentropyResponsibility}$$

First appearance

Volume One, Chapter Twelve, §12.1

References

  1. Schrödinger, E. (1944). What is Life? Cambridge University Press.
  2. Prigogine, I., & Stengers, I. (1984). Order Out of Chaos. Bantam Books.
  3. Schneider, E. D., & Kay, J. J. (1994). "Life as a Manifestation of the Second Law of Thermodynamics." Mathematical and Computer Modelling, 19(6-8), 25-48.

A.3.4 Reversibility

【Reversibility】(Reversibility)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{Reversibility}(a) \triangleq \exists a^{-1}: S(t_0) \xrightarrow{a} S(t_1) \xrightarrow{a^{-1}} S(t_0') \land d(S(t_0), S(t_0')) < \epsilon$$

Where:

  • $a$ is an action
  • $a^{-1}$ is the inverse action
  • $S(t)$ is a state
  • An action is reversible if there exists an inverse action that can restore a state close to the original

II. Degrees of Reversibility

$$\text{Reversibility}(a) \in [0, 1]$$

Where:

  • 1 denotes fully reversible
  • 0 denotes fully irreversible
  • Intermediate values denote partially reversible

III. Natural-Language Definition

Reversibility refers to the degree to which the consequences of an action or decision can be undone or reversed. Under conditions of deep uncertainty, preferring reversible actions is a prudent strategy, because it allows adjustment after new information is obtained.

IV. Core Features

FeatureContentDifference from related concepts
Consequences undoableConsequences can be undoneFlexibility: changing direction
State restorationCan be restored to the original stateAdaptivity: adapting to change
Information dependenceDepends on information acquisitionRobustness: resisting perturbation
Cost-relatedReversal may have a costResilience: capacity to recover

Positive Examples

  1. Software version control: can roll back to a previous version
  2. Revocable decisions: can cancel orders, rescind contracts
  3. Modular design: can replace modules without affecting the whole

Negative Examples

  1. Species extinction: an extinct species cannot be restored
  2. Nuclear war: the consequences of nuclear detonation are irreversible
  3. Resource depletion: exhausted fossil fuels are non-renewable

V. Relations to Related Concepts

Related conceptRelationExplanation
→Deep Uncertainty (A.2.4)ResponseReversibility is the strategy for responding to deep uncertainty
→Epistemic Humility (A.2.3)EntailmentEpistemic humility supports the Principle of Reversibility
→Forbidden Red Lines (A.3.5)BoundaryForbidden red lines mark irreversible boundaries

VI. Theoretical Anchoring

Reversibility is the core normative concept of this work. It is the conceptual basis of the Principle of Reversibility (REV) and the conceptual basis of the protocol-stack methodology's "versioned rollback" mechanism.

$$\text{REV} \Leftarrow \text{Reversibility}$$

First appearance

Volume One, Chapter Thirteen, §13.1

References

  1. Collingridge, D. (1980). The Social Control of Technology. St. Martin's Press.
  2. Sunstein, C. R. (2005). Laws of Fear: Beyond the Precautionary Principle. Cambridge University Press.
  3. Taleb, N. N. (2012). Antifragile. Random House.

A.3.5 Forbidden Red Lines

【Forbidden Red Lines】(Forbidden Red Lines)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{ForbiddenRedLines} \triangleq \{a \in \mathcal{A}: \text{Catastrophic}(a) \land \text{Irreversible}(a) \land \text{Unconditional}(\neg a)\}$$

Where:

  • $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of actions
  • $\text{Catastrophic}(a)$ means the action would lead to catastrophic consequences
  • $\text{Irreversible}(a)$ means the consequences of the action are irreversible
  • $\text{Unconditional}(\neg a)$ means the prohibition of the action is unconditional

II. Natural-Language Definition

Forbidden red lines refer to boundaries of action that absolutely must not be crossed. These boundaries mark actions that would lead to catastrophic, irreversible consequences; the prohibition of these actions is unconditional and not subject to utilitarian calculation.

III. Core Features

FeatureContentDifference from ordinary norms
AbsolutenessUnconditional prohibitionOrdinary norms may have exceptions
CatastrophicityInvolves catastrophic consequencesOrdinary norms involve ordinary consequences
IrreversibilityInvolves irreversible consequencesOrdinary norms may be reversible
PriorityPrior to other considerationsOrdinary norms may be weighed

IV. List of Forbidden Red Lines (Examples)

Red lineContentReason
FRL-1Prohibit triggering irreversible global catastropheCatastrophic, irreversible
FRL-2Prohibit systematically eliminating the possibility space of an entire class of subjectsCatastrophic, irreversible
FRL-3Prohibit closing off the basic options of future generationsCatastrophic, irreversible

Positive Examples

  1. Prohibition of genocide: unconditional prohibition of eliminating a specific group
  2. Prohibition of nuclear war: unconditional prohibition of launching all-out nuclear war
  3. Prohibition of ecocide: unconditional prohibition of causing mass species extinction

Negative Examples

  1. Ordinary resource use: can be decided by weighing
  2. Reversible policy choices: can be adjusted and modified
  3. Local conflicts: can be resolved through negotiation

A.3.6 Cosmic Responsibility Ethics

【Cosmic Responsibility Ethics】(Cosmic Responsibility Ethics)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{CosmicResponsibilityEthics} \triangleq \langle \text{NC}, \text{NL}, \text{NK}, \text{BP}, \text{RFP}, \text{NRP}, \text{REV} \rangle$$

Cosmic Responsibility Ethics is the normative ethical framework proposed by this work. Taking the New Three Views as its ontological-epistemological basis, it derives three core normative principles (recursive freedom, negentropy responsibility, reversibility) through the bridge principle, providing guidance for normative questions in the era of interstellar civilization.

A.3.7 Other Normative Terms

This section collects other important normative terms.

A.3.7.1 Bridge Principles

【Bridge Principles】(Bridge Principles)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{BridgePrinciples} = \{BP\text{-}1, BP\text{-}2, BP\text{-}3\}$$

Where:

  • $BP\text{-}1$: the principle of rational persistence
  • $BP\text{-}2$: the principle of epistemic humility
  • $BP\text{-}3$: the principle of intersubjectivity

II. Natural-Language Definition

Bridge principles are intermediate principles connecting descriptive propositions (the New Three Views) with normative propositions (the three principles). They resolve the "is-ought" problem, making the derivation from facts to norms possible.

III. Core Features

FeatureContent
IntermediaryConnects description and norm
MinimalityAdopts the weakest assumptions
DefensibilityCan be independently defended
NecessityNecessary for the derivation

IV. Theoretical Anchoring: Volume One, Chapter Five

First appearance: Volume One, Chapter Five, §5.1

A.3.7.2 Recursive Freedom Principle (RFP)

【Recursive Freedom Principle】(Recursive Freedom Principle, RFP)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{RFP}: \forall a \in \mathcal{A}, \forall S \in \mathcal{S}: \text{Permissible}(a) \Leftrightarrow \neg(\Delta \mathcal{P}(S | a) < -\epsilon \text{ (systematic)})$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

The Principle of Recursive Freedom is the first core normative principle of this work, holding that no action should systematically reduce the possibility spaces of other subjects.

First appearance: Volume One, Chapter Eleven, §11.1

A.3.7.3 Negentropy Responsibility Principle (NRP)

【Negentropy Responsibility Principle】(Negentropy Responsibility Principle, NRP)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{NRP}: \forall S \in \mathcal{S}_{\text{neg}}: \text{Capability}(S, J) \Rightarrow \text{Obligation}(S, \text{Maintain}(J))$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

The Principle of Negentropy Responsibility is the second core normative principle of this work, holding that negentropic organizations bear responsibility for maintaining the negentropic structures of the universe.

First appearance: Volume One, Chapter Twelve, §12.1

A.3.7.4 Reversibility Principle (REV)

【Reversibility Principle】(Reversibility Principle, REV)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{REV}: \text{DeepUncertainty} \Rightarrow \text{Prefer}(\text{Reversible}(a))$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

The Principle of Reversibility is the third core normative principle of this work, holding that under conditions of deep uncertainty, reversible actions should be preferred.

First appearance: Volume One, Chapter Thirteen, §13.1

A.3.7.5 Intergenerational Justice

【Intergenerational Justice】(Intergenerational Justice)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{IntergenerationalJustice} \triangleq \forall G_i, G_j \in \mathcal{G}: \text{Rights}(G_i) \approx \text{Rights}(G_j)$$

Where $\mathcal{G}$ is the set of generations.

II. Natural-Language Definition

Intergenerational justice is a theory of justice concerning fair relations among different generations, holding that the present generation bears responsibility toward future generations and should not harm the interests of future generations.

First appearance: Volume Three, Chapter Twenty-Six, §26.1

A.3.7.6 Existential Risk

【Existential Risk】(Existential Risk)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{ExistentialRisk} \triangleq \text{Risk}(E): \text{Severity}(E) = \text{Extinction} \lor \text{Severity}(E) = \text{PermanentCurtailment}$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

Existential risk refers to risks that could lead to human extinction or the permanent severe curtailment of humanity's potential.

First appearance: Introduction, §I.1.1

A.3.7.7 Long-range Responsibility

【Long-range Responsibility】(Long-range Responsibility)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{LongRangeResponsibility} \triangleq \text{Responsibility}(A, E): T(E) - T(A) \gg T_{\text{human}}$$

Where $T(E)$ is the time at which the consequence occurs and $T(A)$ is the time of the action.

II. Natural-Language Definition

Long-range responsibility refers to responsibility for consequences in the far future—responsibility that must still be borne when the causal chain extends into the far future.

First appearance: Introduction, §I.1.3

A.3.7.8 Intersubjectivity

【Intersubjectivity】(Intersubjectivity)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{Intersubjectivity} \triangleq \forall S_i, S_j \in \mathcal{S}: \exists \text{CommonGround}(S_i, S_j)$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

Intersubjectivity refers to the property whereby a basis of shared understanding exists among different subjects. In this work, intersubjectivity is the basis of bridge principle BP-3.

First appearance: Volume One, Chapter Five, §5.3

A.4 Indicator Terms

This section collects core terms related to the indicator system. These indicators are the operationalization of abstract normative principles into measurable metrics.

A.4.1 UCS (Universal Consciousness Scale)

【UCS】(Universal Consciousness Scale, Universal Consciousness Scale)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{UCS}(E) = w_1 \cdot \Phi(E) + w_2 \cdot I(E) + w_3 \cdot A(E) + w_4 \cdot S(E) + w_5 \cdot R(E)$$

Where:

  • $E$ is the entity being assessed
  • $\Phi(E)$ is the degree of integrated information (based on IIT theory)
  • $I(E)$ is the complexity of the self-model
  • $A(E)$ is the capacity for autonomous action
  • $S(E)$ is sentience
  • $R(E)$ is the capacity for reflection
  • $w_1, ..., w_5$ are weight coefficients satisfying $\sum w_i = 1$

II. Natural-Language Definition

The Universal Consciousness Scale (UCS) is a multidimensional indicator for assessing an entity's degree of consciousness. It does not attempt to solve the philosophical question of "what consciousness is," but rather provides an operational assessment framework for assessing the degree of consciousness of different entities (including humans, animals, AI, etc.).

A.4.2 RFD (Recursive Freedom Degree)

【RFD】(Recursive Freedom Degree, Recursive Freedom Degree)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{RFD}(a, S) = \frac{|\mathcal{P}(S, t_1)| - |\mathcal{P}(S, t_0)|}{|\mathcal{P}(S, t_0)|} \cdot \text{SignificanceWeight}$$

Where:

  • $a$ is an action
  • $S$ is the affected subject
  • $\mathcal{P}(S, t)$ is the subject's possibility space at time $t$
  • $t_0$ is before the action and $t_1$ is after the action
  • $\text{SignificanceWeight}$ is the significance weight of the possibilities

A more detailed definition:

$$\text{RFD}(a, S) = \sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}} w(p) \cdot \Delta \text{Accessibility}(p | a)$$

Where $w(p)$ is the weight of possibility $p$ and $\Delta \text{Accessibility}$ is the change in accessibility.

II. Natural-Language Definition

The Recursive Freedom Degree (RFD) is an indicator for assessing the effect of an action on a subject's possibility space. A positive RFD indicates that the action expanded the possibility space; a negative RFD indicates that the action reduced it. RFD is the operationalization of the Principle of Recursive Freedom (RFP).

III. Interpretation of RFD Values

RFD valueInterpretationNormative implication
> 0Expands the possibility spaceUsually good
≈ 0Does not change the possibility spaceNeutral
< 0Reduces the possibility spaceRequires justification
<< 0Severely reduces the possibility spaceMay violate RFP

IV. Calculation Method (Conceptual)

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  RFD calculation steps (conceptual)                             │ 
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 1: Identify the affected subject S                        │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 2: Determine the pre-action possibility space P(S, t₀)     │
│        - Identify possible future states                        │ 
│        - Assess the accessibility of each state                 │ 
│        - Assess the significance of each state                  │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 3: Determine the post-action possibility space P(S, t₁)    │
│        - Reassess possible states                               │ 
│        - Reassess accessibility                                 │ 
│        - Reassess significance                                  │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 4: Compute the change                                     │ 
│        RFD = Σ w(p) · ΔAccessibility(p)                         │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 5: Comprehensive assessment                               │ 
│        - Consider multiple affected subjects                    │ 
│        - Consider time discounting (if applicable)              │ 
│        - Consider uncertainty                                   │ 
│                                                                 │ 
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

A.4.3 CRV (Commitment-Reversibility-Verifiability)

【CRV】(Commitment-Reversibility-Verifiability, Commitment-Reversibility-Verifiability)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{CRV}(a) = \langle C(a), R(a), V(a) \rangle$$

Where:

  • $C(a)$ is commitment strength (Commitment): $C \in [0, 1]$
  • $R(a)$ is the degree of reversibility (Reversibility): $R \in [0, 1]$
  • $V(a)$ is the degree of verifiability (Verifiability): $V \in [0, 1]$

Composite score:

$$\text{CRV}_{\text{score}}(a) = w_C \cdot C(a) + w_R \cdot R(a) + w_V \cdot V(a)$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

CRV is a three-dimensional indicator used to assess three key attributes of an action or commitment:

  • Commitment (C): the strength and credibility of the commitment made
  • Reversibility (R): the degree to which the consequences of the action are reversible
  • Verifiability (V): the degree to which fulfillment of the commitment can be verified

A.5 Institutional Terms

This section collects core terms related to institutional design. These terms describe the institutional framework and governance mechanisms proposed by this work.

A.5.1 Protocol Stack

【Protocol Stack】(Protocol Stack)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{ProtocolStack} = \langle L_0, L_1, L_2, L_3, L_4, \text{Rules} \rangle$$

Where:

  • $L_0$: the physical constraint layer
  • $L_1$: the ontological-epistemological framework layer (the New Three Views)
  • $L_2$: the normative principle layer (the three principles)
  • $L_3$: the institutional design layer
  • $L_4$: the operational protocol layer
  • $\text{Rules}$: the rules governing inter-layer relations

II. Rules Governing Inter-Layer Relations

$$\forall i < j: L_j \text{ must be consistent with } L_i$$

(Upper layers must be consistent with lower layers)

III. Natural-Language Definition

The protocol stack is the governance architecture proposed by this work, borrowing the modular design of computer network protocol stacks. It divides the governance framework into five layers, each with a different degree of stability and difficulty of revision, achieving a unity of "principle stability" and "operational flexibility."

IV. Detailed Explanation of the Five-Layer Architecture

LayerNameContentStabilityDifficulty of revision
L₀Physical constraint layerLaws of thermodynamics, information-theoretic boundariesHighestNot revisable
L₁Ontological-epistemological framework layerthe New Three Views (NC, NL, NK)HighExtremely difficult to revise
L₂Normative principle layerThe three principles (RFP, NRP, REV)Medium-highDifficult to revise
L₃Institutional design layerTribunal, IRB, trust, etc.MediumRevisable
L₄Operational protocol layerIndicators, procedures, formsLowEasily revisable

V. Design Principles of the Protocol Stack

PrincipleContentExplanation
Layer separationContents of different stability are separated into layersAvoids confusion
Load-bearing constraintLower layers bear upper layersUpper layers must not violate lower layers
VersioningEach layer can be versioned independentlyFacilitates tracking revisions
Rollback-abilityUpper layers can be rolled back without affecting lower layersFacilitates error correction

A.5.2 Multi-Intelligence Tribunal

【Multi-Intelligence Tribunal】(Multi-Intelligence Tribunal)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{MIT} = \langle \text{Jurisdiction}, \text{Composition}, \text{Procedure}, \text{Remedies} \rangle$$

Where:

  • $\text{Jurisdiction}$: scope of jurisdiction (disputes involving multiple kinds of intelligent subjects)
  • $\text{Composition}$: composition (representatives of multiple kinds of intelligent subjects)
  • $\text{Procedure}$: procedure (deliberative procedure)
  • $\text{Remedies}$: remedies

II. Natural-Language Definition

The Multi-Intelligence Tribunal is an institutional prototype proposed by this work for handling disputes involving multiple kinds of intelligent subjects (humans, AI, possible extraterrestrial intelligences, etc.). Its design principle is to ensure that the interests of all relevant subjects can be represented and considered.

III. Core Design Principles

PrincipleContentExplanation
Plurality of subjectsMultiple kinds of intelligent subjects participateNot limited to humans
Procedural fairnessA fair deliberative procedureProcedural justice
Interest representationAll interests are representedIncludes subjects that cannot represent themselves
Decision transparencyThe decision process is transparentAuditable

AI delegationRepresents AI interests (if any)AI or its representatives

Ecological proxyRepresents the interests of non-human lifeHuman representatives

A.5.3 Cosmic-Scale IRB

【Cosmic-Scale IRB】(Cosmic-Scale Institutional Review Board, Cosmic-Scale Institutional Review Board)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{CIRB} = \langle \text{Scope}, \text{Criteria}, \text{Procedure}, \text{Authority} \rangle$$

Where:

  • $\text{Scope}$: scope of review (actions with cosmic-scale impact)
  • $\text{Criteria}$: review criteria (based on CSIA and the three principles)
  • $\text{Procedure}$: review procedure
  • $\text{Authority}$: authority (recommend, approve, veto)

Trigger condition

$$\text{CIRB\_Required}(a) \Leftrightarrow \text{CSIA}(a) \geq \text{Level 3}$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

The Cosmic-Scale IRB is an institutional prototype proposed by this work for reviewing actions or projects that may have cosmic-scale impact. It borrows the concept of the institutional review board (IRB) in biomedical research and extends it to cosmic-scale decision review.

III. Review Criteria

Possibility-space impactDoes it systematically reduce the possibility space?RFP
Negentropy impactDoes it destroy negentropic structures?NRP
ReversibilityAre the consequences reversible?REV
Subject impactWhich subjects are affected?Plurality of subjects
Temporal impactHow long does the impact last?Deep-time consideration

Enhanced reviewCSIA Level 3In-depthRecommendation
Full reviewCSIA Level 4ComprehensiveApproval/veto

A.5.4 Intergenerational Trust

【Intergenerational Trust】(Intergenerational Trust)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{IGT} = \langle \text{Beneficiaries}, \text{Assets}, \text{Trustees}, \text{Duties}, \text{Oversight} \rangle$$

Where:

  • $\text{Beneficiaries}$: beneficiaries (future generations)
  • $\text{Assets}$: trust assets (natural resources, knowledge, institutions, etc.)
  • $\text{Trustees}$: trustees (representatives of the present generation)
  • $\text{Duties}$: fiduciary duties
  • $\text{Oversight}$: oversight mechanism

Fiduciary duties

$$\text{Duties} = \{\text{Preservation}, \text{Prudence}, \text{Impartiality}, \text{Accountability}\}$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

The Intergenerational Trust is an institutional prototype proposed by this work for representing and protecting the interests of future generations. It borrows the concept of trust law, treating the present generation as trustees of the assets of future generations, with the responsibility to protect and transmit these assets.

III. Core Elements

A.5.5 Versioned Governance

【Versioned Governance】(Versioned Governance)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{VersionedGovernance} = \langle \text{Versions}, \text{ChangeLog}, \text{RollbackRules}, \text{UpdateProcedure} \rangle$$

Where:

  • $\text{Versions}$: the version sequence of governance rules
  • $\text{ChangeLog}$: the change log
  • $\text{RollbackRules}$: rollback rules
  • $\text{UpdateProcedure}$: update procedure

Version control rules

$$\text{Version}(t+1) = \text{Update}(\text{Version}(t), \Delta, \text{Procedure})$$

$$\text{Rollback}: \text{Version}(t) \rightarrow \text{Version}(t-k), \quad k \geq 1$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

Versioned governance is a governance methodology proposed by this work, borrowing the concept of version control in software development. It treats governance rules as updatable "code," achieving continuous improvement of governance rules through version control while retaining the ability to roll back to previous versions.

III. Core Features

FeatureContentExplanation
VersioningEach version has a clear identifierFacilitates tracking
Change logRecords each changeFacilitates auditing
Rollback-abilityCan roll back to a previous versionErrors can be corrected
ProceduralityUpdates must follow procedurePrevents arbitrary modification

IV. Version Number Rules (Examples)

Version formatMeaningType of revision
X.0.0Major versionMajor revision (e.g., L₁-L₂ layer revisions)
x.Y.0Minor versionModerate revision (e.g., L₃ layer revisions)
x.y.ZPatch versionSmall revision (e.g., L₄ layer revisions)

V. Update Procedure (by Layer)

LayerUpdate procedureApproval requirementRollback condition
L₀Not updatable——
L₁Major academic consensusHighest-level deliberationAlmost impossible to roll back
L₂Broad consultationHigh-level deliberationStrict conditions
L₃Standard procedureStandard deliberationStandard conditions
L₄Simplified procedureSimplified deliberationEasy to roll back

VI. Rollback Mechanism

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Rollback mechanism                                             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  Trigger conditions:                                            │
│  ├─ Discovery of a serious error                                │
│  ├─ Occurrence of unexpected serious consequences               │
│  ├─ Violation of lower-layer principles                         │
│  └─ Rollback decided through deliberation                       │
│                                                                 │
│  Rollback procedure:                                            │
│  1. Identify the problematic version                            │
│  2. Determine the target version for rollback                   │
│  3. Assess the impact of the rollback                           │
│  4. Execute the rollback                                        │
│  5. Record the rollback log                                     │
│  6. Analyze the cause of the problem                            │
│  7. Formulate improvement measures                              │
│                                                                 │
│  Rollback constraints:                                          │
│  ├─ L₀ layer: not rollback-able (physical laws)                 │
│  ├─ L₁ layer: almost impossible to roll back (requires highest- │
│  │           level consensus)                                   │
│  ├─ L₂ layer: difficult to roll back (requires broad consensus) │
│  ├─ L₃ layer: rollback-able (standard procedure)                │
│  └─ L₄ layer: easy to roll back (simplified procedure)          │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

A.5.6.1 One Loop

【One Loop】(One Loop)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{OneLoop} = \langle \text{Monitor}, \text{Evaluate}, \text{Adapt}, \text{Iterate} \rangle$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

One Loop is the governance iteration mechanism proposed by this work, achieving continuous improvement of the governance framework through continuous monitoring, evaluation, adaptation, and iteration. Combined with the hierarchical structure of the protocol stack, it forms a "four-layer, one-loop" architecture.

III. Core Features

FeatureContent
MonitorContinuously monitor governance effects
EvaluatePeriodically evaluate the governance framework
AdaptAdapt according to the evaluation results
IterateContinuously iterate and improve
