A.5.6.2 Proxy Representation

【Proxy Representation】(Proxy Representation)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{ProxyRepresentation}(S, P) \triangleq \text{Represents}(P, \text{Interests}(S)) \land \neg \text{CanRepresentSelf}(S)$$

Where $S$ is the subject being represented and $P$ is the proxy.

II. Natural-Language Definition

Proxy representation refers to an institutional arrangement in which a proxy represents the interests of subjects that cannot represent themselves (such as future generations or non-human subjects).

III. Situations of Application

Subject being representedProxyReason
Future generationsIntergenerational trust trusteesNot yet born
Non-human animalsAnimal-welfare proxiesCannot participate in human deliberation
EcosystemsEcological proxiesNot subjects
Early AIHuman proxiesAgency status uncertain

IV. Theoretical Anchoring: Multi-Intelligence Tribunal, Intergenerational Trust

First appearance: Volume Two, Chapter Eighteen, §18.2

A.5.6.3 Layer Loading

【Layer Loading】(Layer Loading)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{LayerLoading}: \forall i < j: L_j \text{ is constrained by } L_i$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

Layer loading is the core design principle of the protocol stack, meaning that upper-layer rules must be consistent with lower-layer rules, that lower layers bear upper layers, and that upper layers must not violate lower layers.

III. Load-Bearing Relations

Lower layerUpper layerConstraint relation
L₀L₁The New Three Views must not violate physical laws
L₁L₂The three principles must not violate the New Three Views
L₂L₃Institutional design must not violate the three principles
L₃L₄Operational protocols must not violate institutional design

IV. Theoretical Anchoring: Protocol-Stack Methodology

First appearance: Volume Two, Chapter Sixteen, §16.3

A.5.6.4 Deliberation Procedure

【Deliberation Procedure】(Deliberation Procedure)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{DeliberationProcedure} = \langle \text{Participants}, \text{Rules}, \text{Stages}, \text{DecisionRule} \rangle$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

The deliberation procedure refers to the decision procedure used in institutions such as the Multi-Intelligence Tribunal and the Cosmic-Scale IRB, emphasizing the reaching of consensus through rational discussion.

III. Core Elements

ElementContent
ParticipantsAll relevant subjects (or their proxies)
RulesDeliberation rules (speaking, responding, etc.)
StagesInformation gathering, discussion, decision
Decision ruleConsensus, majority rule, veto power, etc.

IV. Theoretical Anchoring: NK-4 (Negotiated Truth)

First appearance: Volume Two, Chapter Eighteen, §18.3

A.5.6.5 Soft Law Mechanism

【Soft Law Mechanism】(Soft Law Mechanism)

I. Formal Definition

$$\text{SoftLaw} \triangleq \text{Norm}: \neg \text{LegallyBinding} \land \text{Influential}$$

II. Natural-Language Definition

A soft law mechanism refers to normative documents or practices that are not legally binding but have practical influence, such as guidelines, recommendations, and best practices. This work recommends advancing the implementation of the framework gradually through soft law mechanisms.

III. Comparison of Soft Law and Hard Law

FeatureSoft lawHard law
Binding forceNon-coerciveCoercive
FlexibilityHighLow
Difficulty of formulationLowHigh
Enforcement mechanismReputation, peer pressureLegal sanctions

A.7 Notes on the Evolution of Terms

This section explains the origin, evolution, and development of the core terms of this work.

A.7.1 Classification of Term Origins

The terms of this work can be classified by origin as follows:

Table A.7.1 Classification of term origins

Type of originExplanationExamples of terms
Original termsTerms first proposed in this workrecursive freedom, negentropy responsibility, Cosmic Responsibility Ethics
Borrowed termsBorrowed from other disciplines, with meaning essentially unchangednegentropy, emergence, self-organization
Adapted termsBorrowed from other disciplines, with meaning adjustedprotocol stack, versioned governance
Extended termsExtensions of existing termsparticipatory cognition (extending 4E cognition), Cosmic-Scale IRB (extending IRB)

A.7.2 Notes on Original Terms

The main original terms of this work and the background of their creation:

Table A.7.2 Notes on original terms

TermBackground of creationDesign consideration
New Three ViewsA summary concept was needed to collectively designate the New Cosmological View, the New View of Life, and the New View of CognitionEchoes the traditional "three views" (worldview, view of life, values) while emphasizing a higher-dimensional extension relation
Recursive freedomA concept was needed to express "freedom includes the responsibility to protect the freedom of others"Uses the word "recursive" to emphasize self-reference
Negentropy responsibilityA concept was needed to express a concept of responsibility based on thermodynamicsCombines negentropy and responsibility, anchored in physics
Cosmic Responsibility EthicsA name was needed for the ethical framework of this workEmphasizes cosmic scale and responsibility orientation
Intergenerational TrustA concept was needed to express an institution representing the interests of future generationsBorrows the concept of trust law, extended to the intergenerational level
Multi-Intelligence TribunalA concept was needed to express an institution for handling disputes among multiple kinds of intelligent subjectsEmphasizes the plurality of subjects

A.7.3 Adjustments to Borrowed Terms

The meanings of some terms borrowed by this work have been adjusted:

Table A.7.3 Adjustments to borrowed terms

TermOriginal meaningMeaning in this workNote on the adjustment
Protocol stackThe layered protocol architecture of computer networksThe layered architecture of the governance frameworkExtended from the technical domain to the governance domain
VersioningVersion management of software codeVersion management of governance rulesExtended from the software domain to the governance domain
IRBThe ethics review board of biomedical researchThe ethics review board for cosmic-scale actionsExtended to the cosmic scale
Stress testRisk testing of the financial systemRobustness testing of a theoretical frameworkExtended from the financial domain to theory testing

A.7.4 Versioned Management of Terms

The term definitions of this work adopt versioned management:

Table A.7.4 Term version information

VersionDateMain changes
v0.9.0[pre-publication]Initial version, "first-generation rough model"
v1.0.0[publication]Revised in light of academic feedback
v1.x.x[planned]Continuous iterative revision

Revision principles

  1. Principle of stability: core terms (such as the New Three Views and the three principles) should be kept as stable as possible
  2. Principle of consistency: term revisions should maintain consistency with lower layers of the protocol stack
  3. Principle of traceability: term changes should be recorded in the change log
  4. Principle of community participation: suggestions from the academic community for improving term definitions are welcome

A.7.5 Notes on Term Translation

The term translations of this work follow these principles:

Table A.7.5 Principles of term translation

PrincipleContentExample
Sense priorityPrior to convey the conceptual meaningRecursive Freedom → a rendering that conveys the sense
Established usageRespect existing translation conventionsEmergence → an established rendering
Retention of the originalTechnical terms retain their English abbreviationsUCS, RFD, CRV
CoinageCoin new terms when necessaryNegentropy Responsibility → a newly coined rendering

A.7.6 Recommendations for Term Usage

Table A.7.6 Recommendations for term usage

SituationRecommendation
Academic writingGive a full definition on first use and cite this work as the source
TeachingUse the standard definitions of Appendix A, together with the relation diagrams of A.6
Policy discussionUse the natural-language definitions and avoid excessive formalization
Interdisciplinary exchangeExplain the relations and differences between the terms and those of other disciplines
Criticism and discussionClearly indicate the version of the definition being used

Summary of Appendix A

This appendix provides systematic definitions and explanations of the core terms of The Normative Foundations of Interstellar Civilization.

Content statistics

CategoryNumber of termsMain content
A.1 Ontological terms12relational reality, processuality, participatory nature, emergence, complexity, self-organization, etc.
A.2 Epistemological terms10participatory cognition, social knowledge, epistemic humility, deep uncertainty, negotiability, etc.
A.3 Normative terms14recursive freedom, negentropy responsibility, reversibility, forbidden red lines, Cosmic Responsibility Ethics, etc.
A.4 Indicator terms6UCS, RFD, CRV, CDI, MBCL, CSIA
A.5 Institutional terms10protocol stack, Multi-Intelligence Tribunal, Cosmic-Scale IRB, Intergenerational Trust, versioned governance, etc.
A.6 Term relation diagrams4overall relation diagram, New Three Views relation diagram, three principles and indicators relation diagram, institutional term relation diagram
A.7 Notes on term evolution—term origins, adjustments, versioned management, translation, usage recommendations

Usage recommendations

  1. First reading: browse the A.6 term relation diagrams first to grasp the overall structure
  2. Deeper understanding: consult the detailed definitions of each term as needed
  3. Critical use: pay attention to the boundary conditions and limitations of use of the terms
  4. Continuous updating: follow version updates of the term definitions

Index of Argument NodesAppendix B

I. The Task and Positioning of This Appendix

This appendix provides a systematic summary and analysis of the argument nodes of the entire book The Normative Foundations of Interstellar Civilization. As a foundational work of Interstellar Civilization Studies (ICS), the book's chain of argumentation must satisfy the requirements of traceability, testability, and revisability. The task of this appendix is to render the book's argumentative structure explicit, so that readers can:

  1. Trace arguments: trace any conclusion back to its premises and reasoning process
  2. Test arguments: assess the strength and validity of each argument
  3. Critique arguments: identify potential weaknesses and objections
  4. Revise arguments: locate the nodes requiring revision when problems are found

II. The Concept of an Argument Node

Definition B.0.1 (Argument Node)

$$\text{ArgumentNode} \triangleq \langle \text{ID}, \text{Premises}, \text{Inference}, \text{Conclusion}, \text{Strength}, \text{Dependencies} \rangle$$

where:

  • $\text{ID}$: the unique identifier of the node
  • $\text{Premises}$: the set of premises
  • $\text{Inference}$: the rule or method of inference
  • $\text{Conclusion}$: the conclusion
  • $\text{Strength}$: the argumentative strength
  • $\text{Dependencies}$: the other argument nodes on which it depends

III. Standard Format of an Argument Node

This appendix presents each argument node in the following standard format:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Standard Format of Argument Node                               │    
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │    
│  [Node ID] Node Name                                            │    
│                                                                 │    
│  Premises:                                                      │    
│  P1. [Premise 1]                                                │    
│  P2. [Premise 2]                                                │    
│  ...                                                            │    
│                                                                 │    
│  Inference:                                                     │    
│  [Description of the rule or method of inference]               │    
│                                                                 │    
│  Conclusion:                                                    │    
│  C. [Conclusion]                                                │    
│                                                                 │    
│  Formal representation:                                         │    
│  [Formal expression using logical symbols]                      │    
│                                                                 │    
│  Argument strength: [Necessary/Highly Probable/Probable/Speculative]│
│                                                                 │    
│  Depends on: [List the other nodes it depends on]               │    
│                                                                 │    
│  Depended on by: [List the other nodes that depend on it]       │    
│                                                                 │    
│  Potential objections:                                          │    
│  [List possible objections]                                     │    
│                                                                 │    
│  Response:                                                      │    
│  [Response to the objections]                                   │    
│                                                                 │    
│  First appearance: [Chapter/section location]                   │    
│                                                                 │    
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

IV. Grading of Argument Strength

This appendix divides argument strength into four grades:

Table B.0.1 Grading of Argument Strength

GradeNameDefinitionSymbol
S1Necessary argumentIf the premises are true, the conclusion is necessarily true◆
S2Highly probable argumentIf the premises are true, the conclusion is highly probably true◇
S3Probable argumentIf the premises are true, the conclusion is probably true○
S4Speculative argumentIf the premises are true, the conclusion has a certain reasonableness△

V. Classification of Argument Types

This appendix classifies argument types into the following categories:

Table B.0.2 Classification of Argument Types

Type CodeArgument TypeExplanation
DEDDeductive argumentNecessary inference from the general to the particular
INDInductive argumentProbable inference from the particular to the general
ABDAbductive argumentInference to the best explanation
ANAAnalogical argumentInference based on similarity
TRATranscendental argumentInference exploring the conditions of possibility
CONConstructive argumentInference of conceptual construction
NORNormative argumentInference from facts to norms

VI. Relation to the New Three Views

The argument nodes in this appendix are organized around the New Three Views. The New Three Views (NC, NL, NK) constitute the core of this book's chain of argumentation, and all normative conclusions can be traced back to the foundational propositions of the New Three Views.

VII. Instructions for Use

  1. Mode of consultation: readers may consult argument nodes by chapter, topic, or argument type
  2. Tracing dependencies: trace the premises and consequences of arguments via the dependency diagrams
  3. Strength assessment: assess the reliability of conclusions with reference to the grading of argument strength
  4. Critical use: engage in critical thinking with reference to the potential objections and responses

VIII. Boundary Statement

In accordance with the "first-generation draft-model positioning" of Chapter Zero §0.6, the summary of argument nodes in this appendix is in a state of continuous revision. We welcome criticism and suggestions for improvement from the academic community regarding the validity of the arguments.

B.2 Detailed Account of Volume 1 Argument Nodes

This section unfolds in detail all the argument nodes of Volume 1 (theoretical foundations).

B.2.1 New Cosmology Argument Nodes (1.1-1.12)

[Node 1.1] Relational Interpretation of Quantum Entanglement

Premises:

P1. The phenomenon of quantum entanglement shows that the states of entangled particles cannot be fully described independently of one another P2. The correlations of entangled particles cannot be attributed to hidden variables or local interactions (the violation of Bell's inequalities) P3. The best physical explanation should explain the phenomenon without introducing unnecessary assumptions

Inference:

Abductive inference (Abduction): the best explanation of the phenomenon of quantum entanglement is relational ontology—the state of an entity is constituted by its relations.

Conclusion:

C. Quantum mechanics supports a relational-ontology interpretation

Formal representation:

$$\text{QuantumEntanglement} \land \text{BellViolation} \land \text{Parsimony} \xrightarrow{\text{ABD}} \text{RelationalOntology}$$

Argument strength: ◇ (highly probable)

Depends on: none (empirical foundation of physics)

Depended on by: 1.2, 1.11

Potential objections:

R1. Quantum mechanics has multiple interpretations (Copenhagen, many-worlds, hidden variables, etc.), and the relational interpretation is only one of them R2. The leap from physics to metaphysics may be too quick

Response:

To R1: acknowledge the plurality of interpretations of quantum mechanics, but the relational interpretation is more consistent with other developments in physics (such as quantum gravity) To R2: this argument claims only that the relational interpretation is "supported," not "proven"

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 1, §1.1.1

[Node 1.2] Argument that Relations Are Prior to Entities

Premises:

P1. Quantum mechanics supports a relational-ontology interpretation (from 1.1) P2. If relations are constitutive, then relations are ontologically prior to entities P3. The tradition of process philosophy provides a philosophical framework for the priority of relations

Inference:

Transcendental argument (Transcendental): if the identity of an entity is constituted by relations, then relations are the condition for the existence of the entity, and therefore relations are ontologically prior.

Conclusion:

C. Relations are prior to entities (NC-1)

Formal representation:

$$\text{RelationalOntology} \land \text{ConstitutiveRelations} \xrightarrow{\text{TRA}} \text{NC-1: Relations Prior to Entities}$$

Argument strength: ◇ (highly probable)

Depends on: 1.1

Depended on by: 1.11, 2.10, 3.11, 5.8

Potential objections:

R1. Relations require relata, and therefore entities are ontologically prior to relations R2. Everyday experience supports the priority of entities

Response:

To R1: this presupposes an entity-relation dichotomy; in relational ontology, the relata are themselves nodes in a network of relations To R2: everyday experience reflects the appearances at the macroscopic level; ontology discusses a more fundamental structure

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 1, §1.1.2

[Node 1.3] Physical Support for Process Philosophy

Premises:

P1. Modern physics (quantum mechanics, relativity) describes events and processes, not static entities P2. In quantum field theory, particles are excitations of fields, the results of processes P3. In relativity, spacetime is dynamic, affected by the distribution of matter-energy

Inference:

Abductive inference (Abduction): process philosophy's description of the nature of existence is consistent with the picture of modern physics.

Conclusion:

C. Modern physics supports process ontology

Formal representation:

$$\text{QM} \land \text{QFT} \land \text{GR} \xrightarrow{\text{ABD}} \text{ProcessOntology}$$

Argument strength: ◇ (highly probable)

Depends on: none (empirical foundation of physics)

Depended on by: 1.4, 1.11

Potential objections:

R1. The equations of physics describe states, not processes R2. Process philosophy is an independent philosophical position and should not be simply derived from physics

Response:

To R1: the equations of physics describe the evolution of states, i.e., processes; a state is only a cross-section of a process To R2: this argument does not "derive" process philosophy from physics, but rather claims that the two are consistent

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 1, §1.2.1

[Node 1.4] Argument that Process Is Prior to State

Premises:

P1. Modern physics supports process ontology (from 1.3) P2. If the essence of existence is process, then a state is an abstraction or cross-section of a process P3. Process is a more fundamental category, and state is derivative

Inference:

Transcendental argument (Transcendental): if a state is a cross-section of a process, then the process is the condition for the existence of the state, and therefore process is ontologically prior.

Conclusion:

C. Process is prior to state (NC-2)

Formal representation:

$$\text{ProcessOntology} \land \text{StateAsSection} \xrightarrow{\text{TRA}} \text{NC-2: Process Prior to State}$$

Argument strength: ◇ (highly probable)

Depends on: 1.3

Depended on by: 1.11, 2.10, 3.11, 5.8

Potential objections:

R1. A process requires something to change in the process, and therefore presupposes an entity or state R2. Physics in fact often deals with instantaneous states

Response:

To R1: in process ontology, the "something" is itself a pattern of process; no entity needs to be presupposed To R2: instantaneous states are analytical tools and do not represent ontological priority

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 1, §1.2.2

[Node 1.5] Participatory Interpretation of Quantum Measurement

Premises:

P1. In quantum measurement, the act of observation affects the state of the observed system P2. Measurement results do not pre-exist but are produced through the measurement process P3. Wheeler's concept of the "participatory universe" provides a philosophical framework

Inference:

Abductive inference (Abduction): the best explanation of the phenomenon of quantum measurement is participatory ontology—the observer participates in constituting the observation result.

Conclusion:

C. Quantum mechanics supports a participatory-ontology interpretation

Formal representation:

$$\text{QuantumMeasurement} \land \text{ObserverEffect} \xrightarrow{\text{ABD}} \text{ParticipatoryOntology}$$

Argument strength: ◇ (highly probable)

Depends on: none (empirical foundation of physics)

Depended on by: 1.6, 1.11

Potential objections:

R1. The quantum measurement problem remains unsolved, and the participatory interpretation is only one of many interpretations R2. "Participation" is an anthropomorphic description that may mislead

Response:

To R1: acknowledge the plurality of interpretations, but the participatory interpretation forms a consistent whole with the relational and process interpretations To R2: "participation" here is a technical term, referring to the interaction between observer and system

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 1, §1.3.1

[Node 1.6] Argument that Participation Is Prior to Observation

Premises:

P1. Quantum mechanics supports a participatory-ontology interpretation (from 1.5) P2. If the observer participates in constituting the observation result, then passive observation is impossible P3. The act of cognition is itself a kind of intervention

Inference:

Transcendental argument (Transcendental): if observation is impossible, then participation is the condition of cognition, and therefore participation is epistemologically prior to observation.

Conclusion:

C. Participation is prior to observation (NC-3)

Formal representation:

$$\text{ParticipatoryOntology} \land \text{CognitionAsIntervention} \xrightarrow{\text{TRA}} \text{NC-3: Participation Prior to Observation}$$

Argument strength: ◇ (highly probable)

Depends on: 1.5

Depended on by: 1.11, 2.10, 3.11, 3.1, 5.8

Potential objections:

R1. At the macroscopic level, passive observation appears to be possible R2. This blurs the boundary between ontology and epistemology

Response:

To R1: macroscopic "passive observation" is an approximation; strictly speaking, any observation involves interaction To R2: NC-3 does indeed cross ontology and epistemology, and this is precisely the characteristic of the New Three Views

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 1, §1.3.2

[Node 1.7] Normative Implication of the Second Law of Thermodynamics

Premises:

P1. The second law of thermodynamics stipulates that the entropy of a closed system tends to increase P2. Life and civilization, as negentropic organizations, depend for their survival on the acquisition of negentropy flow P3. One source of normativity is the conditions of survival

Inference:

Normative argument (Normative): if the conditions of survival have normative implications, and negentropy flow is a condition of survival, then maintaining negentropy flow is normative.

Conclusion:

C. The second law of thermodynamics implies the normative requirement of maintaining negentropy flow

Formal representation:

$$\text{SecondLaw} \land \text{NegentropyForSurvival} \land \text{SurvivalAsNormative} \xrightarrow{\text{NOR}} \text{NormativeImplication}$$

Argument strength: ○ (probable)

Depends on: none (foundation of physics)

Depended on by: 1.8, 5.2, 12.2

Potential objections:

R1. Deriving norms from facts (the laws of physics) is the naturalistic fallacy R2. Survival itself has no intrinsic normativity

Response:

To R1: this argument does not derive norms directly from facts, but rather through the bridge principles (the principle of survival rationality) To R2: the justification of the principle of survival rationality will be argued in detail in Chapter 5

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 1, §1.4.1

[Node 1.8] Argument on Negentropy Flow and the Conditions of Survival

Premises:

P1. Life and civilization are dissipative structures and require a continuous flow of energy and matter P2. The survival of a dissipative structure depends on obtaining negentropy from the environment (Schrödinger) P3. If the negentropy flow is interrupted, the dissipative structure will collapse

Inference:

Deductive argument (Deduction): from the definition of dissipative structures and the principles of thermodynamics, it can be deduced that negentropy flow is a necessary condition of survival.

Conclusion:

C. Negentropy flow is a necessary condition of the survival of life and civilization

Formal representation:

$$\text{DissipativeStructure}(S) \land \text{SecondLaw} \xrightarrow{\text{DED}} \text{Necessity}(\text{NegentropyFlow}, \text{Survival}(S))$$

Argument strength: ◆ (necessary)

Depends on: 1.7

Depended on by: 2.1, 12.1, 12.2

Potential objections:

R1. This is only a necessary condition at the physical level and is unrelated to normativity

Response:

To R1: the physical-level necessary condition becomes a constraint on normative considerations; normative construction must fall within the range of physical possibility

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 1, §1.4.2

[Node 1.9] Argument on the Directionality of Cosmic Evolution

Premises:

P1. Since the Big Bang, the universe has undergone evolution from the simple to the complex P2. The formation of stars, planets, life, and civilization shows a growth of complexity P3. The trend of the growth of complexity is statistical and does not violate the second law of thermodynamics

Inference:

Inductive argument (Induction): from the empirical evidence of cosmic history, infer the trend of the growth of complexity.

Conclusion:

C. Cosmic evolution exhibits a directional trend of the growth of complexity

Formal representation:

$$\text{CosmicHistory} \land \text{ComplexityEmergence} \xrightarrow{\text{IND}} \text{DirectionalTrend}$$

Argument strength: ○ (probable)

Depends on: none (empirical evidence)

Depended on by: 1.10, 2.1

Potential objections:

R1. This may be an observer selection effect (we can exist only in a universe of sufficiently high complexity) R2. Local growth of complexity may come at the cost of entropy increase on a larger scale

Response:

To R1: acknowledge the possibility of the observer selection effect, but this does not negate the fact of the growth of complexity To R2: correct, the local growth of complexity is compatible with a global increase of entropy; this is precisely the characteristic of dissipative structures

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 1, §1.5.1

[Node 1.10] Argument on the Physical Basis of the Growth of Complexity

Premises:

P1. Cosmic evolution exhibits a trend of the growth of complexity (from 1.9) P2. The growth of complexity can be explained by mechanisms such as self-organization and emergence P3. These mechanisms have a solid foundation in physics and complex systems science

Inference:

Abductive inference (Abduction): the growth of complexity can be explained by mechanisms of physics and complex systems science.

Conclusion:

C. The growth of complexity has a physical basis

Formal representation:

$$\text{DirectionalTrend} \land \text{SelfOrganization} \land \text{Emergence} \xrightarrow{\text{ABD}} \text{PhysicalBasis}$$

Argument strength: ◇ (highly probable)

Depends on: 1.9

Depended on by: 1.11, 2.1

Potential objections:

R1. The mechanisms of self-organization and emergence are not yet fully understood

Response:

To R1: acknowledge the incompleteness of understanding, but existing theories provide strong support

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 1, §1.5.2

[Node 1.11] Argument for the Consistency of the Three Propositions of the New Cosmology

Premises:

P1. NC-1 (relations prior to entities) is supported by quantum mechanics (from 1.1, 1.2) P2. NC-2 (process prior to state) is supported by modern physics (from 1.3, 1.4) P3. NC-3 (participation prior to observation) is supported by quantum measurement (from 1.5, 1.6) P4. There is no logical contradiction among the three propositions

Inference:

Constructive argument (Construction): the three propositions can be integrated into a consistent cosmological framework.

Conclusion:

C. The three propositions of the New Cosmology constitute a consistent framework

Formal representation:

$$\text{NC-1} \land \text{NC-2} \land \text{NC-3} \land \neg \text{Contradiction} \xrightarrow{\text{CON}} \text{Consistency(NC)}$$

Argument strength: ◇ (highly probable)

Depends on: 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.5, 1.6, 1.10

Depended on by: 1.12, 2.10, 3.11, 5.8

Potential objections:

R1. The support for the three propositions comes from different domains, and the integration may be too forced

Response:

To R1: all three propositions point to the common themes of relationality, dynamism, and participatoriness, and the integration is natural

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 1, §1.6.1

[Node 1.12] Argument on the Dimension-Raising Relation between the New Cosmology and the Old Cosmology

Premises:

P1. The old cosmology (priority of entities, priority of states, priority of observation) is effective at everyday scales and within the domain of classical physics P2. The new cosmology is more accurate at the quantum and cosmic scales P3. The relation between the new cosmology and the old cosmology is analogous to the relation between relativity and Newtonian mechanics

Inference:

Analogical argument (Analogy): just as relativity contains Newtonian mechanics as a low-speed approximation, the new cosmology contains the old cosmology as an approximation at a particular scale.

Conclusion:

C. The new cosmology is a "dimension-raising extension" of the old cosmology rather than a "replacement"

Formal representation:

$$\text{NC} \supset \text{OldCosmology} \text{ (as approximation)}$$

Argument strength: ○ (probable)

Depends on: 1.11

Depended on by: 2.9, 3.10, 5.8

Potential objections:

R1. The relation between relativity and Newtonian mechanics has a precise mathematical expression; the relation between the new and old cosmologies does not R2. This may be merely a rhetorical strategy

Response:

To R1: acknowledge the lack of mathematical precision, but the conceptual relation of containment still holds To R2: this is not merely rhetoric, but a substantive claim about the relation between the two

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 1, §1.6.2 B.2.2 New View of Life Argument Nodes (2.1-2.10)

[Node 2.1] Argument for the Negentropic-Organization Definition of Life

Premises:

P1. Life is a dissipative structure and depends on a negentropy flow to maintain its survival (from 1.8) P2. Traditional definitions of life (based on chemistry, heredity, etc.) are too narrow P3. A functional definition is more suited to cross-substrate application than a substrate-based definition

Inference:

Constructive argument (Construction): construct a negentropy-based, functional definition of life.

Conclusion:

C. Life can be defined as "a self-organizing system that maintains a negentropic state" (the basis of NL-2)

Formal representation:

$$\text{Life} \triangleq \text{SelfOrganizingSystem}(S) \land \text{Maintains}(S, \text{Negentropy})$$

Argument strength: ◇ (highly probable)

Depends on: 1.8, 1.9, 1.10

Depended on by: 2.2, 2.4, 2.8, 12.1

Potential objections:

R1. This definition may be too broad, including non-living systems (such as crystals) R2. This definition may ignore other essential features of life

Response:

To R1: a crystal is a static structure, not a dynamic process of maintaining negentropy; the definition can be further refined To R2: acknowledge that life has multiple features, but negentropy maintenance is the most basic physical feature

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 2, §2.1.1

[Node 2.2] Argument for the Continuum of Life

Premises:

P1. Life is negentropic organization (from 2.1) P2. The degree of negentropy varies continuously P3. There is no clear ontological boundary between life and non-life

Inference:

Inductive argument (Induction): from borderline cases such as viruses, viroids, and protocells, infer that life is a continuum.

Conclusion:

C. Life is a continuum rather than a binary classification (NL-1)

Formal representation:

$$\text{Life} \in [0, 1] \text{ (continuous spectrum)}$$

Argument strength: ○ (probable)

Depends on: 2.1

Depended on by: 2.7, 2.8, 7.1

Potential objections:

R1. In practice, we can usually distinguish life from non-life R2. The continuum view may lead to moral relativism

Response:

To R1: the practical distinction is operational and does not represent a clear ontological boundary To R2: the continuum does not lead to relativism, but to graded moral consideration

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 2, §2.2.1

[Node 2.3] Functionalist Argument for Agency Status

Premises:

P1. Agency status is usually based on certain capacities or functions (sentience, autonomy, interests, etc.) P2. These capacities or functions can be realized on different material substrates P3. Functionalism is more universally applicable than substrate-ism

Inference:

Transcendental argument (Transcendental): if agency status is based on functions rather than substrate, then agency status can be realized across substrates.

Conclusion:

C. Agency status is functional and can be realized across substrates (the basis of NL-3)

Formal representation:

$$\text{AgencyStatus}(E) = f(\text{Functions}(E)) \neq g(\text{Substrate}(E))$$

Argument strength: ◇ (highly probable)

Depends on: none (conceptual analysis)

Depended on by: 2.4, 2.7, 7.1, 7.2

Potential objections:

R1. Functionalism is controversial in the philosophy of mind R2. Certain functions may depend on a particular substrate

Response:

To R1: acknowledge that functionalism is controversial, but it is currently the position best able to accommodate cross-substrate situations To R2: this argument does not exclude the causal influence of substrate on function, but merely denies that substrate is a definitional element of agency status

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 2, §2.3.1

[Node 2.4] Argument for the Possibility of Cross-Substrate Life

Premises:

P1. Life is negentropic organization (from 2.1) P2. Agency status is functional (from 2.3) P3. Silicon-based life, digital life, etc., are logically possible

Inference:

Abductive inference (Abduction): the possibility of cross-substrate life can explain why we need functional definitions of life and agency status.

Conclusion:

C. Cross-substrate life is possible

Formal representation:

$$\exists S_1, S_2: \text{Life}(E, S_1) \land \text{Life}(E', S_2) \land S_1 \neq S_2$$

Argument strength: ○ (probable)

Depends on: 2.1, 2.3

Depended on by: 2.8, 7.1, 18.3

Potential objections:

R1. There is currently no empirical evidence of cross-substrate life R2. Carbon-based life may have a special physical necessity

Response:

To R1: the absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; this is an argument about possibility To R2: even if carbon-based life has advantages, this does not exclude the possibility of other substrates

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 2, §2.4.1

[Node 2.5] Integrated Information Theory Support for Consciousness

Premises:

P1. Integrated Information Theory (IIT) provides a formal framework for consciousness P2. IIT associates consciousness with information integration (the Φ value) P3. IIT is substrate-neutral and applicable to any information-processing system

Inference:

Abductive inference (Abduction): IIT provides formal support for a functionalist understanding of consciousness.

Conclusion:

C. Integrated information theory supports a functionalist understanding of consciousness

Formal representation:

$$\text{IIT} \xrightarrow{\text{ABD}} \text{FunctionalistConsciousness}$$

Argument strength: ○ (probable)

Depends on: none (foundation of consciousness science)

Depended on by: 2.6, 7.2, 7.3

Potential objections:

R1. IIT is controversial and is not a consensus of consciousness science R2. The calculation of the Φ value is infeasible in complex systems

Response:

To R1: acknowledge that IIT is controversial, but it is currently one of the most formalized theories To R2: the computational difficulty is a practical problem and does not affect the validity of the conceptual framework

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 2, §2.5.1

[Node 2.6] Argument for the UCS Conceptual Framework

Premises:

P1. Consciousness is graded (from the continuum of life) P2. Integrated information theory supports a functionalist understanding of consciousness (from 2.5) P3. An operationalized framework for assessing consciousness is needed

Inference:

Constructive argument (Construction): construct a multi-dimensional framework for assessing consciousness (UCS).

Conclusion:

C. The UCS provides an operationalized framework for assessing consciousness

Formal representation:

$$\text{UCS}(E) = f(\Phi, I, A, S, R)$$

Argument strength: ○ (probable)

Depends on: 2.2, 2.5

Depended on by: 2.8, 7.1, 7.2

Potential objections:

R1. A multi-dimensional framework may obscure the importance of a single dimension R2. The choice of dimensions may be arbitrary

Response:

To R1: multiple dimensions are meant to capture the complexity of consciousness, and do not exclude the possibility that some dimensions are more important To R2: the choice of dimensions is based on the literature of consciousness science and is not arbitrary

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 2, §2.5.2

[Node 2.7] Argument for the Gradualness of Moral Status

Premises:

P1. Life is a continuum (from 2.2) P2. Agency status is functional (from 2.3) P3. Moral status is based on agency status

Inference:

Normative argument (Normative): if agency status is graded, then moral status is also graded.

Conclusion:

C. Moral status is graded rather than binary

Formal representation:

$$\text{MoralStatus}(E) \in [0, 1]$$

Argument strength: ◇ (highly probable)

Depends on: 2.2, 2.3

Depended on by: 2.8, 7.1, 11.3

Potential objections:

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 11, §11.3.1

[Node 11.4] Argument for the Consistency of the RFP with the New Three Views

Premises:

P1. The RFP requires protecting the possibility space P2. The New Cosmology emphasizes relationality, processuality, and participatoriness P3. The New View of Life emphasizes the functionality and gradualness of agency status P4. The New View of Cognition emphasizes the sociality and negotiability of cognition

Inference:

Constructive argument (Construction): argue for the consistency of the RFP with the New Three Views.

Conclusion:

C. The RFP is consistent with the New Three Views

Formal representation:

$$\text{Consistent}(\text{RFP}, \text{NC} \land \text{NL} \land \text{NK})$$

Argument strength: ◇ (highly probable)

P1. The RFP is an abstract normative principle P2. Operational indicators are needed to apply the RFP P3. The RFD (recursive freedom degree) is the operationalization of the RFP

[Node 11.6] Argument on the Relation between the RFP and Existing Concepts of Freedom

P1. Negative freedom focuses on freedom from interference P2. Positive freedom focuses on the capacity for realization P3. Republican freedom focuses on freedom from domination

C. The RFP is an extension of existing concepts of freedom, integrating the negative, positive, and republican dimensions

B.2.6 Principle of Negentropy Responsibility Argument Nodes (12.1-12.5)

[Node 12.1] Argument for the Concept of Negentropy Responsibility

Premises:

P1. Life and civilization are negentropic organizations (from 2.1) P2. The survival of a negentropic organization depends on a negentropy flow (from 1.8) P3. Maintaining the negentropy flow is a necessary condition of survival

Inference:

Constructive argument (Construction): construct the concept of negentropy responsibility.

Conclusion:

C. Negentropy responsibility is the responsibility of a negentropic organization to maintain the negentropic structure

Formal representation:

$$\text{NegentropyResponsibility}(S) \triangleq \text{Obligation}(S, \text{Maintain}(\text{NegentropyStructure}))$$

Argument strength: ◇ (highly probable)

Depends on: 1.8, 2.1

Depended on by: 12.2, 12.3

To R1: negentropy responsibility is a requirement on agents, based on physical facts

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 12, §12.1.1

[Node 12.2] Argument for the Derivation of the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility

Premises:

P1. The normative principles can be derived from the New Three Views + the bridge principles (from 5.8) P2. BP-1 (survival rationality) requires maintaining the conditions of survival (from 5.2) P3. Negentropy flow is a condition of survival (from 1.7, 1.8) P4. The concept of negentropy responsibility (from 12.1)

Inference:

Normative argument (Normative): derive the principle of negentropy responsibility.

Conclusion:

C. Principle of negentropy responsibility (NRP): a negentropic organization is responsible for maintaining the negentropic structure

Formal representation:

$$\text{NRP}: \forall S \in \mathcal{S}_{\text{neg}}: \text{Capability}(S, J) \Rightarrow \text{Obligation}(S, \text{Maintain}(J))$$

$$\text{Consistent}(\text{NRP}, \text{NC} \land \text{NL} \land \text{NK})$$

B.2.7 Principle of Reversibility Argument Nodes (13.1-13.5)

[Node 13.1] Argument for the Concept of Reversibility

Premises:

P1. The consequences of an action can be reversible or irreversible P2. Reversibility is graded P3. Irreversible actions close off certain possibilities

Inference:

Constructive argument (Construction): construct the concept of reversibility.

Conclusion:

C. Reversibility is the degree to which the consequences of an action can be undone

Formal representation:

$$\text{Reversibility}(a) \triangleq \exists a^{-1}: S(t_0) \xrightarrow{a} S(t_1) \xrightarrow{a^{-1}} S(t_0') \land d(S(t_0), S(t_0')) < \epsilon$$

Argument strength: ◇ (highly probable)

Depends on: none (conceptual construction)

Depended on by: 13.2, 13.3, 8.3

Potential objections:

R1. Strict reversibility is physically impossible (the second law of thermodynamics)

Response:

To R1: reversibility is graded; the point is to return to a "functionally equivalent" state

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 13, §13.1.1

[Node 13.2] Argument for the Derivation of the Principle of Reversibility

Premises:

P1. The normative principles can be derived from the New Three Views + the bridge principles (from 5.8) P2. BP-2 (epistemic humility) requires acknowledging the boundaries of knowledge (from 5.3) P3. Deep uncertainty exists (from 3.6) P4. Under deep uncertainty, reversible action is more prudent

Inference:

Normative argument (Normative): derive the principle of reversibility.

Conclusion:

C. Principle of reversibility (REV): under conditions of deep uncertainty, reversible action should be preferred

Formal representation:

$$\text{REV}: \text{DeepUncertainty} \Rightarrow \text{Prefer}(\text{Reversible}(a))$$

Argument strength: ◇ (highly probable)

Depends on: 3.6, 3.7, 5.3, 5.8, 13.1

Depended on by: 13.3, 13.4, 14.1, 14.2

Potential objections:

R1. Sometimes irreversible action is necessary

Response:

To R1: the REV is a "preference," not an "absolute prohibition"; irreversible action requires additional justification

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 13, §13.2.1

[Node 13.3] Argument for the Concept of the Forbidden Red Lines

Premises:

P1. The consequences of certain actions are catastrophic and irreversible P2. Such actions should be absolutely prohibited P3. The extreme form of the principle of reversibility is the forbidden red lines

Inference:

Constructive argument (Construction): construct the concept of the forbidden red lines.

Conclusion:

C. The forbidden red lines are the absolute prohibition of catastrophic, irreversible actions

Formal representation:

$$\text{ForbiddenRedLines} \triangleq \{a \in \mathcal{A}: \text{Catastrophic}(a) \land \text{Irreversible}(a) \land \text{Unconditional}(\neg a)\}$$

Argument strength: ◇ (highly probable)

Depends on: 13.1, 13.2

Depended on by: 13.4, 9.3

Potential objections:

R1. An absolute prohibition may be too strict

Response:

To R1: the forbidden red lines target only the most extreme cases (such as civilization-level catastrophes)

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 13, §13.3.1

[Node 13.4] Argument for the Consistency of the REV with the New Three Views

Premises:

P1. The REV is based on epistemic humility P2. Epistemic humility comes from the New View of Cognition P3. The REV protects the possibility space and is consistent with the RFP and the NRP

Inference:

Constructive argument (Construction): argue for the consistency of the REV with the New Three Views.

Conclusion:

C. The REV is consistent with the New Three Views

Formal representation:

$$\text{Consistent}(\text{REV}, \text{NC} \land \text{NL} \land \text{NK})$$

Argument strength: ◇ (highly probable)

Depends on: 1.11, 2.8, 3.9, 13.2, 13.3

Depended on by: 14.2

Potential objections:

R1. The consistency may be superficial

Response:

To R1: the consistency is not only superficial; the core concept of the REV (epistemic humility) comes directly from the New Three Views

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 13, §13.4.1

[Node 13.5] Argument on the Relation between the REV and the Precautionary Principle

Premises:

P1. The precautionary principle requires taking precautionary measures under uncertainty P2. The REV requires preferring reversible action under deep uncertainty P3. Both concern prudence under uncertainty

Inference:

Argument strength: ○ (probable)

First appearance: Volume 1, Chapter 13, §13.5.1

Premises:

P1. The RFP protects the possibility space (from 11.3) P2. The NRP maintains the negentropic structure (from 12.2) P3. The REV ensures reversibility (from 13.2) P4. The three principles are mutually complementary, with no contradiction

B.5 Summary Table of Argument Strength

This section summarizes all argument nodes classified by argumentative strength.

B.5.1 List of Necessary Arguments

Table B.5.1 List of Necessary Arguments (◆)

A necessary argument is an argument in which the conclusion is necessarily true if the premises are true; it is usually a deductive argument.

Node IDNode NameLogical FormChapter/Section
1.8Argument on Negentropy Flow and the Conditions of SurvivalDeduced from the definition of dissipative structures and the principles of thermodynamics§1.4
17.1Argument for the Content of the L₀ LayerNecessity of physical constraints§17.1

Characteristics of Necessary Arguments

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Characteristics of Necessary Arguments                         │         
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │         
│  1. The premise-conclusion relation is necessary                │         
│     P₁ ∧ P₂ ∧ ... ∧ Pn ⊨ C                                      │         
│                                                                 │         
│  2. The conclusion cannot be negated without contradiction      │         
│     ¬C is incompatible with (P₁ ∧ P₂ ∧ ... ∧ Pn)               │          
│                                                                 │         
│  3. Condition of refutability                                   │         
│     The conclusion can be negated only if a premise is negated  │         
│                                                                 │         
│  Example: Node 1.8                                               │        
│  P1. Life is a dissipative structure                            │         
│  P2. A dissipative structure requires a negentropy flow to be maintained │
│  C.  Life requires a negentropy flow to be maintained (necessary) │       
│                                                                 │         
│  To refute C, a critic must refute P1 or P2                     │         
│                                                                 │         
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

B.6 Summary of Potential Objections and Responses

This section systematically summarizes the potential objections faced by the core arguments of this work and the responses to them. This reflects the critical openness and commitment to revisability of this work.

B.6.1 Framework for Classifying Potential Objections

Definition B.6.1 (Potential Objection)

$$\text{PotentialObjection} \triangleq \langle \text{Target}, \text{Type}, \text{Content}, \text{Severity}, \text{Response} \rangle$$

where:

  • $\text{Target}$: the argument node that the objection targets
  • $\text{Type}$: the type of objection
  • $\text{Content}$: the content of the objection
  • $\text{Severity}$: the degree of severity (fatal/major/moderate/minor)
  • $\text{Response}$: the strategy of response

Table B.6.1 Classification of Objection Types

Type CodeObjection TypeExplanationTypical Form
OBJ-PPremise objectionQuestions the truth of the premises of the argument"P does not hold"
OBJ-IInference objectionQuestions the validity of the reasoning process"C cannot be derived from P"
OBJ-CConclusion objectionDirectly questions the conclusion"C is wrong"
OBJ-AAlternative objectionProposes a better alternative"A is better than C"
OBJ-OOperational objectionQuestions the operability of the concept"C cannot be operationalized"
OBJ-EEmpirical objectionRefutes with empirical evidence"Evidence E refutes C"

Grading of Severity

GradeNameDefinitionCoping Strategy
S1Fatal objectionIf it holds, the argument fails completelyRequires reconstruction of the argument
S2Major objectionIf it holds, the argument is significantly weakenedRequires revision or supplementation
S3Moderate objectionIf it holds, the argument is partially weakenedRequires clarification or qualification
S4Minor objectionIf it holds, the impact on the argument is limitedCan be resolved by a response

Detailed Objection and Response: R-NC-1

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Objection R-NC-1: Plurality of Interpretations of Quantum Mechanics │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │     
│  Content of the objection:                                     │      
│  Quantum mechanics has multiple interpretations (Copenhagen,    │     
│  many-worlds, hidden variables, relational quantum mechanics,   │     
│  etc.), and the relational interpretation is only one of them   │     
│  and cannot serve as a determinate ontological foundation.      │     
│                                                                 │     
│  Type of objection: OBJ-A (alternative objection)              │      
│  Severity: S2 (major)                                           │     
│  Target node: 1.1                                               │     
│                                                                 │     
│  Response strategy:                                             │     
│                                                                 │     
│  1. Acknowledge the plurality of interpretations                │     
│     This work does not claim that the relational interpretation │     
│     is the only correct interpretation, but rather maintains    │     
│     that it is a "supported" interpretation "compatible with    │     
│     the purposes of this work."                                 │     
│                                                                 │     
│  2. Point to a convergent trend                                  │    
│     In the contemporary philosophy of physics, relational/       │    
│     structural realism is receiving increasing attention,       │     
│     consistent with frontier research trends such as quantum    │     
│     gravity.                                                    │     
│                                                                 │     
│  3. Emphasize practicality                                       │    
│     Even if the relational interpretation is not the ultimate   │     
│     truth, it provides a useful conceptual framework for        │     
│     thinking about ethical problems across substrates, species, │     
│     and civilizations.                                          │     
│                                                                 │     
│  4. Retain room for revision                                     │    
│     If future developments in physics refute the relational     │     
│     interpretation, the normative conclusions of this work can  │     
│     still obtain support through other paths (such as           │     
│     functionalism or process philosophy).                       │     
│                                                                 │     
│  Assessment of the response:                                    │     
│  The response effectively downgrades "the relational            │     
│  interpretation is the only correct one" to "the relational     │     
│  interpretation is supported and useful," preserving the core   │     
│  force of the argument.                                         │     
│                                                                 │     
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Detailed Objection and Response: R-NC-7

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Objection R-NC-7: The Naturalistic Fallacy                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  Content of the objection:                                     │ 
│  Deriving normative requirements from the second law of         │
│  thermodynamics (a fact) is the naturalistic fallacy.           │
│  Hume's problem shows that "ought" cannot be derived from "is." │
│                                                                 │
│  Type of objection: OBJ-I (inference objection)                │ 
│  Severity: S1 (fatal)                                           │
│  Target nodes: 1.7, 5.8                                         │
│                                                                 │
│  Response strategy:                                             │
│                                                                 │
│  1. Clarify the structure of the argument                       │
│     This work does not derive norms directly from facts. The    │
│     structure of the argument is:                               │
│     fact + bridge principles → norm                             │
│     The bridge principles themselves contain a normative        │
│     component and are the connecting point.                     │
│                                                                 │
│  2. Independent defense of the bridge principles                │
│     The bridge principles (survival rationality, epistemic      │
│     humility, intersubjectivity) can be defended independently  │
│     of physical facts, drawing on traditions such as rational   │
│     choice theory, decision theory, and social contract theory. │
│                                                                 │
│  3. The principle "ought implies can"                           │
│     Any normative claim must be compatible with physical        │
│     possibility. Physical constraints are not the source of     │
│     norms, but the boundary conditions of norms.                │
│                                                                 │
│  4. Contemporary metaethical responses                          │
│     Contemporary metaethics provides various strategies for     │
│     responding to the naturalistic fallacy, including           │
│     naturalism, non-cognitivism, and constructivism. This work  │
│     adopts the position of "weak naturalism + bridge            │
│     principles."                                                │
│                                                                 │
│  Assessment of the response:                                    │
│  This is one of the most serious potential objections. The      │
│  response strategy is viable, but it must be acknowledged that  │
│  the legitimacy of the bridge principles remains contestable.   │
│                                                                 │
│  See: Chapter 5 §5.1-§5.7, argument nodes 5.1, 5.7             │ 
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Detailed Objection and Response: R-NL-2

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Objection R-NL-2: The Continuum Leads to Moral Relativism      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  Content of the objection:                                     │ 
│  If life and agency status are a continuum, then moral status   │
│  is also continuous.                                            │
│  This may lead to moral relativism and weaken the protection    │
│  of human rights.                                               │
│                                                                 │
│  Type of objection: OBJ-C (conclusion objection)              │  
│  Severity: S2 (major)                                           │
│  Target nodes: 2.2, 2.7                                         │
│                                                                 │
│  Response strategy:                                             │
│                                                                 │
│  1. Distinguish the continuum from relativism                   │
│     The continuum is an ontological claim, while relativism is  │
│     a normative claim.                                          │
│     From "moral status is graded" it cannot be derived that     │
│     "any moral judgment is relative."                           │
│                                                                 │
│  2. Gradualness does not negate thresholds                      │
│     Graded moral status can set thresholds. For example,        │
│     an agent reaching a certain threshold of consciousness      │
│     obtains the protection of basic rights. Human rights can    │
│     serve as the rights of high-degree agents.                  │
│                                                                 │
│  3. Extension rather than weakening                             │
│     The graded view extends the scope of moral concern          │
│     (including animals, ecosystems, and potential AI agents)    │
│     rather than weakening the protection of humans.             │
│                                                                 │
│  4. Practical operability                                       │
│     Indicators such as the UCS provide operationalized methods  │
│     for assessing the degree of moral status, making graded     │
│     judgments practicable.                                      │
│                                                                 │
│  Assessment of the response:                                    │
│  The response effectively shows that the continuum and          │
│  relativism are not equivalent. But the specific method of      │
│  threshold-setting needs further development.                   │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Detailed Objection and Response: R-NK-5

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Objection R-NK-5: Negotiable Truth and Anti-Realism            │ 
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │ 
│  Content of the objection:                                     │  
│  If truth is negotiable, then truth depends on social consensus │ 
│  rather than objective facts.                                   │ 
│  This appears to be anti-realism, denying the existence of      │ 
│  objective truth.                                               │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Type of objection: OBJ-C (conclusion objection)              │   
│  Severity: S2 (major)                                           │ 
│  Target node: 3.5                                               │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Response strategy:                                             │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  1. Distinguish truth from the establishment of truth           │ 
│     Negotiable truth does not deny the existence of objective   │ 
│     truth, but maintains that the establishment of truth        │ 
│     (how we know what is true) depends on social processes.     │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  2. Support from scientific practice                             │
│     Scientific knowledge obtains recognition through social     │ 
│     processes such as peer review, replicated experiments, and  │ 
│     open discussion, which is precisely the manifestation of    │ 
│     negotiability. But this does not mean that scientific truth │ 
│     is arbitrary or relative.                                   │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  3. Convergent constraints                                      │ 
│     The negotiation process is constrained by empirical         │ 
│     evidence, logical consistency, etc., and tends to converge  │ 
│     rather than diverge. This provides a basis for objectivity. │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  4. Pragmatist position                                         │ 
│     This work adopts a pragmatist position, focusing on the     │ 
│     practical utility of knowledge rather than the abstract     │ 
│     realism/anti-realism debate.                                │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Assessment of the response:                                    │ 
│  The response clarifies the meaning of negotiable truth and     │ 
│  shows that it is compatible with moderate realism.             │ 
│                                                                 │ 
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Detailed Objection and Response: R-BP-8

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Objection R-BP-8: The Covert Naturalistic Fallacy              │   
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │   
│  Content of the objection:                                     │

Key Findings

  1. The hierarchical character of the argumentative structure: the argumentative structure of this work strictly follows the load-bearing hierarchical relations of the protocol stack, with upper-layer arguments depending on lower-layer arguments.
  2. The distribution of argument strength: necessary arguments account for only about 2% (concentrated in the layer of physical constraints), highly probable arguments account for about 50% (the core conceptual layer), probable arguments account for about 45% (the operationalization layer), and speculative arguments account for about 3% (the layer of practical feasibility).
  3. Core dependency points: the consistency arguments of the New Three Views (1.11, 2.8, 3.9) and the complete derivation of the bridge principles (5.8) are the key nodes of the entire argumentative structure.
  4. Main weaknesses: the objections related to the naturalistic fallacy (R-NC-7, R-BP-8) and the objection related to the quantification of the possibility space (R-RFP-2) are the most serious challenges.
  5. Open attitude: this work maintains an open attitude toward all objections, acknowledges the revisability of the arguments, and welcomes criticism and improvement from the academic community.

Recommendations for Use

  1. Quick consultation: use the index tables of B.1 to quickly locate argument nodes
  2. Dependency tracing: use the dependency diagrams of B.4 to trace the premises and consequences of arguments
  3. Strength assessment: use the strength lists of B.5 to assess the reliability of conclusions
  4. Critical use: use the objections and responses of B.6 for critical thinking
  5. Research direction: use the list of open problems of B.6.7 to determine research directions

Indicator Computation GuideAppendix C

I. The Task and Positioning of This Appendix

This appendix provides a calculation guide for the six major indicator systems of the book Normative Foundations of Interstellar Civilization. As a foundational work of Interstellar Civilizatology, this treatise requires not only an abstract theoretical framework but also operable assessment tools. The task of this appendix is to convert the conceptual framework of Part Two (the indicator systems) into executable calculation procedures.

C.1 General Introduction to Indicator Calculation

This section explains the general principles, data requirements, uncertainty handling, result interpretation, and calculation tools for the calculation of the six major indicator systems.

C.1.1 General Principles of Calculation

C.1.1.1 The Philosophical Basis of Indicator Calculation

The fundamental purpose of indicator calculation is to operationalize the New Three Views and the normative principles, so that abstract philosophical concepts can be applied to concrete situations.

Definition C.1.1 (Operationalization)

$$\text{Operationalization} \triangleq \text{Concept} \xrightarrow{\text{Indicator}} \text{Measurement} \xrightarrow{\text{Calculation}} \text{Numerical Value}$$

The operationalization process must satisfy the following conditions:

ConditionDefinitionTest Method
Concept validityThe indicator indeed measures the concept it is intended to measureExpert review, theoretical argumentation
Construct validityThe internal structure of the indicator is consistent with the theoryFactor analysis, structural equation modeling
ReliabilityThe consistency and stability of measurement resultsRepeated measurement, inter-rater agreement
FeasibilityThe measurement can be carried out in practicePilot testing

C.1.1.2 Core Principles of Indicator Design

The indicator design of this treatise follows these core principles:

Principle One: Anchoring

Every indicator must be anchored to the New Three Views and the normative principles.

$$\forall I \in \{\text{UCS}, \text{RFD}, \text{CRV}, \text{CDI}, \text{MBCL}, \text{CSIA}\}: \exists A \in \{L_1, L_2\}: \text{Anchored}(I, A)$$

Principle Two: Multidimensionality

Complex concepts should be captured through multiple dimensions.

$$I = f(D_1, D_2, ..., D_n) \text{ where } n \geq 2$$

Principle Three: Gradualism

Indicators should reflect the graded nature of concepts, rather than binary classification.

$$I: \mathcal{E} \rightarrow [0, 1] \text{ (continuous spectrum)}$$

Principle Four: Revisability

Indicator design should remain open and can be revised based on feedback.

$$I_{v+1} = \text{Revise}(I_v, \text{Feedback})$$

Principle Five: Transparency

The calculation process should be fully transparent, traceable, and auditable.

$$\forall \text{step} \in \text{Calculation}: \text{Documented}(\text{step}) \land \text{Auditable}(\text{step})$$

C.1.1.3 The Formal Framework of Calculation

Definition C.1.2 (Indicator Calculation Framework)

$$\text{IndicatorCalculation} \triangleq \langle \mathcal{D}, \mathcal{M}, f, \mathcal{I}, \mathcal{U} \rangle$$

Where:

  • $\mathcal{D}$: the set of Dimensions
  • $\mathcal{M}$: the set of Measurement Methods
  • $f$: the Aggregation Function
  • $\mathcal{I}$: the Interpretation Framework
  • $\mathcal{U}$: the Uncertainty Model

The General Flow of Calculation

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  The General Flow of Indicator Calculation                       │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 1: Determine the object of assessment                      │
│  └─ Specify the subject, action, system, or situation           │ 
│     being assessed                                              │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 2: Collect data                                            │
│  └─ Collect the necessary information according to the          │ 
│     data requirements of each dimension                         │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 3: Score the dimensions                                    │
│  └─ Score or measure each dimension                             │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 4: Aggregation computation                                 │
│  └─ Use the aggregation function to synthesize the dimension    │ 
│     scores into a composite indicator                           │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 5: Uncertainty quantification                              │
│  └─ Assess the uncertainty range of the result                  │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 6: Interpretation of results                               │
│  └─ Interpret the result according to the interpretation        │ 
│     framework                                                   │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 7: Recording and archiving                                 │
│  └─ Record the calculation process for auditing and revision    │ 
│                                                                 │ 
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

C.1.1.4 Types of Aggregation Functions

This treatise uses the following types of aggregation functions:

Type One: Weighted Arithmetic Mean

$$I = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \cdot D_i \quad \text{where} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i = 1$$

Applicable scenario: there is compensability among dimensions (a high score on one dimension can compensate for a low score on another)

Type Two: Weighted Geometric Mean

$$I = \prod_{i=1}^{n} D_i^{w_i} \quad \text{where} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i = 1$$

Applicable scenario: dimensions are partially complementary, but extremely low values produce significant penalties

Type Three: Minimum Function

$$I = \min_{i=1}^{n} D_i$$

Applicable scenario: there is no compensability among dimensions; limited by the weakest link

Type Four: Mixed Function

$$I = \alpha \cdot \text{Mean}(D_1, ..., D_n) + (1-\alpha) \cdot \min(D_1, ..., D_n)$$

Applicable scenario: combines average performance and the weakest link

Table C.1.1 Aggregation Functions Used by Each Indicator

IndicatorPrimary Aggregation FunctionAlternative FunctionReason for Selection

RFDDifference computationRatio computationMeasure spatial change
CRVWeighted arithmetic meanMixed functionCommitment dimensions are compensable
CDIWeighted geometric meanWeighted arithmetic meanCivilizational dimensions are partially complementary
MBCLMaximum function—Risk is determined by the highest term
CSIAMultidimensional vector—Preserve multidimensional information

C.1.2.4 Handling Missing Data

When data are incomplete, the following strategies may be adopted:

Strategy One: Downgraded Assessment

$$\text{If } D_i \text{ is unavailable, then } I = f(D_1, ..., D_{i-1}, D_{i+1}, ..., D_n) \text{ with a downgrade annotation}$$

Strategy Two: Conservative Estimation

$$\text{If } D_i \text{ is unavailable, then } D_i = D_i^{\text{conservative}} \text{ (adopt the most conservative estimate)}$$

Strategy Three: Range Estimation

$$\text{If } D_i \text{ is unavailable, then } D_i \in [D_i^{\min}, D_i^{\max}] \text{, and report the range of results}$$

Strategy Four: Suspension of Assessment

$$\text{If a critical dimension is unavailable, then } I = \text{N/A} \text{ (no assessment)}$$

C.1.3 Uncertainty Handling

C.1.3.1 Sources of Uncertainty

Uncertainty in indicator calculation comes from multiple sources:

Table C.1.5 Classification of Sources of Uncertainty

Type of UncertaintyDefinitionExample of SourceTractability
Measurement uncertaintyError introduced by the measurement processInstrument precision, observer biasQuantifiable
Model uncertaintyThe gap between the model and realitySimplifying assumptions, omitted variablesPartially quantifiable
Parameter uncertaintyUncertainty in parameter valuesWeight selection, threshold settingAddressable via sensitivity analysis
Deep uncertaintyProbability distributions are unknowableFuture scenarios, black-swan eventsDifficult to quantify

C.1.3.2 Uncertainty Quantification Methods

Method One: Confidence Intervals

$$I \in [I_{\text{lower}}, I_{\text{upper}}] \text{ with confidence level } \alpha$$

Applicable to: measurement uncertainty, parameter uncertainty

Method Two: Sensitivity Analysis

$$\frac{\partial I}{\partial p} \text{ for key parameters } p$$

Applicable to: parameter uncertainty, model uncertainty

Method Three: Scenario Analysis

$$I_{\text{optimistic}}, I_{\text{baseline}}, I_{\text{pessimistic}}$$

Applicable to: deep uncertainty

Method Four: Fuzzy Set Methods

$$\mu_I(x) \text{ (membership function for indicator value)}$$

Applicable to: situations with fuzzy conceptual boundaries

C.1.3.3 Uncertainty Propagation

When the uncertainties of multiple dimensions need to be propagated to the composite indicator:

Definition C.1.4 (Uncertainty Propagation)

Let the uncertainty of each dimension be $\sigma_{D_i}$; the uncertainty of the composite indicator is:

$$\sigma_I = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial D_i}\right)^2 \sigma_{D_i}^2}$$

For a weighted-mean aggregation function:

$$\sigma_I = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i^2 \sigma_{D_i}^2}$$

C.1.3.4 Uncertainty Reporting Format

│                                                                 │

│                                                                 │ 
│  Breakdown of uncertainty sources:                              │ 
│  - Measurement uncertainty: accounts for Y₁%                    │ 
│  - Model uncertainty: accounts for Y₂%                          │ 
│  - Parameter uncertainty: accounts for Y₃%                      │ 
│  - Deep uncertainty: cannot be quantified                       │ 
│                                                                 │

C.1.4 Result Interpretation

C.1.4.1 General Principles of Interpretation

Principle One: Context Dependence

The meaning of an indicator value depends on the specific context; there is no "absolutely good" or "absolutely bad" that is detached from context.

$$\text{Meaning}(I) = f(I, \text{Context})$$

Principle Two: Priority of Relative Comparison

Indicators are better suited to relative comparison than to absolute judgment.

$$\text{Comparison}(I_1, I_2) > \text{AbsoluteJudgment}(I)$$

Principle Three: Multidimensional Synthesis

A single indicator should not serve as the sole basis for decision; multiple indicators should be synthesized.

$$\text{Decision} = g(\text{UCS}, \text{RFD}, \text{CRV}, \text{CDI}, \text{MBCL}, \text{CSIA}, \text{Context})$$

Principle Four: Incorporation of Uncertainty

The range of uncertainty must be considered in interpretation.

$$\text{Interpretation}(I) = h(I, \sigma_I, \text{Context})$$

C.1.4.2 Interpretation Framework

Definition C.1.5 (Interpretation Framework)

$$\text{InterpretationFramework} \triangleq \langle \text{Thresholds}, \text{Categories}, \text{Implications}, \text{Caveats} \rangle$$

Table C.1.7 Summary of the Interpretation Framework for Each Indicator

IndicatorValue RangeGeneral InterpretationKey Threshold
UCS[0, 1]Degree of consciousness0.3 (reference threshold for subjecthood)
RFD(-∞, +∞)Change in the possibility space0 (baseline of no change)
CRV[0, 1]Credibility of commitment0.5 (reference threshold for credibility)
CDI[0, 1]Level of civilizational developmentMultiple thresholds
MBCL{1, 2, 3, 4}Risk levelLevel boundaries
CSIAMultidimensional vectorMultidimensional impactThresholds for each dimension

C.1.4.3 Common Pitfalls in Interpretation

Pitfall One: Excessive Precision

Incorrect: UCS = 0.5723 indicates that the subject has a precise 57.23% degree of consciousness Correct: UCS ≈ 0.57 (95% CI: [0.45, 0.69]) indicates that the subject's degree of consciousness is at a medium level, but there is substantial uncertainty

Pitfall Two: Single-Indicator Determinism

Incorrect: RFD < 0, therefore this action should be prohibited Correct: RFD < 0 is a signal that warrants attention, but the final judgment requires comprehensively considering other indicators such as CRV and CSIA, as well as the specific contextual factors

Pitfall Three: Ignoring Context

Incorrect: CDI = 0.8 indicates that this is a highly developed civilization Correct: CDI = 0.8 needs to be interpreted within the context of a specific assessment framework and comparison object; different assessment frameworks may yield different conclusions

Pitfall Four: Causal Inference

Incorrect: High UCS causes high CDI Correct: There may be a correlation between UCS and CDI, but causation requires further argumentation
