F.1.3 Proof Format

F.1.3.1 Proof Structure

Rule F.1.2 (Proof Format)

This appendix adopts the following standardized proof format:

┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Proof Format Template                                           │ 
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │  
│  [Theorem/Lemma/Proposition Number]                              │ 
│  [Natural-language statement of the theorem/lemma/proposition]   │ 
│                                                                 │  
│  [Formal Statement]                                              │ 
│  [Precise statement using the formal language]                   │ 
│                                                                 │  
│  [Proof]                                                         │ 
│  [Numbered proof steps]                                          │ 
│  1. [Premise or already-proved proposition] ....... [Basis]      │ 
│  2. [Derivation step] .............................. [Rule]       │
│  3. ...                                                          │ 
│  n. [Conclusion] .................................... Q.E.D.      │
│                                                                 │  
│  [Boundary Conditions]                                           │ 
│  [Conditions and assumptions under which the proof holds]        │ 
│                                                                 │  
│  [Relation to the New Three Views]                               │ 
│  [Explanation of this proof's relation to the New Three Views]   │ 
│                                                                 │  
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

F.1.3.2 Inference Rules

Table F.1.5 Inference Rules Used

Rule NameSymbolForm
Modus ponensMP$\phi, \phi \rightarrow \psi \vdash \psi$
Universal instantiationUI$\forall x.\phi(x) \vdash \phi(a)$
Existential generalizationEG$\phi(a) \vdash \exists x.\phi(x)$
Hypothetical syllogismHS$\phi \rightarrow \psi, \psi \rightarrow \chi \vdash \phi \rightarrow \chi$
Conjunction introduction$\land$I$\phi, \psi \vdash \phi \land \psi$
Conjunction elimination$\land$E$\phi \land \psi \vdash \phi$
Disjunction introduction$\lor$I$\phi \vdash \phi \lor \psi$
Reductio ad absurdumRAA$\phi \rightarrow \bot \vdash \neg\phi$

F.1.4 Statement of the Limitations of Formalization

F.1.4.1 General Limitations

Rule F.1.3 (Limitations of Formalization)

The formalization work of this appendix has the following limitations:

Limitation TypeDescriptionImpact
IncompletenessNot all intuitions can be formalizedSome arguments retain a non-formal form
AbstractnessFormalization is distant from concrete experienceRequires interpretive bridging
Language dependenceDepends on a specific symbol systemTranslation may introduce ambiguity
Axiom choiceThe choice of axioms is controversialThe axioms themselves require justification

F.1.4.2 Specific Statement

Statement F.1.1 (Statement of the Limitations of Formalization)

  1. Non-finality: All formal statements may be revised in future versions
  2. Non-exclusivity: Other formalization schemes are not excluded
  3. Instrumentality: Formalization is a tool, not an end
  4. Criticizability: Criticism of the formalization scheme is welcome

F.2 Formalization of the New Three Views

F.2.1 Formalized Statement of the New Cosmology

F.2.1.1 Formalization of NC-1

Proposition NC-1 (Relation Precedes Entity)

At the ontological level, relations have priority over entities. The properties of an entity are determined by its relational network.

Formal Statement

Axiom NC-1.1 (Relational Ontology)

$$\forall x \in \mathcal{E}.\exists R \subseteq \mathcal{R}.\text{Properties}(x) = f(R)$$

Read as: For any entity $x$, there exists a set of relations $R$ such that the properties of $x$ are a function of $R$.

Axiom NC-1.2 (Priority of Relations)

$$\forall x, y \in \mathcal{E}.[\text{Distinguishable}(x, y) \leftrightarrow \exists r \in \mathcal{R}.(r(x) \neq r(y))]$$

Read as: Any two entities are distinguishable if and only if there exists some relation under which they behave differently.

Axiom NC-1.3 (Constitutivity of Relations)

$$\forall x \in \mathcal{E}.[\text{Exists}(x) \rightarrow \exists y \in \mathcal{E}.\text{Rel}(x, y)]$$

Read as: If $x$ exists, then there must exist some $y$ that has a relation to $x$.

Definition NC-1.1 (Relational Network)

$$\mathcal{N}(x) \triangleq \{(y, r) : y \in \mathcal{E}, r \in \mathcal{R}, r(x, y)\}$$

The relational network of entity $x$ is the set of all entity-relation pairs related to $x$.

Lemma NC-1.1 (Relational Determination of Properties)

$$\forall x \in \mathcal{E}.\forall p \in \text{Properties}(x).\exists \mathcal{N}(x).p = g(\mathcal{N}(x))$$

Proof

  1. Let x ∈ ℰ, p ∈ Properties(x) ........................ Assumption
  2. By Axiom NC-1.1, Properties(x) = f(R) ................. NC-1.1
  3. Hence p ∈ f(R) ....................................... 2, set theory
  4. R ⊆ the relational part of 𝒩(x) ...................... Definition NC-1.1
  5. Hence there exists g such that p = g(𝒩(x)) ........... 3, 4, function construction

Q.E.D.

Boundary Conditions

  1. This formalization does not presuppose any particular type of relation (causal, spatial, temporal, etc.)
  2. "Priority" means ontological priority, not temporal priority
  3. Compatible with the relational interpretation of quantum field theory

Relation to the New Three Views

NC-1 provides the ontological basis for the New View of Life (NL) and the New View of Cognition (NK): both life and cognition are relational processes.

F.2.1.2 Formalization of NC-2

Proposition NC-2 (Process Precedes State)

At the ontological level, processes have priority over states. A state is an instantaneous slice of a process.

Formal Statement

Axiom NC-2.1 (Process Ontology)

$$\forall s \in \mathcal{S}_{tate}.\exists p \in \mathcal{P}.\exists t \in \mathcal{T}.s = \text{Snapshot}(p, t)$$

Read as: Any state $s$ is a snapshot of some process $p$ at some moment $t$.

Axiom NC-2.2 (Persistence of Processes)

$$\forall p \in \mathcal{P}.\exists I \subseteq \mathcal{T}.\forall t \in I.\text{Exists}(p, t)$$

Read as: Any process $p$ exists over some time interval $I$.

Axiom NC-2.3 (Derivedness of States)

$$\forall x \in \mathcal{E}.\forall t_1, t_2 \in \mathcal{T}.[t_1 \neq t_2 \rightarrow \text{State}(x, t_1) \neq \text{State}(x, t_2)]$$

Read as: At different moments, the states of an entity are generally different (the weak form of the Heraclitean principle).

Definition NC-2.1 (Process)

$$p \in \mathcal{P} \triangleq \langle \text{Trajectory}, \text{Duration}, \text{Dynamics} \rangle$$

A process consists of a trajectory (a sequence of states), a duration, and dynamical rules.

Lemma NC-2.1 (States Are Subordinate to Processes)

$$\forall s \in \mathcal{S}_{tate}.\neg\text{Independent}(s)$$

Proof

  1. Let s ∈ 𝒮_tate ..................................... Assumption
  2. By Axiom NC-2.1, ∃p, t. s = Snapshot(p, t) ........... NC-2.1
  3. Assume Independent(s) ............................... For reductio
  4. Then s does not depend on any process ............... 3, definition
  5. But by 2, s depends on p ............................. Contradiction
  6. Hence ¬Independent(s) ................................ RAA, 3-5

Q.E.D.

Relation to Thermodynamics

$$\text{Entropy}(p) = \int_I \frac{dS}{dt}dt$$

The entropy change of a process is a time integral; the entropy of a state is an instantaneous value.

Boundary Conditions

  1. The use of state descriptions in specific contexts is not excluded
  2. "Priority" means explanatory priority
  3. Compatible with the tradition of process philosophy (Whitehead)

F.2.1.3 Formalization of NC-3

Proposition NC-3 (Participation Precedes Spectatorship)

The cognitive subject is not an external observer of the universe but a participant. The act of cognition itself changes the system being cognized.

Formal Statement

Axiom NC-3.1 (Participatoriness of Cognition)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.\forall x \in \mathcal{E}.[\text{Observe}(a, x) \rightarrow \text{Interact}(a, x)]$$

Read as: If agent $a$ observes $x$, then $a$ interacts with $x$.

Axiom NC-3.2 (Physicality of Observation)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.\forall x \in \mathcal{E}.[\text{Observe}(a, x) \rightarrow \Delta\text{State}(x) \neq 0]$$

Read as: The act of observation causes a change in the state of the observed object (at least at the microscopic level).

Axiom NC-3.3 (Immanence of the Subject)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.a \in \mathcal{U}_{niverse}$$

Read as: All subjects are constituents of the universe; no "external" observer exists.

Definition NC-3.1 (Participatory Cognition)

$$\text{ParticipatoryKnowledge}(a, \phi) \triangleq \text{Know}(a, \phi) \land \text{Contributed}(a, \text{Truth}(\phi))$$

Participatory knowledge means that the knower contributes to the truth that is known.

Lemma NC-3.1 (The Impossibility of Spectatorship)

$$\neg\exists a \in \mathcal{A}.\forall x \in \mathcal{E}.[\text{Observe}(a, x) \land \neg\text{Interact}(a, x)]$$

Proof

  1. Assume there exists a such that for all x, Observe(a, x) ∧ ¬Interact(a, x) .. For reductio
  2. Take any x₀ ∈ ℰ ..................................... Choice
  3. Observe(a, x₀) ∧ ¬Interact(a, x₀) .................. 1, UI
  4. By Axiom NC-3.1, Observe(a, x₀) → Interact(a, x₀) ..... NC-3.1
  5. Observe(a, x₀) ..................................... 3, ∧E
  6. Interact(a, x₀) .................................... 4, 5, MP
  7. But ¬Interact(a, x₀) ................................ 3, ∧E
  8. Contradiction ....................................... 6, 7
  9. Hence the assumption fails ......................... RAA

Q.E.D.

Boundary Conditions

  1. Does not imply that objective knowledge is impossible, but re-understands "objectivity"
  2. Related to, but not identical with, the measurement problem in quantum mechanics
  3. Does not lead to extreme subjectivism

F.2.2 Formalized Statement of the New View of Life

F.2.2.1 Formalization of NL-1

Proposition NL-1 (Cross-substrate Nature of Life)

Life is not confined to a particular material substrate (such as carbon-based organic matter); its essential features are information organization and negentropy maintenance.

Formal Statement

Axiom NL-1.1 (Substrate Independence)

$$\forall x.[\text{Life}(x) \leftrightarrow \text{InfoOrganization}(x) \land \text{NegentropyMaintenance}(x)]$$

Read as: $x$ is alive if and only if $x$ has information organization and the capacity for negentropy maintenance.

Axiom NL-1.2 (Substrate Diversity)

$$\exists x, y.[\text{Life}(x) \land \text{Life}(y) \land \text{Substrate}(x) \neq \text{Substrate}(y)]$$

Read as: There exist life forms with different substrates.

Axiom NL-1.3 (Functional Equivalence)

$$\forall x, y.[\text{FunctionalEquivalent}(x, y) \rightarrow (\text{Life}(x) \leftrightarrow \text{Life}(y))]$$

Read as: Functionally equivalent systems have the same status with respect to life.

Definition NL-1.1 (Information Organization)

$$\text{InfoOrganization}(x) \triangleq \exists I.\text{Information}(I) \land \text{Embodies}(x, I) \land \text{SelfMaintaining}(I)$$

Definition NL-1.2 (Negentropy Maintenance)

$$\text{NegentropyMaintenance}(x) \triangleq \frac{dS(x)}{dt} < \frac{dS_{eq}}{dt}$$

The system $x$ maintains an entropy production rate lower than that of the thermal equilibrium state.

Lemma NL-1.1 (The Non-material Essence of Life)

$$\forall x.[\text{Life}(x) \rightarrow \neg\text{EssentiallyMaterial}(x)]$$

Proof

  1. Let Life(x) ......................................... Assumption
  2. By Axiom NL-1.1, InfoOrganization(x) ∧ NegentropyMaintenance(x) .. NL-1.1
  3. InfoOrganization(x) is a functional property, not a material property ......... Definition NL-1.1
  4. NegentropyMaintenance(x) is a dynamical property, not a material property .. Definition NL-1.2
  5. The essence of life is determined by functional and dynamical properties .................. 3, 4
  6. Hence ¬EssentiallyMaterial(x) ......................... 5

Q.E.D.

Boundary Conditions

  1. Does not deny the carbon-based character of currently known life
  2. Provides a conceptual framework for identifying non-carbon-based life
  3. Compatible with artificial life research

F.2.2.2 Formalization of NL-2

Proposition NL-2 (Life as Negentropy Organization)

The essence of life is the process of maintaining and increasing local complexity by acquiring and utilizing negentropy flows.

Formal Statement

Axiom NL-2.1 (Negentropy Requirement)

$$\forall x.[\text{Life}(x) \rightarrow \exists \mathcal{S}_{ext}.\text{Acquires}(x, \mathcal{S}_{ext})]$$

Read as: Any living thing acquires negentropy from outside.

Axiom NL-2.2 (Entropy Export)

$$\forall x.[\text{Life}(x) \rightarrow \exists \mathcal{S}_{waste}.\text{Exports}(x, \mathcal{S}_{waste})]$$

Read as: Any living thing exports entropy to the outside.

Axiom NL-2.3 (Negentropy Balance)

$$\forall x.[\text{Life}(x) \rightarrow \mathcal{S}_{ext} > \mathcal{S}_{waste,internal}]$$

Read as: The negentropy acquired by life is greater than the entropy produced internally.

Definition NL-2.1 (Negentropy Flow)

$$\text{NegentropyFlow}(x) \triangleq \frac{d\mathcal{S}_{ext}}{dt} - \frac{dS_{internal}}{dt}$$

Negentropy flow is the external negentropy acquisition rate minus the internal entropy production rate.

Definition NL-2.2 (Conditions for the Persistence of Life)

$$\text{Viable}(x, t) \triangleq \text{NegentropyFlow}(x) > 0 \text{ at } t$$

Lemma NL-2.1 (Thermodynamic Constraints on Life)

$$\forall x.[\text{Life}(x) \rightarrow \exists E_{environment}.\text{NegentropySource}(E_{environment})]$$

Proof

  1. Let Life(x) ......................................... Assumption
  2. By Axiom NL-2.1, ∃𝒮_ext. Acquires(x, 𝒮_ext) ........... NL-2.1
  3. 𝒮_ext must have a source ........................... Second law of thermodynamics
  4. Let this source be E_environment ................... Naming
  5. NegentropySource(E_environment) ..................... Definition

Q.E.D.

Relation to Physics

$$\frac{dS_{universe}}{dt} \geq 0, \text{ but } \frac{dS_{life}}{dt} < 0 \text{ locally}$$

Life locally violates the tendency toward entropy increase, but at the cost of a greater environmental entropy increase.

F.2.2.3 Formalization of NL-3

Proposition NL-3 (The Continuum of Consciousness and Subjecthood)

Consciousness and subjecthood are not binary properties but degree-based properties, forming a continuum from simple to complex.

Formal Statement

Axiom NL-3.1 (Degree-based Nature of Consciousness)

$$\text{Conscious}: \mathcal{E} \rightarrow [0, 1]$$

Read as: Consciousness is a function from entities to the interval $[0,1]$, not a binary predicate.

Axiom NL-3.2 (Degree-based Nature of Subjecthood)

$$\text{Agenthood}: \mathcal{E} \rightarrow [0, 1]$$

Read as: Subjecthood is degree-based.

Axiom NL-3.3 (Consciousness-Subjecthood Association)

$$\forall x.\text{Agenthood}(x) \leq f(\text{Conscious}(x))$$

Read as: Subjecthood is constrained by the level of consciousness.

Definition NL-3.1 (Universal Consciousness Scale)

$$\text{UCS}(x) \triangleq \text{Conscious}(x)$$

UCS directly measures the degree of consciousness.

Definition NL-3.2 (Consciousness Threshold)

$$\theta_c \triangleq \inf\{u : \text{MoralPatienthood}(x) \text{ if } \text{UCS}(x) \geq u\}$$

The consciousness threshold $\theta_c$ is the minimum level of consciousness required for eligibility for moral consideration.

Lemma NL-3.1 (The Non-binary Nature of Consciousness)

$$\neg\forall x.[\text{Conscious}(x) \in \{0, 1\}]$$

Proof

  1. Consider the neural correlates of consciousness ................. Empirical premise
  2. Neural complexity is a continuous variable ......................... Neuroscience
  3. Consciousness correlates with neural complexity ................... Theories such as IIT
  4. Hence consciousness should be a continuous variable ................. 2, 3
  5. That is, there exists x such that Conscious(x) ∈ (0, 1) ............ 4
  6. Hence ¬∀x.[Conscious(x) ∈ {0, 1}] ................................... 5

Q.E.D.

Boundary Conditions

  1. Does not presuppose any particular theory of consciousness (IIT, GWT, etc.)
  2. The threshold $\theta_c$ requires empirical calibration
  3. Acknowledges the difficulty of measuring consciousness

F.2.3 Formalized Statement of the New View of Cognition

F.2.3.1 Formalization of NK-1

Proposition NK-1 (Participatoriness of Cognition)

Cognition is not a passive mirroring of an external world but an interactive process between the subject and the environment; the knower participates in constructing the world that is known.

Formal Statement

Axiom NK-1.1 (Interactivity of Cognition)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.\forall \phi.[\text{Know}(a, \phi) \rightarrow \text{Interacted}(a, \text{ReferentOf}(\phi))]$$

Read as: If $a$ knows $\phi$, then $a$ has interacted with the referent of $\phi$.

Axiom NK-1.2 (Constructivity of Cognition)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.\forall \phi.[\text{Know}(a, \phi) \rightarrow \text{Contributed}(a, \text{Representation}(\phi))]$$

Read as: $a$ contributes to the representation of $\phi$.

Definition NK-1.1 (Participatory Knowledge)

$$\text{Know}_{part}(a, \phi) \triangleq \text{Know}(a, \phi) \land \text{Interacted}(a, \text{ReferentOf}(\phi)) \land \text{Contributed}(a, \text{Representation}(\phi))$$

Lemma NK-1.1 (The Non-mirror Nature of Knowledge)

$$\neg\forall a, \phi.[\text{Know}(a, \phi) \rightarrow \text{Represents}(\phi, \text{ReferentOf}(\phi), \text{exactly})]$$

Proof

  1. By Axiom NK-1.2, knowledge involves the knower's contribution ................ NK-1.2
  2. The knower's contribution means the representation is not a pure mirror .......... Definition
  3. Hence knowledge is not an exact mirror of the object ........................ 2

Q.E.D.

F.2.3.2 Formalization of NK-2

Proposition NK-2 (Sociality of Knowledge)

Knowledge is essentially social; individual knowledge depends on the practices and norms of an epistemic community.

Formal Statement

Axiom NK-2.1 (Social Dependence of Knowledge)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.\forall \phi.[\text{Know}(a, \phi) \rightarrow \exists C.\text{Community}(C) \land a \in C \land \text{Enables}(C, \text{Know}(a, \phi))]$$

Read as: Individual knowledge presupposes an epistemic community.

Axiom NK-2.2 (Normativity of Knowledge)

$$\forall \phi.[\text{Knowledge}(\phi) \rightarrow \text{NormativelyConstrained}(\phi)]$$

Read as: Knowledge is constrained by norms.

Definition NK-2.1 (Epistemic Community)

$$\text{Community}(C) \triangleq \exists \text{Practices}, \text{Norms}.\text{Shares}(C, \text{Practices}) \land \text{Shares}(C, \text{Norms})$$

F.2.3.3 Formalization of NK-3

Proposition NK-3 (Recognition of Deep Uncertainty)

There exists deep uncertainty—uncertainty that cannot be reduced to a probability distribution—requiring new epistemological and decision-making frameworks.

Formal Statement

Definition NK-3.1 (Deep Uncertainty)

$$\text{DeepUncertainty}(\phi) \triangleq \neg\exists P.\text{ProbabilityDistribution}(P) \land \text{Represents}(P, \text{Uncertainty}(\phi))$$

Read as: $\phi$ is deeply uncertain if and only if there exists no probability distribution that can represent that uncertainty.

Axiom NK-3.1 (Existence of Deep Uncertainty)

$$\exists \phi.\text{DeepUncertainty}(\phi)$$

Read as: Deep uncertainty exists.

Axiom NK-3.2 (Irreducibility of Deep Uncertainty)

$$\forall \phi.[\text{DeepUncertainty}(\phi) \rightarrow \neg\exists t > t_0.\neg\text{DeepUncertainty}(\phi, t)]$$

Read as: Some deep uncertainties cannot be eliminated over time.

Lemma NK-3.1 (The Limits of Probabilistic Methods)

$$\exists \phi.[\text{DeepUncertainty}(\phi) \land \neg\text{ApplicableExpectedUtility}(\phi)]$$

Proof

  1. By Definition NK-3.1, deep uncertainty has no corresponding probability distribution ............. NK-3.1
  2. Expected utility requires a probability distribution ............................... Expected utility theory
  3. Hence for deep uncertainty, expected utility is not applicable ..................... 1, 2

Q.E.D.

F.2.3.4 Formalization of NK-4

Proposition NK-4 (Deliberativeness of Norms)

Norms are not given in advance but constructed through intersubjective deliberation and require continuous revision.

Formal Statement

Axiom NK-4.1 (Deliberative Construction of Norms)

$$\forall n \in \text{Norms}.\exists C, P.\text{Community}(C) \land \text{NegotiationProcess}(P) \land \text{ResultOf}(n, P)$$

Read as: Any norm is the result of some deliberation process.

Axiom NK-4.2 (Revisability of Norms)

$$\forall n \in \text{Norms}.\Diamond\text{Revised}(n)$$

Read as: Any norm may be revised.

Definition NK-4.1 (Norm Deliberation)

$$\text{NegotiationProcess}(P) \triangleq \exists A \subseteq \mathcal{A}.\forall a \in A.\text{Participates}(a, P) \land \text{VoiceHeard}(a, P)$$

F.3 Formal Proofs of the Bridge Principles

F.3.1 Proof of the Persistence Rationality Principle

Bridge Principle BP-1 (Persistence Rationality Principle)

Maintaining one's own persistence and capacity for development is a basic disposition of rational agents, from which normative requirements can be derived.

F.3.1.1 Formal Statement

Axiom BP-1.1 (Disposition to Persist)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.[\text{Rational}(a) \rightarrow \text{Tends}(a, \text{SelfPersistence})]$$

Read as: Rational agents tend toward self-persistence.

Axiom BP-1.2 (Capacity Maintenance)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.[\text{Rational}(a) \rightarrow \text{Tends}(a, \text{CapacityMaintenance})]$$

Read as: Rational agents tend to maintain their own capacities.

Axiom BP-1.3 (Conditionality of Persistence)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.[\text{SelfPersistence}(a) \rightarrow \text{NegentropyAccess}(a)]$$

Read as: Self-persistence requires the acquisition of negentropy.

F.3.1.2 Core Theorem

Theorem BP-1.1 (From the Disposition to Persist to Normativity)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.[\text{Rational}(a) \rightarrow O(\text{MaintainNegentropyAccess}(a))]$$

Read as: Rational agents are obligated to maintain the capacity to acquire negentropy.

Proof

  1. Let Rational(a) ..................................... Assumption
  2. By Axiom BP-1.1, Tends(a, SelfPersistence) ............ BP-1.1, MP
  3. By Axiom BP-1.3, SelfPersistence(a) → NegentropyAccess(a) .. BP-1.3
  4. If a tends toward X, and X requires Y, then a tends toward Y ......... Principle of instrumental rationality
  5. Tends(a, NegentropyAccess) .......................... 2, 3, 4
  6. Tending toward X means having reason to realize X ....................... Desire-belief model
  7. Having reason to realize X means O(realize X) ..................... Normativity of reasons
  8. O(MaintainNegentropyAccess(a)) ...................... 5, 6, 7

Q.E.D.

Boundary Conditions

  1. "Rational" is understood as instrumental rationality
  2. Does not presuppose any particular form of rational agent
  3. The obligation is conditional (given the goal of persistence)

F.3.1.3 Corollary

Corollary BP-1.1 (Normative Basis for Environmental Protection)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.[\text{Rational}(a) \land \text{NegentropySource}(E) \rightarrow O(\text{Preserve}(a, E))]$$

Proof

  1. By Theorem BP-1.1, O(MaintainNegentropyAccess(a)) ......... Theorem BP-1.1
  2. NegentropySource(E) ................................. Assumption
  3. MaintainNegentropyAccess(a) requires Preserve(E) ........ Causal dependence
  4. O(X) ∧ (X requires Y) → O(Y) ........................... Transmission of obligation
  5. O(Preserve(a, E)) ................................... 1, 3, 4

Q.E.D.

F.3.2 Proof of the Epistemic Humility Principle

Bridge Principle BP-2 (Epistemic Humility Principle)

Given the existence of deep uncertainty, rational agents should maintain epistemic humility and adopt conservative decision strategies.

F.3.2.1 Formal Statement

Axiom BP-2.1 (Acknowledgement of Uncertainty)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.[\text{Rational}(a) \rightarrow \text{Acknowledges}(a, \text{DeepUncertainty})]$$

Read as: Rational agents acknowledge deep uncertainty.

Axiom BP-2.2 (Cognitive Limitations)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.\exists \phi.\neg\Box_K\text{Know}(a, \phi) \land \neg\Box_K\neg\text{Know}(a, \phi)$$

Read as: There exist propositions that an agent neither definitely knows nor definitely does not know.

F.3.2.2 Core Theorem

Theorem BP-2.1 (Humility Principle)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.[\text{Rational}(a) \land \text{DeepUncertainty}(\phi) \rightarrow O(\text{EpistemicHumility}(a, \phi))]$$

Read as: In the face of deep uncertainty, rational agents are obligated to maintain epistemic humility.

Proof

  1. Let Rational(a) ∧ DeepUncertainty(φ) ................. Assumption
  2. By Definition NK-3.1, no probability distribution represents Uncertainty(φ) ........ NK-3.1
  3. Hence standard decision methods are not applicable ........................... Lemma NK-3.1
  4. When methods are not applicable, overconfidence leads to error ................... Epistemic risk
  5. Rationality requires avoiding avoidable errors ............................... Norm of rationality
  6. Hence rationality requires maintaining humility ................................. 4, 5
  7. O(EpistemicHumility(a, φ)) .......................... 6, obligatorification

Q.E.D.

F.3.2.3 Corollary

Corollary BP-2.1 (Reversibility Preference)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.[\text{Rational}(a) \land \text{DeepUncertainty}(\phi) \rightarrow \text{Prefer}(a, \text{ReversibleAction}, \text{IrreversibleAction})]$$

Proof

  1. By Theorem BP-2.1, O(EpistemicHumility(a, φ)) ............ Theorem BP-2.1
  2. Epistemic humility means acknowledging that one may err ......... Definition
  3. If one may err, reversible actions allow correcting errors ..................... Value of reversibility
  4. Irreversible actions cannot be corrected ................................. Definition
  5. Rationality prefers correctable options ............................... 3, 4, rationality
  6. Prefer(a, ReversibleAction, IrreversibleAction) ...... 5

Q.E.D.

F.3.3 Proof of the Intersubjectivity Principle

Bridge Principle BP-3 (Intersubjectivity Principle)

The legitimacy of a norm derives from intersubjective recognition, not external imposition.

F.3.3.1 Formal Statement

Axiom BP-3.1 (Intersubjective Basis of Norms)

$$\forall n \in \text{Norms}.[\text{Legitimate}(n) \leftrightarrow \exists C.\text{Community}(C) \land \text{Accepted}(n, C)]$$

Read as: A norm is legitimate if and only if it is accepted by a community.

Axiom BP-3.2 (Deliberativeness of Acceptance)

$$\forall n, C.[\text{Accepted}(n, C) \rightarrow \exists P.\text{NegotiationProcess}(P) \land \text{ResultOf}(n, P)]$$

Read as: Acceptance presupposes a deliberation process.

F.3.3.2 Core Theorem

Theorem BP-3.1 (Conditions for Norm Legitimacy)

$$\forall n \in \text{Norms}.[\text{Legitimate}(n) \rightarrow \forall a \in C.\text{CouldHaveVoice}(a, n)]$$

Read as: A legitimate norm requires that all relevant agents have an opportunity to be heard.

Proof

  1. Let Legitimate(n) .................................... Assumption
  2. By Axiom BP-3.1, ∃C. Accepted(n, C) .................... BP-3.1
  3. By Axiom BP-3.2, ∃P. NegotiationProcess(P) ∧ ResultOf(n, P) .. BP-3.2
  4. By Definition NK-4.1, ∀a ∈ A. Participates(a, P) ∧ VoiceHeard(a, P) .. NK-4.1
  5. A ⊆ C (the relevant participants are members of the community) .......... Assumption
  6. ∀a ∈ C. CouldHaveVoice(a, n) ........................ 4, 5

Q.E.D.

F.4 Formal Proofs of the Normative Principles

F.4.1 Derivational Proof of the Recursive Freedom Principle

Normative Principle RFP (Recursive Freedom Principle)

Any action should protect or expand the possibility space for choice and development of all agents (including future agents).

F.4.1.1 Formal Statement

Definition RFP.1 (Possibility Space)

$$\Omega(a, t) \triangleq \{\omega : \omega \text{ is a state that agent } a \text{ may reach at time } t\}$$

Definition RFP.2 (Recursive Freedom Degree)

$$\text{RFD}(a, t) \triangleq \log|\Omega(a, t)| - \log|\Omega_{min}|$$

After normalization:

$$\text{RFD}_{norm}(a, t) = \frac{\log|\Omega(a, t)| - \log|\Omega_{min}|}{\log|\Omega_{max}| - \log|\Omega_{min}|} \in [0, 1]$$

Axiom RFP.1 (Value of the Possibility Space)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.\text{Value}(\Omega(a)) > 0$$

Read as: The possibility space has intrinsic value.

Axiom RFP.2 (Recursiveness of Possibility)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.\forall t.[\Omega(a, t+1) \subseteq f(\Omega(a, t), \text{Actions}(t))]$$

Read as: Future possibilities depend on current possibilities and actions.

F.4.1.2 Core Theorem

Theorem RFP.1 (Recursive Freedom Principle)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.\forall \alpha \in \text{Actions}.O(\Delta\Omega(\alpha) \geq 0)$$

Read as: For any action $\alpha$, there is an obligation that the possibility space not decrease.

Proof

  1. By Axiom RFP.1, Value(Ω(a)) > 0 ....................... RFP.1
  2. By Axiom RFP.2, Ω(a, t+1) depends on Actions(t) ........... RFP.2
  3. If α makes ΔΩ(α) < 0, then it diminishes something of value ............. 1, definition
  4. By Theorem BP-1.1, rational agents should maintain the capacity to persist .............. BP-1.1
  5. The capacity to persist depends on the possibility space ........................... Conceptual analysis
  6. Hence rational agents should maintain the possibility space ......................... 4, 5
  7. But the possibility spaces of free agents are mutually related ..................... NC-1
  8. Hence the possibility space of all agents should be maintained ....................... 7, universalization
  9. O(ΔΩ(α) ≥ 0) ....................................... 6, 8, obligatorification

Q.E.D. F.4.1.3 Corollary

Corollary RFP.1 (Obligations Toward Future Agents)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}_{present}.\forall a' \in \mathcal{A}_{future}.O(\neg\text{Foreclose}(a, \Omega(a')))$$

Read as: Present agents are obligated not to foreclose the possibility space of future agents.

Proof

  1. By Theorem RFP.1, O(ΔΩ(α) ≥ 0) .......................... Theorem RFP.1
  2. "All agents" includes future agents ............................. Temporal neutrality
  3. Foreclose(a, Ω(a')) means making ΔΩ(a') < 0 ............ Definition
  4. Hence O(¬Foreclose(a, Ω(a'))) .......................... 1, 2, 3

Q.E.D.

Corollary RFP.2 (Reversibility Requirement)

$$\forall \alpha.[\text{Irreversible}(\alpha) \land \text{ΔΩ}(\alpha) < 0 \rightarrow F(\alpha)]$$

Read as: Actions that irreversibly reduce the possibility space are forbidden.

F.4.2 Derivational Proof of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle

Normative Principle NRP (Negentropy Responsibility Principle)

Agents have a responsibility to maintain negentropy resources and complexity structures, not only for their own persistence but also for all agents that depend on these resources.

F.4.2.1 Formal Statement

Definition NRP.1 (Negentropy Responsibility)

$$\text{NegentropyResponsibility}(a) \triangleq O(\text{Maintain}(a, \mathcal{S}_{sources}))$$

Definition NRP.2 (Complexity Maintenance)

$$\text{ComplexityMaintenance}(a) \triangleq O(\neg\text{Degrade}(a, C_{ecosystem}))$$

Axiom NRP.1 (Negentropy Dependence)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.[\text{Exists}(a) \rightarrow \text{Depends}(a, \mathcal{S}_{sources})]$$

Read as: The existence of any agent depends on negentropy sources.

Axiom NRP.2 (Sharedness of Negentropy Sources)

$$\forall a, b \in \mathcal{A}.\exists \mathcal{S}.\text{Depends}(a, \mathcal{S}) \land \text{Depends}(b, \mathcal{S})$$

Read as: Agents share negentropy sources.

F.4.2.2 Core Theorem

Theorem NRP.1 (Negentropy Responsibility Principle)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.\text{NegentropyResponsibility}(a)$$

Read as: All agents have negentropy responsibility.

Proof

  1. By Axiom NRP.1, Exists(a) → Depends(a, 𝒮_sources) ...... NRP.1
  2. By Axiom NRP.2, 𝒮_sources is shared ..................... NRP.2
  3. By Theorem BP-1.1, O(MaintainNegentropyAccess(a)) ......... BP-1.1
  4. MaintainNegentropyAccess(a) requires Maintain(𝒮_sources) . 1, causal
  5. Because of sharedness, a's maintaining 𝒮 also benefits others .................... 2
  6. Hence there is an obligation to maintain shared negentropy sources ........... 3, 4, 5
  7. NegentropyResponsibility(a) .......................... 6, Definition NRP.1

Q.E.D.

F.4.2.3 Corollary

Corollary NRP.1 (Obligation of Anti-entropy Actions)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.O(\frac{d\mathcal{S}_{contribution}}{dt} \geq 0)$$

Read as: Agents are obligated to make a non-negative contribution to negentropy sources.

Corollary NRP.2 (Intergenerational Responsibility)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}_{present}.O(\text{Preserve}(a, \mathcal{S}_{sources}, t_{future}))$$

Read as: Present agents are obligated to preserve negentropy sources for the future.

F.4.3 Derivational Proof of the Reversibility Principle

Normative Principle REV (Reversibility Principle)

Under conditions of deep uncertainty, reversible actions should be preferred, and a higher standard of justification should be imposed on irreversible actions.

F.4.3.1 Formal Statement

Definition REV.1 (Reversibility)

$$\text{Reversible}(\alpha) \triangleq \exists \beta.\text{Action}(\beta) \land \text{Undoes}(\beta, \alpha)$$

Definition REV.2 (Irreversibility)

$$\text{Irreversible}(\alpha) \triangleq \neg\text{Reversible}(\alpha)$$

Definition REV.3 (Reversibility Preference)

$$\text{REV-Preference} \triangleq \forall \alpha, \beta.[\text{Outcome}(\alpha) \approx \text{Outcome}(\beta) \land \text{Reversible}(\alpha) \land \text{Irreversible}(\beta) \rightarrow \text{Prefer}(\alpha, \beta)]$$

Axiom REV.1 (Risk of Irreversibility)

$$\forall \alpha.[\text{Irreversible}(\alpha) \rightarrow \text{HigherRisk}(\alpha)]$$

Read as: Irreversible actions carry higher risk.

F.4.3.2 Core Theorem

Theorem REV.1 (Reversibility Principle)

$$\forall \alpha.[\text{Irreversible}(\alpha) \rightarrow \text{RequiresHigherJustification}(\alpha)]$$

Read as: Irreversible actions require a higher degree of justification.

Proof

  1. By Axiom REV.1, Irreversible(α) → HigherRisk(α) ........ REV.1
  2. By Theorem BP-2.1, in the face of deep uncertainty one should maintain humility ............. BP-2.1
  3. Humility means acknowledging that one may err ............................. Definition
  4. If an action is reversible, errors can be corrected ............................. Definition REV.1
  5. If an action is irreversible, errors cannot be corrected ......................... Definition REV.2
  6. Uncorrectable errors cause greater harm ......................... Risk assessment
  7. Greater harm requires stronger reasons ............................... Principle of proportionality
  8. RequiresHigherJustification(α) ...................... 1, 6, 7

Q.E.D.

F.4.3.3 Corollary

Corollary REV.1 (Procedural Requirements for Irreversible Actions)

$$\forall \alpha.[\text{Irreversible}(\alpha) \rightarrow O(\text{ExtendedDeliberation}(\alpha) \land \text{BroadConsultation}(\alpha))]$$

Corollary REV.2 (Reversibility Constraints on Technological Development)

$$\forall T.[\text{Technology}(T) \land \text{Irreversible}(\text{Deployment}(T)) \rightarrow O(\text{ReversibilityAnalysis}(T))]$$

F.5 Proof of Consistency of the Three Principles

F.5.1 Proof of Independence

Proposition F.5.1 (Independence of the Three Principles)

RFP, NRP, and REV are mutually independent; the third cannot be derived from any two of them.

F.5.1.1 Formal Statement

Definition of Independence

$$\text{Independent}(P_1, P_2, P_3) \triangleq \neg(P_1 \land P_2 \vdash P_3) \land \neg(P_1 \land P_3 \vdash P_2) \land \neg(P_2 \land P_3 \vdash P_1)$$

Theorem F.5.1 (Independence of the Three Principles)

$$\text{Independent}(\text{RFP}, \text{NRP}, \text{REV})$$

F.5.1.2 Proof

Proof strategy: Construct models in which two principles hold but the third does not.

Model M₁: RFP ∧ NRP ∧ ¬REV

Construction: A world in which:

  • The possibility space remains sufficient (RFP satisfied)
  • Negentropy sources are maintained (NRP satisfied)
  • But irreversible actions are treated on a par with reversible ones (REV not satisfied)

For example: A world without deep uncertainty, in which all consequences are predictable, so a reversibility preference is unnecessary.

Conclusion: RFP ∧ NRP ⊬ REV

Model M₂: RFP ∧ REV ∧ ¬NRP

Construction: A world in which:

  • The possibility space remains sufficient (RFP satisfied)
  • Reversible actions are preferred (REV satisfied)
  • But negentropy sources can be consumed without maintenance (NRP not satisfied)

For example: A world with unlimited negentropy sources, so a maintenance responsibility does not apply.

Conclusion: RFP ∧ REV ⊬ NRP

Model M₃: NRP ∧ REV ∧ ¬RFP

Construction: A world in which:

  • Negentropy sources are maintained (NRP satisfied)
  • Reversible actions are preferred (REV satisfied)
  • But the possibility space can be restricted (RFP not satisfied)

For example: A highly determinate world with an inherently limited space of choice, so the requirement to maintain the possibility space does not apply.

Conclusion: NRP ∧ REV ⊬ RFP

Overall Conclusion

$$\text{Independent}(\text{RFP}, \text{NRP}, \text{REV})$$ Q.E.D.

F.5.2 Proof of Compatibility

Proposition F.5.2 (Compatibility of the Three Principles)

RFP, NRP, and REV are logically consistent and can hold simultaneously.

F.5.2.1 Formal Statement

Definition of Compatibility

$$\text{Compatible}(P_1, P_2, P_3) \triangleq \neg(P_1 \land P_2 \land P_3 \vdash \bot)$$

Theorem F.5.2 (Compatibility of the Three Principles)

$$\text{Compatible}(\text{RFP}, \text{NRP}, \text{REV})$$

F.5.2.2 Proof

Proof strategy: Construct a model that satisfies all three principles.

Construction of Model M:

Let world W satisfy:

  1. There exists a sufficient possibility space Ω, |Ω| > Ω_min
  2. There exists a maintainable negentropy source 𝒮
  3. There exists deep uncertainty, giving the reversibility preference meaning

In W:

  • RFP satisfied: there exists a space of actions that does not shrink Ω
  • NRP satisfied: there exists a strategy for maintaining 𝒮
  • REV satisfied: one can choose between reversible and irreversible actions

Checking consistency:

  • RFP and NRP do not conflict: maintaining 𝒮 helps maintain Ω
  • RFP and REV do not conflict: the reversibility preference protects Ω
  • NRP and REV do not conflict: reversible actions generally protect 𝒮 better

Conclusion: ∃M. M ⊨ RFP ∧ NRP ∧ REV Hence: Compatible(RFP, NRP, REV) Q.E.D.

F.5.2.3 Analysis of Potential Conflicts

RFP-REV conflictMaintaining possibilities may require irreversible actionsProcedural constraints, higher justification

Conflict Resolution Principle

F.6 Formalization of the Indicator System

F.6.1 Formalized Definition of UCS

F.6.1.1 Basic Definition

Definition F.6.1 (UCS - Universal Consciousness Scale)

$$\text{UCS}: \mathcal{E} \rightarrow [0, 1]$$

$$\text{UCS}(x) \triangleq f(\Phi(x), G(x), A(x), M(x))$$

Where:

  • $\Phi(x)$: integrated information (the $\Phi$ of IIT)
  • $G(x)$: global workspace capacity
  • $A(x)$: subjecthood indicator
  • $M(x)$: metacognitive capacity

F.6.1.2 Axiomatic Constraints

Axiom UCS.1 (Boundary Conditions)

$$\forall x \in \mathcal{E}. 0 \leq \text{UCS}(x) \leq 1$$

Axiom UCS.2 (Monotonicity)

$$\forall x, y.[\Phi(x) > \Phi(y) \land G(x) \geq G(y) \land A(x) \geq A(y) \land M(x) \geq M(y) \rightarrow \text{UCS}(x) > \text{UCS}(y)]$$

Axiom UCS.3 (Continuity)

$$\forall \epsilon > 0.\exists \delta > 0.\forall x, y.[d(x, y) < \delta \rightarrow |\text{UCS}(x) - \text{UCS}(y)| < \epsilon]$$

F.6.1.3 Calculation Formula

Definition F.6.2 (UCS Calculation Formula)

$$\text{UCS}(x) = \alpha \cdot \hat{\Phi}(x) + \beta \cdot \hat{G}(x) + \gamma \cdot \hat{A}(x) + \delta \cdot \hat{M}(x)$$

where $\hat{X}$ denotes the normalized value, and $\alpha + \beta + \gamma + \delta = 1$.

Default Weights

WeightSymbolDefault ValueRationale
Integrated information weight$\alpha$0.35Centrality of IIT
Global workspace weight$\beta$0.25Importance of GWT
Subjecthood weight$\gamma$0.25Value of subjecthood
Metacognition weight$\delta$0.15Discriminative power of metacognition

F.6.2 Formalized Definition of RFD

F.6.2.1 Basic Definition

Definition F.6.3 (RFD - Recursive Freedom Degree)

$$\text{RFD}: \mathcal{E} \times \mathcal{T} \rightarrow [-1, 1]$$

$$\text{RFD}(x, t) \triangleq \frac{|\Omega(x, t+\Delta t)| - |\Omega(x, t)|}{|\Omega(x, t)|}$$

Normalized form:

$$\text{RFD}_{norm}(x, t) = \frac{\text{RFD}(x, t) - \text{RFD}_{min}}{\text{RFD}_{max} - \text{RFD}_{min}}$$

F.6.2.2 Axiomatic Constraints

Axiom RFD.1 (Boundary Conditions)

$$\forall x \in \mathcal{E}.\forall t \in \mathcal{T}. -1 \leq \text{RFD}(x, t) \leq 1$$

Axiom RFD.2 (Association with RFP)

$$\text{RFP-Compliance}(x, t) \leftrightarrow \text{RFD}(x, t) \geq 0$$

Axiom RFD.3 (Temporal Cumulativeness)

$$\text{RFD}_{cumulative}(x, t_0, t_1) = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \text{RFD}(x, t) dt$$

F.6.2.3 System RFD

Definition F.6.4 (System Recursive Freedom Degree)

$$\text{RFD}_{sys}(t) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|} \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} w_a \cdot \text{RFD}(a, t)$$

where $w_a$ is the weight of agent $a$ (which may be based on UCS).

F.6.3 Formalized Definition of CRV

F.6.3.1 Basic Definition

Definition F.6.5 (CRV - Commitment-Verification Ratio)

$$\text{CRV}: \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{T} \rightarrow [0, 1]$$

$$\text{CRV}(a, t) \triangleq \frac{|\text{VerifiedCommitments}(a, t)|}{|\text{TotalCommitments}(a, t)|}$$

F.6.3.2 Time-weighted Form

Definition F.6.6 (Time-weighted CRV)

$$\text{CRV}_w(a, t) = \frac{\sum_{i} w(t - t_i) \cdot \mathbb{1}_{verified}(c_i)}{\sum_{i} w(t - t_i)}$$

where $w(t - t_i)$ is the time-decay weight, and $\mathbb{1}_{verified}(c_i)$ is the verification indicator function.

F.6.3.3 Axiomatic Constraints

Axiom CRV.1 (Boundary Conditions)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.\forall t \in \mathcal{T}. 0 \leq \text{CRV}(a, t) \leq 1$$

Axiom CRV.2 (Association with Trust)

$$\text{Trustworthiness}(a, t) = f(\text{CRV}(a, t), \text{History}(a))$$

F.6.4 Formalization of Relations Among Indicators

F.6.4.1 Indicator Dependence Relations

Theorem F.6.1 (UCS-RFD Association)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.\text{UCS}(a) \text{ high} \rightarrow \text{Capacity}(\text{RFD}(a) \text{ high})$$

Read as: A high-UCS agent has the capacity to maintain a high RFD.

Theorem F.6.2 (CRV-RFD Association)

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}.\text{CRV}(a) \text{ high} \rightarrow \text{CooperationPotential}(\text{RFD}_{sys} \text{ increase})$$

Read as: A high CRV promotes growth of the system RFD.

Concordance Appendices

Concordance with International Space LawAppendix G

I. The Task and Positioning of This Appendix

This appendix provides a systematic comparative analysis of The Normative Foundations of Interstellar Civilization in relation to the existing system of international space law. International space law is the most important legal achievement of humanity to date in the field of norms governing space activities. The normative framework of this work must engage in dialogue with this achievement, inheriting its reasonable core while identifying its limitations and proposing directions for extension.

II. The Relationship Between the Comparison and the New Three Views

The comparative work directly embodies the core ideas of the New Three Views:

III. Maturity Statement

Rule G.0.1 (Maturity Statement)

In accordance with the statement in Chapter Zero §0.4, the comparative analysis in this appendix is at the conceptual prototype stage:

ContentMaturityScope of ApplicationUsage Constraints
Interpretation of provisionsScholarly analysisScholarly researchNot a legal opinion
Comparative analysisConceptual prototypeTheoretical explorationRequires validation by legal experts
Bridging suggestionsPolicy draftReference for discussionNot policy recommendations
Compatibility assessmentPreliminary analysisResearch-orientedRequires further argumentation

IV. Disclaimer

The comparative analysis in this appendix is for scholarly research reference only and does not constitute legal advice or policy recommendations. Interpretations of international space law should defer to authoritative legal texts and the professional interpretations of international law scholars.

G.1 Explanation of the Comparative Method

G.1.1 The Purpose of the Comparison

G.1.1.1 Definition of the Purpose of the Comparison

Definition G.1.1 (Comparison)

$$\text{Comparison} \triangleq \text{Mapping}(\text{Framework}_{this}, \text{Framework}_{ISL}) \rightarrow \text{Analysis}$$

Comparison is the process of mapping this work's normative framework onto the framework of international space law and carrying out an analysis.

G.1.1.2 The Fourfold Purpose of the Comparison

Rule G.1.1 (Purpose of Comparison)

The comparative work in this appendix serves the following fourfold purpose:

PurposeDescriptionFormalized Expression
HeritageIdentify inheritable legal achievements$\text{Heritage} = \text{ISL} \cap \text{Valid}$
SupplementIdentify this work's supplementary contributions$\text{Supplement} = \text{Framework} - \text{ISL}$
ExtensionIdentify areas requiring extension$\text{Extension} = \text{Needed} - \text{ISL}$
BridgingPropose bridging suggestions$\text{Bridge} = f(\text{ISL}, \text{Framework})$

G.2 Comparison with the Outer Space Treaty

G.2.1 Comparison of Article I

G.2.1.1 Text of the Provision

Outer Space Treaty, Article I

"The exploration and use of outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, shall be carried out for the benefit and in the interests of all countries, irrespective of their degree of economic or scientific development, and shall be the province of all mankind.

Outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, shall be free for exploration and use by all States without discrimination of any kind, on a basis of equality and in accordance with international law, and there shall be free access to all areas of celestial bodies.

There shall be freedom of scientific investigation in outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, and States shall facilitate and encourage international cooperation in such investigation."

Key Points in Chinese

Key PointContent
Principle of common benefitThe exploration and use of outer space shall be for the benefit and interests of all countries
Common province of mankindOuter space activities are the province of all mankind
Principle of equal freedomAll states may freely explore and use outer space on a basis of equality
Freedom of scientific investigationFreedom of scientific investigation in outer space
International cooperationEncourage international cooperation in scientific investigation

$$\text{OST-I} \subseteq \text{Framework-I}_{restricted}$$

where $\text{Framework-I}_{restricted}$ is this work's framework restricted to the scope of human subjects.

G.2.4 Comparison of Article IV

G.2.4.1 Text of the Provision

Outer Space Treaty, Article IV

"States Parties to the Treaty undertake not to place in orbit around the Earth any objects carrying nuclear weapons or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, install such weapons on celestial bodies, or station such weapons in outer space in any other manner.

The Moon and other celestial bodies shall be used by all States Parties to the Treaty exclusively for peaceful purposes. The establishment of military bases, installations and fortifications, the testing of any type of weapons and the conduct of military manoeuvres on celestial bodies shall be forbidden. The use of military personnel for scientific research or for any other peaceful purposes shall not be prohibited. The use of any equipment or facility necessary for peaceful exploration of the Moon and other celestial bodies shall also not be prohibited."

Peaceful use of celestial bodiesCelestial bodies shall be used exclusively for peaceful purposes
Restriction of military activitiesProhibits military activities on celestial bodies
Exception clausePermits military personnel and equipment for peaceful purposes

G.2.5 Comparison of Article V

G.2.5.1 Text of the Provision

Outer Space Treaty, Article V

"States Parties to the Treaty shall regard astronauts as envoys of mankind in outer space and shall render to them all possible assistance in the event of accident, distress, or emergency landing on the territory of another State Party or on the high seas. When astronauts make such a landing, they shall be safely and promptly returned to the State of registry of their space vehicle.

In carrying on activities in outer space and on celestial bodies, the astronauts of one State Party shall render all possible assistance to the astronauts of other States Parties.

States Parties to the Treaty shall immediately inform the other States Parties to the Treaty or the Secretary-General of the United Nations of any phenomena they discover in outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, which could constitute a danger to the life or health of astronauts."

Key Points in Chinese

Key PointContent
Status of envoys of mankindAstronauts are regarded as envoys of mankind
Obligation of assistanceObligation to assist astronauts in distress
Mutual assistanceMutual assistance among astronauts
Notification of dangerObligation to notify discovered dangerous situations

Core Findings

Rule G.S.1 (Core Findings)

  1. High compatibility: this work's framework is highly compatible with existing international space law at the level of core principles
  2. Need for extension: extensions are mainly needed in the scope of subjects, temporal scope, and the concept of damage
  3. Deepening of foundations: this work provides a deeper normative foundation for existing space law principles
  4. Gradual path: bridging can be achieved through a gradual path of soft law—protocol—new treaty

Relationship to the New Three Views

New Three Views PropositionManifestation in the Comparison
NC-1 (relationality)Concern with the evolution of relational structures among legal subjects
NC-2 (processuality)Emphasis on the dynamic evolution of legal frameworks
NC-3 (participation)Concern with the participation of multiple subjects
NL-1 (cross-substrate)Promoting the extension of the scope of subjects
NL-2 (negentropy)Introducing the concept of negentropy responsibility
NL-3 (continuum)Handling graded subjecthood
NK-1 (participatory)Adopting a participatory interpretive method
NK-2 (sociality)Concern with the social construction of law
NK-3 (deep uncertainty)Acknowledging the uncertainty of interpretation
NK-4 (deliberativeness)Emphasizing the deliberability of comparative conclusions

Usage Suggestions

  1. Legal researchers: refer to G.2-G.5 for the article-by-article comparative analysis
  2. Policymakers: refer to G.6 for the bridging suggestions
  3. Academic researchers: refer to G.7 for the comprehensive concordance table
  4. Critics: attend to the statement of limitations in G.1.3

Key Warnings

  1. Not a legal opinion: this comparative analysis does not constitute legal advice or recommendations
  2. Interpretive dependence: the comparative conclusions depend on a particular interpretation of the treaties
  3. Dynamism: international law is in evolution, and the comparative conclusions may need updating
  4. Requires validation: the comparative conclusions require validation by legal experts

Concordance with the AI-Ethics LiteratureAppendix H

I. The Task and Positioning of This Appendix

This appendix provides a systematic comparative analysis of The Normative Foundations of Interstellar Civilization against contemporary AI ethics literature. The development of artificial intelligence is one of the most important technological variables of the interstellar-civilization era, and AI ethics research represents humanity's most recent thinking on the technology-ethics relationship. The normative framework of this work must engage in dialogue with this field—absorbing its insights while identifying its limitations, and clarifying the unique contributions of this work.

II. The Relationship between the Comparison and the New Three Views

The comparative work directly embodies the core ideas of the New Three Views:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

III. Maturity Statement

Rule H.0.1 (Maturity Statement)

In accordance with the statement in Chapter 0 §0.4, the comparative analysis in this appendix is at the conceptual prototype stage:

ContentMaturityScope of ApplicationUsage Limitations
Literature interpretationAcademic analysisAcademic researchDifferences in interpretation may exist
Comparative analysisConceptual prototypeTheoretical explorationRequires further validation
Contribution assessmentPreliminary analysisResearch-orientedRequires examination by the academic community
Interface recommendationsPolicy draftDiscussion referenceNot a policy recommendation

IV. Disclaimer

The comparative analysis in this appendix is for academic research reference only. Interpretations of AI ethics literature should defer to the original texts. This comparison aims to promote academic dialogue, not to judge superiority or inferiority.

H.1 Explanation of the Comparative Method

H.1.1 The Purpose of the Comparison

Definition H.1.1 (Comparison)

$$\text{Comparison} \triangleq \text{Mapping}(\text{Framework}_{this}, \text{Literature}_{AI-Ethics}) \rightarrow \text{Analysis}$$

A comparison is the process of mapping the normative framework of this work against AI ethics literature and performing an analysis.

H.1.2 The Fourfold Purpose of the Comparison

Rule H.1.1 (Purpose of the Comparison)

PurposeDescriptionFormalized Expression
LearningAbsorb insights from the field of AI ethics$\text{Learn} = \text{AI-Ethics} \cap \text{Valuable}$
PositioningClarify the position of this work within the field of AI ethics$\text{Position} = \text{Framework} \cap \text{AI-Ethics}$
ContributionIdentify the unique contributions of this work$\text{Contribution} = \text{Framework} - \text{AI-Ethics}$
InterfacePropose recommendations for interfacing with AI ethics research$\text{Bridge} = f(\text{Framework}, \text{AI-Ethics})$

H.3.1.4 Formalized Comparison

Definition H.3.1 (Formalization of Russell's Framework)

Russell's value-alignment framework:

$$\text{Russell} = \text{MaximizeHumanPreference} \land \text{InitialUncertainty} \land \text{BehaviorLearning}$$

Objective function:

$$\text{Objective}_{Russell} = \max_a \mathbb{E}[U(human\_preferences) | a]$$

The corresponding item in the framework of this work:

$$\text{Framework-Alignment} = \text{RFP} \land \text{NK-3} \land (\text{NK-1} \land \text{NK-2})$$

Objective function:

$$\text{Objective}_{Framework} = \max_a \mathbb{E}[\sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} w_i \cdot \Delta\Omega_i | a]$$

Where $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of all subjects and $\Omega_i$ is the space of possibilities of subject $i$.

Definition H.3.2 (Formalization of the Orthogonality Thesis)

Bostrom's orthogonality thesis:

$$\text{Orthogonality}: \neg\text{Correlation}(\text{IntelligenceLevel}, \text{GoalContent})$$

The partial revision of this work:

$$\text{WeakOrthogonality}: \text{PartialCorrelation}(\text{IntelligenceLevel}, \text{GoalStructure})$$

$$\forall a.[\text{UCS}(a) > \theta \rightarrow \text{Tends}(a, \text{NegentropyAcquisition})]$$

Read as: subjects exceeding a certain consciousness threshold tend toward negentropy acquisition (an instrumental goal).

Concordance with the Longtermism LiteratureAppendix I

I. The Task and Positioning of This Appendix

This appendix provides a systematic comparative analysis of The Normative Foundations of Interstellar Civilization in relation to the contemporary literature on longtermism. Longtermism is an important philosophical movement that emerged in the early twenty-first century, holding that we bear significant moral responsibility toward the distant future. This work and longtermism share a concern with long-term consequences, but differ markedly in normative foundations, methodology, and institutional design. Through systematic comparison, this appendix aims to clarify the similarities and differences between the two approaches, to identify possibilities for complementarity, and to provide a clearer positioning for the normative foundations of Interstellar Civilization Studies.

I.2 Comparison with MacAskill's What We Owe the Future

I.2.1 Comparison of the Temporal Neutrality Argument

I.2.1.1 MacAskill's Temporal Neutrality Argument

Background Information

ItemContent
WorkWhat We Owe the Future
AuthorWilliam MacAskill
Publication2022
Core conceptsTemporal neutrality, longtermism, trajectory change

The Core of the Temporal Neutrality Argument

MacAskill's temporal neutrality argument:

"The date at which someone exists does not, in itself, affect the value of their life or the moral weight of their interests."

Core claims:

  1. The point in time at which a person exists does not in itself affect the value of their life
  2. The interests of future people have the same moral importance as those of present people
  3. We bear moral obligations to future people similar to those we bear to present people

Formalized Expression

$$\text{TemporalNeutrality}: \forall p, t_1, t_2. \text{Value}(\text{Welfare}(p, t_1)) = \text{Value}(\text{Welfare}(p, t_2))$$

Read as: for any person $p$ and any time points $t_1, t_2$, the value of their welfare is independent of the time point.

$$\text{MoralWeight}(p, t) = f(\text{Welfare}(p)) \text{ independent of } t$$

This work's RFP entails:

$$\text{RFP}: \forall a, t.\text{Action}(a, t) \rightarrow \text{Protect}(\Omega(\text{AllAgents}, t'))$$

where $t' > t$, i.e., when acting, one should protect the space of possibilities of all future subjects.

I.2.2 Comparison of the Future Population Size Argument

I.2.2.1 MacAskill's Future Population Size Argument

Core of the Argument

MacAskill's future population size argument:

"If humanity survives for as long as Earth remains habitable, there could be roughly 10^16 future people. Even if we spread to the stars, the number could be vastly greater still."

Core claims:

  1. The number of people who could exist in the future is enormous
  2. Combined with temporal neutrality, this means that the total welfare of future people may vastly exceed that of the present
  3. Therefore, actions that influence the long-term future carry extremely high moral importance

Formalized Expression

$$\text{ExpectedFutureWelfare} = N_{future} \times \bar{W}_{future}$$

where $N_{future}$ is the future population size and $\bar{W}_{future}$ is average welfare.

Since $N_{future} \gg N_{current}$, therefore:

$$\text{ExpectedFutureWelfare} \gg \text{CurrentWelfare}$$

I.2.2.3 This Work's Alternative Argument

Rule I.2.2 (Space of Possibilities Argument)

This work offers an alternative argument that does not rely on population size estimates:

  1. The value of the space of possibilities: the space of possibilities has value in itself, not merely through realized welfare
  2. The importance of irreversibility: actions that reduce the space of possibilities are irreversible, and therefore require particular caution
  3. Handling deep uncertainty: under deep uncertainty, protecting the space of possibilities is the rational default choice

Formalized:

$$\text{Importance}(\alpha) = f(\Delta\Omega(\alpha), \text{Irreversibility}(\alpha))$$

where $\Delta\Omega(\alpha)$ is the impact of action $\alpha$ on the space of possibilities and $\text{Irreversibility}(\alpha)$ is the degree of irreversibility.

Calculation methodExpected valueChange in space of possibilitiesThis work is more robust
ConclusionThe long-term future mattersProtecting the space of possibilities mattersConvergent in practice

I.2.3 Comparison of the Trajectory Lock-In Argument

I.2.3.1 MacAskill's Trajectory Lock-In Argument

Core of the Argument

MacAskill's value lock-in argument:

"The period in which we live might be particularly influential. We might be at a critical juncture, able to influence which of many possible long-run futures will be ours."

Core concepts:

  1. Trajectory lock-in: certain decisions may permanently determine the direction of human civilization's development
  2. Critical period: we may be in a particularly influential historical period
  3. Window of opportunity: the opportunity to change trajectory may be limited

Formalized Expression

$$\text{TrajectoryLockIn}: \exists t_{critical}.\text{Decision}(t_{critical}) \rightarrow \text{Permanent}(\text{Trajectory})$$

I.3.2 Comparison of Risk Assessment Methods

I.3.2.1 Ord's Risk Assessment Method

Ord's Methodology

Ord adopts a subjective probability estimation method:

  1. Integration of expert judgment: synthesizing estimates from multiple experts
  2. Historical analogy: referring to the frequency of historical events
  3. Causal analysis: analyzing the causal chains that generate risk
  4. Quantification of uncertainty: providing probability intervals

Formalized Expression

$$P(\text{Risk}_i) = \int P(\text{Risk}_i | \theta) \cdot P(\theta) d\theta$$

where $\theta$ is an uncertain parameter.

I.3.2.3 This Work's Alternative Method

Rule I.3.1 (Risk Assessment Under Deep Uncertainty)

This work provides a risk assessment method that does not rely on probability estimation:

  1. MBCL (Model Behavior Concern Level)
  • Does not rely on probability
  • Grading based on behavioral characteristics
  • Triggers corresponding regulatory measures
  1. CSIA (Cross-Scale Impact Assessment)
  • Assesses the spatial and temporal scales of impact
  • Does not rely on probability estimation
  • Based on causal structure analysis
  1. REV (Reversibility Principle)
  • Prioritizes reversible actions under deep uncertainty
  • Does not rely on expected-value calculation
  • A robust default strategy

Formalized Expression

$$\text{RiskAssessment}_{Framework} = \text{MBCL} \times \text{CSIA} \times \text{REV-Score}$$

Does not rely on:

$$\neg\text{Requires}(\text{RiskAssessment}_{Framework}, P(\text{Risk}))$$

I.3.3 Comparison of the Long-Term Potential Argument

I.3.3.1 Ord's Long-Term Potential Argument

Core of the Argument

Ord's long-term potential argument:

"If we can make it through this vulnerable period of our history, we may have a vast and flourishing future ahead of us."

Core claims:

  1. Human civilization has immense long-term potential
  2. This potential may last for billions of years
  3. Protecting this potential is a moral task of extremely high priority

Formalized Expression

$$\text{LongTermPotential} = \int_{t_{now}}^{t_{end}} \text{Value}(t) dt$$

If $t_{end}$ is very far away (billions of years), then $\text{LongTermPotential}$ is very large.

I.4.1 Comparison of the Astronomical Waste Argument

I.4.1.1 Bostrom's Astronomical Waste Argument

Background Information

ItemContent
Paper"Astronomical Waste: The Opportunity Cost of Delayed Technological Development"
AuthorNick Bostrom
Publication2003
Core conceptsAstronomical waste, cosmic colonization potential, cost of delay

Core of the Argument

Bostrom's astronomical waste argument:

"For every second of delay in colonizing the accessible universe, we forgo an immense amount of potential value—what I have called 'astronomical waste.'"

Core claims:

  1. The matter-energy of the accessible universe embodies immense potential value
  2. Every second of delay means the loss of a vast amount of potential value
  3. Therefore, developing technology rapidly carries immense moral urgency

Formalized Expression

$$\text{AstronomicalWaste} = \int_{t_{actual}}^{t_{optimal}} \text{PotentialValue}(t) - \text{ActualValue}(t) dt$$

Waste per second:

$$\frac{d\text{Waste}}{dt} \approx 10^{38} \text{ potential lives/second}$$

(based on Bostrom's estimate)

I.4.2 Comparison of the Vulnerable World Hypothesis

I.4.2.1 Bostrom's Vulnerable World Hypothesis

Background Information

Paper"The Vulnerable World Hypothesis"
AuthorNick Bostrom
Publication2019
Core conceptsVulnerable world, technological urn, black ball

Core of the Hypothesis

Bostrom's vulnerable world hypothesis:

"If technological development continues, then a set of capabilities will eventually be attained that make civilization devastation extremely likely, unless civilization has by then sufficiently established a system of 'defensive technologies' and/or a level of civilizational competence or effective global governance."

Core concepts:

  • Technological urn: technological development is like drawing balls from an urn
  • Black ball: a technology with devastating consequences
  • White ball: a beneficial technology
  • Grey ball: a technology with both benefits and harms

Formalized Expression

$$\text{VWH}: P(\exists t.\text{BlackBall}(t)) > 0$$

$$\text{BlackBall}(t) \triangleq \text{Technology}(t) \land \text{EasyDevastation}(t)$$

I.5 Comparison with Beckstead's On the Overwhelming Importance of Shaping the Far Future

I.5.1 Comparison of the Core Argument

I.5.1.1 Beckstead's Core Argument

Background Information

ItemContent
Dissertation"On the Overwhelming Importance of Shaping the Far Future"
AuthorNick Beckstead
TypeDoctoral dissertation (Rutgers University)
Year2013
StatusFoundational scholarly literature of longtermism

Structure of the Core Argument

Beckstead's "overwhelming importance" argument:

  1. Premise 1: the number of people who could exist in the future vastly exceeds the present generation
  2. Premise 2: the welfare of future people is as important as that of the present generation (temporal neutrality)
  3. Premise 3: we can significantly influence the far future
  4. Conclusion: shaping the far future is a moral task of overwhelming importance

Formalized Expression

$$\text{Importance}(\text{ShapingFuture}) = f(\text{Scale}, \text{Probability}, \text{Influence})$$

where:

  • $\text{Scale}$: the number of future people affected (enormous)
  • $\text{Probability}$: the probability that the future actually exists
  • $\text{Influence}$: the influence we are able to exert

Since $\text{Scale}$ is very large, even if $\text{Probability}$ and $\text{Influence}$ are small, $\text{Importance}$ may still be "overwhelming."

I.6 Comparison of Normative Foundations

I.6.1 The Utilitarian Foundation of Longtermism

I.6.1.1 The Ethical Foundation of Longtermism

The Relationship Between Longtermism and Utilitarianism

Longtermism is usually (but not necessarily) built on a utilitarian foundation:

  1. Total utilitarianism: maximize the total welfare of all beings (past, present, future)
  2. Time-neutral utilitarianism: do not apply moral discounting to time points
  3. Total population ethics: it is better that more happy people exist

Formalized Expression

$$\text{TotalUtilitarianism}: \max \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \sum_{i \in P_t} U_i(t)$$

where $P_t$ is the set of all people existing at time $t$, and $U_i(t)$ is the utility of individual $i$ at time $t$.

The Utilitarian Argument for Longtermism

  1. Future population $\sum_{t>now}|P_t| \gg |P_{now}|$
  2. Therefore, the total future welfare $\sum_{t>now}\sum_{i \in P_t} U_i \gg \sum_{i \in P_{now}} U_i$
  3. Therefore, actions that influence future welfare carry immense moral importance

I.6.1.2 Problems with the Utilitarian Foundation

Table I.6.1 Potential problems with the utilitarian foundation

ProblemDescriptionChallenge Facing Longtermism
Population ethics paradoxParfit's Repugnant Conclusion, etc.How to avoid counterintuitive conclusions?
Computational infeasibilityCannot compute the utility of an infinite futureExpected value may be meaningless
Aggregation problemHow to aggregate the utility of different individuals?Cross-generational aggregation is even more difficult
Sacrifice by the present generationMay require excessive sacrifice by the present generationIntergenerational fairness problem
UncertaintyFuture utility is highly uncertainThe basis for expected-value calculation is unstable

I.6.2 This Work's Foundation in Cosmic Responsibility Ethics

I.6.2.1 Characteristics of Cosmic Responsibility Ethics

This Work's Normative Foundation

This work's normative foundation is not utilitarianism but "Cosmic Responsibility Ethics":

  1. Ontological anchoring: normativity is anchored in the ontology-epistemology of the New Three Views
  2. Space of possibilities: value lies not only in welfare but also in the space of possibilities
  3. Negentropy responsibility: responsibility as maintainers of negentropic organization in the universe
  4. Recursive structure: the recursive structure in which freedom protects freedom

Formalized Expression

$$\text{CosmicResponsibilityEthics} = f(\text{NewThreeViews}, \text{BridgePrinciples}) \rightarrow \text{ThreePrinciples}$$

where:

  • $\text{RFP}$: Recursive Freedom Principle
  • $\text{NRP}$: Negentropy Responsibility Principle
  • $\text{REV}$: Reversibility Principle

I.6.4.3 A Possible Framework for Integration

Rule I.6.2 (Draft Integration Framework)

One possible integration framework:

$$\text{IntegratedFramework} = \text{Longtermism}_{concerns} + \text{Framework}_{foundations} + \text{Framework}_{operations}$$

where:

  • $\text{Longtermism}_{concerns}$: longtermism's concern with the long-term future
  • $\text{Framework}_{foundations}$: this work's normative foundations (the New Three Views, the three principles)
  • $\text{Framework}_{operations}$: this work's operationalization tools (indicators, institutions)

The Core Claims of Integration

  1. Accept that the long-term future matters (shared with longtermism)
  2. Base on the space of possibilities rather than total welfare (this work's normative foundation)
  3. Acknowledge deep uncertainty (this work's epistemology)
  4. Use the protocol stack and indicator systems (this work's operationalization)
  5. Achieve governance through institutional innovation (this work's institutional design)

  2. Foundational concern: the utilitarian foundation faces philosophical challenges
  3. Methodological concern: probabilistic methods may mislead under deep uncertainty
  4. Invitation to complementarity: this work's framework can provide an alternative or supplementary normative foundation for longtermism

Usage Suggestions

  1. Longtermism researchers: refer to I.6 for the comparison of normative foundations
  2. Policymakers: refer to I.2–I.5 for the comparison of specific arguments
  3. Cross-disciplinary researchers: refer to I.7 for the comprehensive concordance table
  4. Critics: attend to the statement of limitations in I.1.5

Key Warnings

  1. Interpretive difference: the interpretation of longtermism literature may differ from the original authors' intentions
  2. Internal diversity: multiple positions exist within longtermism, and this comparison mainly targets the mainstream version
  3. Dynamic development: longtermism is still developing, and the conclusions of the comparison may need updating
  4. Scholarly respect: this comparison aims to promote dialogue rather than to disparage longtermism's contributions

Minimal Argument PathsAppendix J

I. The Task and Positioning of This Appendix

This appendix provides the Minimal Argument Path (MAP) for The Normative Foundations of Interstellar Civilization. The book's overall argumentative system is vast and complex, spanning multiple disciplinary fields and multiple levels of theoretical construction. The minimal argument path aims to distill the most concise and most critical chain of reasoning from the core problem to institutional design, enabling readers to quickly grasp the book's core logic while providing a clear focus for critical examination.

II. The Nature of the Minimal Argument Path

Definition J.0.1 (Minimal Argument Path)

$$\text{MAP} \triangleq \min_{\text{Path}} |\text{Path}| \text{ s.t. } \text{Path} \vdash \text{Conclusions}$$

The minimal argument path is the shortest valid chain of reasoning capable of deriving the core conclusions.

Rule J.0.1 (Properties of the MAP)

PropertyDescription
NecessityEvery step in the path is necessary
SufficiencyThe path suffices to derive the core conclusions
ConcisenessRemoving any step would render the reasoning invalid
TestabilityEvery step can be independently tested

J.2 The Minimal Path from the Problem to the New Three Views

J.2.1 Statement of the Core Problem

J.2.1.1 Formal Statement of the Problem

Definition J.2.1 (Core Problem)

$$\text{CoreProblem} \triangleq \text{How to establish normative framework for } \mathcal{S}_{interstellar}?$$

Where $\mathcal{S}_{interstellar}$ is the set of interstellar-civilization situations, including:

$$\mathcal{S}_{interstellar} = \{\text{AGI}, \text{ASI}, \text{SpaceColonization}, \text{FirstContact}, \text{PostHuman}, ...\}$$

J.2.1.2 The Three Dimensions of the Problem

Rule J.2.1 (The Three Dimensions of the Problem)

DimensionQuestionFormalization
Normative groundingWhere does normativity come from?$\text{Source}(\text{Normativity}) = ?$
Deep uncertaintyHow to decide under deep uncertainty?$\text{Decision}(\text{DeepUncertainty}) = ?$
Long-range responsibilityHow to attribute long-range responsibility?$\text{Attribution}(\text{LongTermResponsibility}) = ?$

Puzzle One: The Cosmic Grounding of Normativity

$$\text{Puzzle}_1: \text{What grounds normativity in a cosmos without pre-given purposes?}$$

Core tension:

  • Naturalism: the cosmos is a purposeless physical process
  • The need for normativity: we need the guidance of "ought"
  • Problem: how to move from "is" to "ought"?

Puzzle Two: Rationality under Deep Uncertainty

$$\text{Puzzle}_2: \text{How to be rational under deep uncertainty?}$$

Core tension:

  • Standard decision theory relies on probabilities
  • Interstellar-civilization situations face deep uncertainty
  • Problem: how to decide when there are no reliable probabilities?

Puzzle Three: The Attribution of Long-Range Responsibility

$$\text{Puzzle}_3: \text{How to attribute responsibility across deep time?}$$

Core tension:

  • Traditional responsibility attribution relies on proximate causation
  • Interstellar-civilization decisions have far-reaching effects
  • Problem: how to be responsible for long-range consequences?

J.2.1.3 The Urgency of the Problem

Rule J.2.2 (Argument for the Urgency of the Problem)

Development TrendTime ScaleNormative Need
Growth of AI capabilitiesYears–decadesAGI governance framework
Acceleration of space explorationDecades–centuriesSpace resource governance
Breakthroughs in biotechnologyDecades–centuriesPosthuman ethics
Potential extraterrestrial contactUncertainFirst Contact protocol

$$\text{Urgency} = f(\text{TechnologyDevelopment}, \text{NormativeGap})$$

Current state: technological development outpaces the establishment of normative frameworks.

J.2.4 The Core Claims of the New Three Views

J.2.4.1 The New Cosmological View (NC)

Definition J.2.2 (Core Propositions of the New Cosmological View)

PropositionStatementFormalization
NC-1Relations precede entities$\text{Relation} \prec \text{Entity}$
NC-2Processes precede states$\text{Process} \prec \text{State}$
NC-3Participation precedes observation$\text{Participation} \prec \text{Observation}$

The Meaning of NC-1

$$\text{NC-1}: \forall e.\text{Entity}(e) \Rightarrow \exists R.\text{ConstitutedBy}(e, R)$$

Entities are constituted by relational networks rather than existing independently.

The Meaning of NC-2

$$\text{NC-2}: \forall s.\text{State}(s) \Rightarrow \exists p.\text{MomentOf}(s, p)$$

States are slices of processes rather than the basis of processes.

The Meaning of NC-3

$$\text{NC-3}: \forall k.\text{Knowledge}(k) \Rightarrow \exists a.\text{InvolvedIn}(a, k)$$

Knowledge involves the participation of a subject rather than passive observation.

J.2.4.2 The New View of Life (NL)

Definition J.2.3 (Core Propositions of the New View of Life)

PropositionStatementFormalization
NL-1Life is cross-substrate$\text{Life} \not\Rightarrow \text{CarbonBased}$
NL-2The essence of life is negentropic organization$\text{Life} \equiv \text{NegentropyOrganization}$
NL-3Subjecthood is a continuum$\text{Agenthood}: \mathcal{E} \rightarrow [0, 1]$

The Meaning of NL-1

$$\text{NL-1}: \Diamond\exists x.[\text{Life}(x) \land \neg\text{CarbonBased}(x)]$$

Life may exist on non-carbon-based substrates (such as silicon-based AI or other forms).

The Meaning of NL-2

$$\text{NL-2}: \text{Life}(x) \Leftrightarrow \text{SelfMaintaining}(\text{NegentropyOrganization}(x))$$

The essence of life is self-maintaining negentropic organization.

The Meaning of NL-3

$$\text{NL-3}: \text{Agenthood}: \mathcal{E} \rightarrow [0, 1]$$

Subjecthood is not binary but a graded continuum.

J.2.4.3 The New View of Cognition (NK)

Definition J.2.4 (Core Propositions of the New View of Cognition)

PropositionStatementFormalization
NK-1Cognition is participatory$\text{Cognition} \equiv \text{Participation}$
NK-2Knowledge is socially constructed$\text{Knowledge} \equiv \text{SocialConstruction}$
NK-3Deep uncertainty exists$\exists \phi.\text{DeepUncertainty}(\phi)$
NK-4Norms are deliberative$\text{Norms} \equiv \text{Negotiated}$

The Meaning of NK-3 (Key)

$$\text{NK-3}: \exists \phi.[\neg\exists P.\text{ProbabilityDistribution}(P) \land \text{Represents}(P, \text{Uncertainty}(\phi))]$$

There exists deep uncertainty that cannot be probabilized.

The Meaning of NK-4

$$\text{NK-4}: \forall n.\text{Norm}(n) \Rightarrow \text{OpenToRevision}(n)$$

All norms are open to deliberation and revision.

J.2.4.4 The Unity of the Three Views

Theorem J.2.2 (Unity of the Three Views)

$$\text{NC} \land \text{NL} \land \text{NK} \vdash \text{Consistent}$$

The three views are conceptually consistent, mutually supporting rather than conflicting.
