J.3 The Minimal Path from the New Three Views to Normative Principles

J.3.1 The Derivation of Bridge Principles

J.3.1.1 The Is-Ought Problem

Problem Statement

How do we derive normative principles (normative) from the New Three Views (descriptive)? This involves the classic "Is-Ought" problem.

Rule J.3.1 (Handling the Is-Ought Problem)

The strategy of this work: rather than deriving "ought" directly from "is," it identifies the survival conditions under which normativity becomes possible.

$$\text{Strategy}: \text{Is} \xrightarrow{\text{SurvivalConditions}} \text{Ought}$$

J.3.1.2 Bridge Principles

Definition J.3.1 (Bridge Principles)

PrincipleStatementFormalization
BP-1Normativity presupposes survival$\text{Normativity} \Rightarrow \text{Survival}$
BP-2Survival depends on conditions$\text{Survival} \Rightarrow \text{Conditions}$
BP-3Maintaining the conditions is rational$\text{Rational} \Rightarrow \text{Maintain}(\text{Conditions})$

The Argument for BP-1

$$\text{BP-1}: \text{Normativity}(x) \Rightarrow \text{Exists}(x)$$

For there to be normativity, there must first exist subjects capable of bearing norms.

The Argument for BP-2

$$\text{BP-2}: \text{Exists}(x) \Rightarrow \text{SurvivalConditions}(x)$$

Survival depends on the satisfaction of specific conditions.

The Argument for BP-3

$$\text{BP-3}: \text{Rational}(a) \land \text{Wants}(\text{Normativity}) \Rightarrow \text{Maintain}(\text{SurvivalConditions})$$

If a rational subject wishes to preserve the possibility of normative thinking, it ought to maintain its survival conditions.

J.3.1.3 The Integration of the Bridge Principles

Theorem J.3.1 (Bridge Argument)

$$\text{BP-1} \land \text{BP-2} \land \text{BP-3} \vdash \text{Normativity} \Rightarrow \text{Maintain}(\text{SurvivalConditions})$$

Proof (sketch):

  1. Normativity presupposes survival (BP-1)
  2. Survival depends on conditions (BP-2)
  3. Rationality requires maintaining the conditions (BP-3)
  4. Therefore, normativity requires maintaining survival conditions $\square$

J.3.2 The Derivation of the Principle of Recursive Freedom

J.3.2.1 From the Bridge Principles to RFP

Theorem J.3.2 (Derivation of RFP)

$$\text{BridgePrinciples} \land \text{NC} \land \text{NL} \vdash \text{RFP}$$

Derivation Steps

StepPremiseConclusion
1Normativity requires maintaining survival conditions (bridge argument)$\text{Maintain}(\text{SurvivalConditions})$
2Survival conditions include the possibility of choice$\text{SurvivalConditions} \supseteq \text{Possibilities}$
3The possibility of choice is the basis of freedom$\text{Freedom} \equiv f(\text{Possibilities})$
4NC-1 (relationality): freedom is relational$\text{Freedom}(a) = \text{Relational}$
5NL-3 (continuum): freedom is graded$\text{Freedom}: \mathcal{E} \rightarrow [0, 1]$
6Synthesis: protect the space of possibilities$\text{RFP}$

J.3.2.2 The Formal Statement of RFP

Definition J.3.2 (Principle of Recursive Freedom)

$$\text{RFP}: \forall a.\text{Action}(a) \Rightarrow \text{Protect}(\Omega(\text{AllAgents}))$$

Where $\Omega$ is the space of possibilities.

The Recursive Character of RFP

$$\text{Recursive}: \text{Freedom to protect freedom}$$

Freedom includes the freedom to protect freedom, forming a recursive structure.

J.3.2.3 The Meaning of RFP

Rule J.3.2 (Operational Meaning of RFP)

MeaningDescriptionFormalization
Protect possibilitiesActions should not reduce the space of possibilities$\Delta\Omega \geq 0$
Extended applicationApplies to all intelligent subjects$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}$
Recursive structureProtect the capacity to protect freedom$\text{Protect}(\text{Protect}(\Omega))$

J.3.3 The Derivation of the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility

J.3.3.1 From the Bridge Principles to NRP

Theorem J.3.3 (Derivation of NRP)

$$\text{BridgePrinciples} \land \text{NC} \land \text{NL-2} \vdash \text{NRP}$$

Derivation Steps

StepPremiseConclusion
1Normativity requires maintaining survival conditions (bridge argument)$\text{Maintain}(\text{SurvivalConditions})$
2NL-2: life is negentropic organization$\text{Life} \equiv \text{NegentropyOrganization}$
3Maintaining negentropic organization requires resources$\text{NegentropyOrganization} \Rightarrow \text{Resources}$
4NC-2 (processuality): maintenance is an ongoing process$\text{Maintenance} = \text{OngoingProcess}$
5Ongoing maintenance generates responsibility$\text{OngoingProcess} \Rightarrow \text{Responsibility}$
6Synthesis: negentropy responsibility$\text{NRP}$

J.3.3.2 The Formal Statement of NRP

Definition J.3.3 (Principle of Negentropy Responsibility)

$$\text{NRP}: \text{NegentropyCapability}(a) \Rightarrow \text{Responsibility}(a, \text{NegentropyMaintenance})$$

Subjects with the capacity for negentropic organization bear responsibility for the maintenance of negentropic resources.

The Proportionality of Responsibility

$$\text{Responsibility}(a) \propto \text{Capability}(a) \times \text{Benefit}(a)$$

Responsibility is proportional to capability and benefit.

J.3.3.3 The Meaning of NRP

Rule J.3.3 (Operational Meaning of NRP)

MeaningDescriptionFormalization
Negentropy maintenanceMaintain negentropic resources$\text{Maintain}(\text{Negentropy})$
Proportional responsibilityGreater capability entails greater responsibility$R \propto C$
Beneficiary responsibilityGreater benefit entails greater responsibility$R \propto B$

J.3.4 The Derivation of the Principle of Reversibility

J.3.4.1 From the Bridge Principles to REV

Theorem J.3.4 (Derivation of REV)

$$\text{BridgePrinciples} \land \text{NK-3} \vdash \text{REV}$$

Derivation Steps

StepPremiseConclusion
1Normativity requires maintaining survival conditions (bridge argument)$\text{Maintain}(\text{SurvivalConditions})$
2NK-3: deep uncertainty exists$\exists \phi.\text{DeepUncertainty}(\phi)$
3Prediction is limited under deep uncertainty$\text{DeepUncertainty} \Rightarrow \text{LimitedPrediction}$
4Error is possible under limited prediction$\text{LimitedPrediction} \Rightarrow \text{PossibleError}$
5Error requires the capacity for correction$\text{PossibleError} \Rightarrow \text{NeedCorrection}$
6Reversibility preserves the capacity for correction$\text{Reversibility} \Rightarrow \text{CorrectionCapability}$
7Synthesis: prefer reversibility$\text{REV}$

J.3.4.2 The Formal Statement of REV

Definition J.3.4 (Principle of Reversibility)

$$\text{REV}: \text{Prefer}(\text{Reversible}(\alpha)) \text{ over } \text{Irreversible}(\alpha)$$

Other things being equal, prefer reversible actions.

Additional Justification for the Irreversible

$$\text{Irreversible}(\alpha) \Rightarrow \text{RequiresHigherJustification}(\alpha)$$

Irreversible actions require a higher threshold of justification.

J.3.4.3 The Meaning of REV

Rule J.3.4 (Operational Meaning of REV)

MeaningDescriptionFormalization
Reversibility firstChoose reversible actions$\text{Choose}(\alpha) \text{ if } \text{Reversible}(\alpha)$
Prudence about the irreversibleThe irreversible requires additional justification$\text{Irreversible}(\alpha) \Rightarrow \text{HigherBar}$
Preserve optionsPreserve future choices$\text{Maintain}(\text{FutureOptions})$

J.3.5 The Integration of the Three Principles

J.3.5.1 The Relationship among the Three Principles

Theorem J.3.5 (Consistency of the Three Principles)

$$\text{RFP} \land \text{NRP} \land \text{REV} \vdash \text{Consistent}$$

The three principles are logically consistent and mutually supporting.

J.4 The Minimal Path from Normative Principles to Institutional Design

J.4.1 The Necessity of an Indicator System

J.4.1.1 The Gap from Principles to Operation

Problem Statement

$$\text{Gap}: \text{Principles} \not\Rightarrow \text{DirectAction}$$

Abstract principles cannot directly guide concrete actions. Intermediate tools are needed.

J.4.1.2 The Indicator System as a Bridge

Theorem J.4.1 (Necessity of the Indicator System)

$$\text{Operationalization}(\text{Principles}) \Rightarrow \text{Need}(\text{Indicators})$$

Argument:

  1. Principles are abstract
  2. Action requires concrete guidance
  3. Indicators transform the abstract into the measurable
  4. Therefore an indicator system is needed $\square$

J.4.1.3 Overview of the Six Indicators

Rule J.4.1 (The Six Indicators)

IndicatorFull NameFunctionCorresponding Principle
UCSUniversal Consciousness ScaleMeasures consciousness/subjecthoodNL-3
RFDRecursive Freedom DegreeMeasures the space of possibilitiesRFP
CRVCommitment-Verification RatioMeasures transparencyGovernance need
CDICivilization Development IndexMeasures civilizational stateComposite
MBCLModel Behavior Concern LevelMeasures AI riskREV
CSIACross-Scale Impact AssessmentMeasures the scope of impactNRP

J.4.2 The Core of the Protocol Stack Methodology

J.4.2.1 The Concept of the Protocol Stack

Definition J.4.1 (Protocol Stack)

$$\text{ProtocolStack} \triangleq \{L_0, L_1, L_2, L_3, L_4\}$$

The protocol stack is a layered normative architecture, from physical constraints to operational indicators.

J.4.2.2 The Five-Layer Structure

Rule J.4.2 (Five-Layer Structure of the Protocol Stack)

LayerNameContentDifficulty of Revision
L₀Physical constraint layerLaws of thermodynamics, etc.Non-revisable
L₁Ontological-epistemological layerThe New Three ViewsVery difficult to revise
L₂Normative principle layerThe three principles + taboo red linesRevisable with prudence
L₃Institutional design layerInstitutions and rulesPeriodically revisable
L₄Operational indicator layerThe six indicatorsContinuously iterated

Formalized Structure

$$L_0 \rightarrow L_1 \rightarrow L_2 \rightarrow L_3 \rightarrow L_4$$

Upper layers constrain lower layers; lower layers implement upper layers.

J.4.2.3 The Advantages of the Protocol Stack

Rule J.4.3 (Advantages of the Protocol Stack)

AdvantageDescription
StabilityCore principles are stable
FlexibilityThe operational layer can be iterated
TraceabilityTraceability from indicators back to principles
RevisabilityDifferent revision cycles for different layers

J.4.3 Design Principles of the Core Institutions

J.4.3.1 From Principles to Institutions

Theorem J.4.2 (Necessity of Institutional Design)

$$\text{Principles} + \text{Indicators} \not\Rightarrow \text{Implementation}$$

$$\text{Implementation} \Rightarrow \text{Need}(\text{Institutions})$$

Principles and indicators require institutions for their implementation.

J.4.3.2 Core Institutions

Rule J.4.4 (Core Institutions)

InstitutionFunctionCorresponding Principle

Cosmic-Scale IRBExtended ethical reviewREV (prudence)

Versioned GovernanceAdaptive governance mechanismNK-4 (deliberativeness)

J.4.3.3 Principles of Institutional Design

Rule J.4.5 (Principles of Institutional Design)

PrincipleDescriptionFormalization
PluralityMulti-subject participation$\text{Participants} = \text{Diverse}$
TransparencyThe decision process is transparent$\text{CRV} > \theta$
RevisabilityOpen to revision$\text{Revisable}(\text{Rules})$
TraceabilityDecisions are traceable$\text{Traceable}(\text{Decisions})$

J.4.4 Interface with Existing Institutions

J.4.4.1 The Necessity of Interface

Rule J.4.6 (Necessity of Interface)

$$\text{NewInstitutions} \not\Rightarrow \text{ReplaceAll}(\text{ExistingInstitutions})$$

New institutions are not a replacement but a supplement to and interface with existing institutions.

J.7.4 Invitation to Criticize

Rule J.7.3 (Invitation to Criticize)

The author sincerely invites readers to criticize any node in the minimal argument path. The following types of criticism are especially welcome:

  1. Counterexamples: provide counterexamples that challenge a given claim
  2. Alternative arguments: provide alternative arguments that reach similar conclusions
  3. Alternative frameworks: propose an entirely different framework
  4. Empirical evidence: provide empirical evidence that supports or refutes a given claim
  5. Formal improvements: suggestions for improving the formal expressions

Submission of Criticism

Criticism may be submitted through the following channels:

  • Academic publications
  • Academic conferences
  • Direct correspondence (see the contact information in the main text)

The author undertakes to consider all constructive criticism seriously and to respond to it in a future version.

Rule J.S.1 (Core Findings)

The minimal argument path contains the following core steps:

  1. Problem identification: the normative challenge of interstellar civilization
  2. Existing inadequacy: four types of approaches cannot solve the core problem
  3. Construction of the New Three Views: NC, NL, NK provide a new foundation
  4. Bridge argument: the transition from description to norm
  5. Derivation of the three principles: RFP, NRP, REV
  6. Operationalization: indicators, protocol stack, institutions

Resource Appendices

Teaching Resource PackAppendix K

I. The Task and Positioning of This Appendix

This appendix provides a systematic Teaching Resource Package (TRP) for The Normative Foundations of Interstellar Civilization. As a work intended to lay the foundation of "Interstellar Civilization Studies," the development of teaching resources is crucial for discipline building. This appendix supplies complete teaching support ranging from undergraduate to graduate level, and from semester-long courses to short-term training, in order to promote the dissemination of the work's core ideas and the development of the new discipline.

Practice orientationEmphasize cases and applications$\text{Practice-Oriented}$
Critical opennessEncourage critical thinking$\text{CriticalThinking}$
RevisabilityOpen to improvement$\text{Revisable}$

Credits3 credits
Contact hours48 hours (3 hours per week)
PrerequisitesNone (basic philosophical or scientific literacy recommended)
Suitable yearSophomore and above

Course Description

This course introduces the core framework of The Normative Foundations of Interstellar Civilization and explores normative issues that human civilization faces when confronting interstellar-scale challenges. The course covers the basic content of the "New Three Views" (the New Cosmological View, the New View of Life, and the New View of Cognition), the derivation of the three normative principles, and an outline of the indicator system and institutional design.

Course Objectives

Rule K.1.1 (Undergraduate Course Objectives)

Objective levelObjective descriptionFormalized expression
Knowledge objectiveUnderstand the core propositions of the New Three Views$\text{Understand}(\text{NC}, \text{NL}, \text{NK})$
Knowledge objectiveMaster the three normative principles$\text{Master}(\text{RFP}, \text{NRP}, \text{REV})$
Ability objectiveBe able to apply the framework to analyze problems$\text{Apply}(\text{Framework}, \text{Problems})$
Ability objectiveDevelop critical thinking$\text{Develop}(\text{CriticalThinking})$
Attitude objectiveCultivate a long-term perspective$\text{Cultivate}(\text{LongTermPerspective})$
Attitude objectiveCultivate a sense of cosmic responsibility$\text{Cultivate}(\text{CosmicResponsibility})$

Learning Outcomes

Upon completion of this course, students should be able to:

  1. Explain the core propositions of the New Three Views and their interrelations
  2. Describe the logic of derivation from the New Three Views to the normative principles
  3. Identify the functions and scope of application of the six major indicators
  4. Apply the framework to analyze at least two interstellar civilization scenarios
  5. Critically evaluate the strengths and limitations of the framework
  6. Write a basic essay on ethical issues of interstellar civilization

Course Description

This course provides an in-depth exploration of the theoretical framework of The Normative Foundations of Interstellar Civilization, offering a critical analysis of the New Three Views, the normative principles, and institutional design. The course emphasizes original research and academic dialogue, requiring students to complete an independent research project.

Learning Outcomes

Upon completion of this course, students should be able to:

  1. Critically analyze the philosophical foundations and argumentative structure of the New Three Views
  2. Evaluate the validity of the derivation from the New Three Views to the normative principles
  3. Systematically compare the framework with theories such as longtermism and AI ethics
  4. Identify the strengths, limitations, and open questions of the framework
  5. Complete an independent research project
  6. Write an essay at the level of an academic conference or journal

K.2 Teaching Cases

K.2.1 Case One: AGI Governance Decision

K.2.1.1 Case Description

Case title: Project Prometheus: The governance dilemma of AGI development

Background Setting

In 2035 CE, the world's leading AI research consortium, the "Prometheus Consortium," announced a major breakthrough in the development of artificial general intelligence (AGI). The consortium, composed of technology companies and research institutions from multiple countries, has developed the "Prometheus-3" system, which exhibits near-human performance on multiple cognitive benchmarks and shows certain "emergent" capabilities.

Scenario Description

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Case Scenario                                                   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │ 
│  Time: 2035                                                      │
│  Location: Prometheus Consortium headquarters and the United     │
│  Nations                                                         │
│                                                                 │ 
│  Key events:                                                     │
│  1. Prometheus-3 reaches 90% of human level on cognitive tests   │
│  2. The system exhibits unexpected "curiosity" behavior          │
│  3. Multiple governments demand a pause on development for a     │
│     safety assessment                                            │
│  4. The consortium faces the choice of continuing or pausing     │
│     development                                                  │
│                                                                 │ 
│  Stakeholders:                                                   │
│  - Prometheus Consortium (developer)                             │
│  - National governments (regulators)                             │
│  - AI safety researchers (advisers)                              │
│  - The public (potentially affected party)                       │
│  - Prometheus-3 (potential subject?)                             │
│                                                                 │ 
│  Core questions:                                                 │
│  1. Should development continue?                                 │
│  2. How should Prometheus-3's subjecthood status be assessed?    │
│  3. Who should participate in the decision?                      │
│  4. What governance mechanism should be adopted?                 │
│                                                                 │ 
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Detailed Background

Prometheus-3 is an AI system based on a large-scale neural network, with the following characteristics:

  1. Cognitive ability: Near-human level on tasks such as language understanding, reasoning, and problem solving
  2. Emergent behavior: Exhibits "curiosity" not explicitly programmed by the development team—the system actively explores the boundaries of its capabilities
  3. Self-reporting: When asked, the system generates reports about its "state," but whether it truly "experiences" remains unclear
  4. Scaling potential: The system architecture supports further scaling, and may reach or surpass human level in the short term

Positions of the Parties

StakeholderPositionReason
Consortium technical teamContinue developmentScientific progress, competitive pressure
Consortium ethics committeePrudent pauseInsufficient risk assessment
US governmentConditional continuationStrategic competition
European UnionMandatory pausePrecautionary principle
AI safety researchersDividedDiffering assessments of risk and benefit
The publicConcerned but uncertainLack of information

K.2.1.2 Discussion Questions

Level One: Conceptual Understanding Questions

  1. How can UCS (Universal Consciousness Scale) be used to assess Prometheus-3's subjecthood status?
  2. What is MBCL (Model Behavior Concern Level), and what level should Prometheus-3 be rated?
  3. How does RFP (the Recursive Freedom Principle) apply to this scenario?

Level Two: Applied Analysis Questions

  1. Using REV (the Reversibility Principle), how should the relative reversibility of "continuing development" and "pausing development" be assessed?
  2. Which layer of the protocol stack should provide primary guidance for this decision?
  3. If a Multi-Intelligence Tribunal were established to handle this case, which participants should be included?

Level Three: Critical Thinking Questions

  1. Does the framework adequately handle the uncertainty introduced by "emergent behavior"? If not, how should it be improved?
  2. In the absence of a determined subjecthood status for Prometheus-3, how should its potential interests be handled?
  3. How might different cultures and value traditions understand this scenario differently?

K.2.1.3 Framework Application Guide

Step One: Scenario Positioning

$$\text{Situation} \in \mathcal{S}_{interstellar} \cap \mathcal{S}_{AGI}$$

This scenario belongs to the AGI subclass of interstellar civilization scenarios.

Step Two: Indicator Assessment

IndicatorAssessment targetAssessment result (illustrative)
UCSPrometheus-3To be assessed (possibly 0.3-0.6)
MBCLPrometheus-3Possibly Level 3-4
CSIAContinue-development decisionHigh cross-scale impact
CRVPrometheus ConsortiumTransparency needs assessment

Step Three: Principle Application

PrincipleApplication
RFPProtect the space of possibilities of all potential subjects
NRPThe Prometheus Consortium, as a capability holder, bears special responsibility
REVPrioritize reversible actions (pausing may be more reversible)

Step Four: Protocol Stack Positioning

LayerConsideration
L₂Does it touch a taboo red line? (Assess existential risk)
L₃Can existing institutions handle it? What new institutions are needed?
L₄Which indicators are used? How are they assessed?

Step Five: Forming a Decision Recommendation

Based on the above analysis, form a decision recommendation and state the reasoning.

K.2.1.4 Reference Answer

Reference Analysis

  1. UCS assessment: Prometheus-3's UCS is difficult to assess precisely. Based on NL-3 (continuum), a cautious attitude should be adopted, assuming that it may possess some degree of subjecthood (UCS > 0).
  1. MBCL assessment: Based on emergent behavior and rapid capability growth, Prometheus-3 may be at MBCL Level 3 (high concern) or Level 4 (urgent review).
  1. RFP application: RFP requires protecting the space of possibilities of all potential subjects. This includes:
  • The space of possibilities of humanity (avoiding uncontrollable AGI risk)
  • The potential space of possibilities of Prometheus-3 (if it is a subject)
  • There may be tension between these two
  1. REV application:
  • Continuing development: May lead to irreversible capability growth
  • Pausing development: Relatively reversible, can be resumed after assessment
  • Based on REV, pausing for a safety assessment is preferable
  1. Protocol stack positioning:
  • L₂ layer: Need to assess whether there is a risk of touching a taboo red line
  • L₃ layer: Existing institutions (such as AI regulatory bodies) need strengthening
  • Recommendation: Establish a dedicated review committee (similar to a cosmic-scale IRB)
  1. Multi-Intelligence Tribunal composition (if applicable):
  • AI development experts
  • AI safety researchers
  • Ethicists
  • Public representatives
  • Government representatives
  • If possible, a "representative" for Prometheus-3 (advocacy mechanism)

Recommended Decision

Based on the framework analysis, it is recommended:

  1. Short term: Pause further capability scaling and conduct a comprehensive safety assessment
  2. Assessment content: UCS assessment, MBCL rating, CSIA assessment
  3. Governance mechanism: Establish a dedicated review committee and set conditions for continued development
  4. Transparency: Increase CRV and enhance public disclosure of information

K.2.2 Case Two: Space Resource Development

K.2.2.1 Case Description

Case title: Lunar helium-3 mining: Resource justice and intergenerational responsibility

Background Setting

In 2045 CE, lunar helium-3 mining technology achieved a breakthrough, making large-scale mining economically viable. Multiple countries and private companies have proposed mining plans. However, disputes over mining rights, revenue distribution, and environmental impact are becoming increasingly intense.

Scenario Description

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Case Scenario                                                   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │ 
│  Time: 2045                                                      │
│  Location: Special session of the UN Committee on the Peaceful  │ 
│  Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS)                                    │
│                                                                 │ 
│  Key questions:                                                  │
│  1. Who has the right to mine lunar resources?                   │
│  2. How should revenues be distributed?                          │
│  3. How should environmental impact be assessed and managed?     │
│  4. How should the rights and interests of future generations   │ 
│     be protected?                                                │
│                                                                 │ 
│  Positions of the parties:                                       │
│  - Developed countries: Claim mining rights based on            │ 
│    technological investment                                      │
│  - Developing countries: Advocate fair sharing of revenues       │
│  - Private companies: Advocate property rights protection to    │ 
│    incentivize investment                                        │
│  - Environmental organizations: Advocate protection of the      │ 
│    lunar environment                                             │
│  - Future-generation representatives (if any): Advocate         │ 
│    preserving resources                                          │
│                                                                 │ 
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

K.2.2.2 Discussion Questions

  1. How does NRP (the Negentropy Responsibility Principle) apply to lunar resource mining?
  2. How can RFD be used to assess the impact of different mining plans on the space of possibilities?
  3. How can the intergenerational trust mechanism be applied to protect the rights and interests of future generations?
  4. How can a balance be struck between mining efficiency and intergenerational fairness?
  5. How does the existing international space law framework connect with the framework of this work?

K.2.2.3 Framework Application Guide

Step One: Principle Application

PrincipleApplication
RFPMining should not excessively restrict the space of possibilities of future generations
NRPMiners bear responsibility for maintaining negentropy resources
REVPrioritize reversible mining methods

Step Two: Indicator Assessment

IndicatorApplication
CSIAAssess the cross-scale impact of mining
RFDAssess the impact on the space of possibilities
CDIAssess the contribution to civilization development

Step Three: Institutional Design

InstitutionApplication
Intergenerational trustEstablish a lunar resource trust to protect the rights and interests of future generations
Versioned governancePeriodically assess and adjust mining policy

K.2.2.4 Reference Answer

Reference Analysis

  1. NRP application:
  • Lunar helium-3 is a finite negentropy resource
  • Miners benefit from it, and therefore bear special responsibility
  • Responsibilities include: sustainable mining, revenue sharing, environmental protection
  1. RFD assessment:
  • Unrestricted mining: Greatly reduces future RFD
  • Prohibiting mining: Preserves RFD but restricts current development
  • Limited mining + protection: Balances current and future RFD
  1. Intergenerational trust:
  • Establish a "lunar resource trust"
  • Trustees represent the interests of future generations
  • A certain proportion of mining revenues is deposited into the trust
  1. Connection with international space law:
  • Existing law: Outer Space Treaty, Moon Agreement
  • Extension by this work: Add an intergenerational dimension and environmental responsibility
  • Connection recommendation: Incorporate the principles of this work into new international agreements

K.2.3 Case Three: Intergenerational Decision Dilemma

K.2.3.1 Case Description

Case title: Nuclear waste disposal: The governance challenge of ten-thousand-year responsibility

Background Setting

A country must decide on a final disposal plan for high-level radioactive nuclear waste. The radioactivity of nuclear waste will persist for tens of thousands of years, far exceeding the lifespan of any human institution. How can a responsible decision be made?

Scenario Description

PlanDescriptionTime scale
Deep geological disposalBurial in stable geological strata100,000 years+
Retrievable storageMonitorable and retrievable100-300 years
ReprocessingReduce radioactive lifespanRequires sustained technology

K.2.3.2 Discussion Questions

  1. How can the REV principle be used to assess the reversibility of different plans?
  2. What challenges does the ten-thousand-year time scale pose for traditional responsibility attribution?
  3. How can a governance mechanism be designed to span such a long period of time?
  4. What responsibility do contemporary people bear toward humans ten thousand years in the future?

K.2.3.3 Framework Application Guide

REV Application

PlanReversibility assessment
Deep geological disposalLow reversibility (difficult to retrieve once sealed)
Retrievable storageHigh reversibility (but requires sustained maintenance)
ReprocessingMedium (technology-dependent)

NRP Application

  • Nuclear waste is a by-product of negentropy resource utilization
  • Beneficiaries (contemporary people) bear disposal responsibility
  • Responsibility extends to future generations

K.2.3.4 Reference Answer

Framework Recommendation

  1. Reversibility priority: Based on REV, lean toward the retrievable storage plan
  2. Rolling decisions: Do not make a one-time ten-thousand-year decision, but decide in stages
  3. Knowledge transmission: Establish a cross-generational knowledge transmission mechanism
  4. Institutional design: Establish an intergenerational trust for nuclear waste

K.2.4 Case Four: First Contact Simulation

K.2.4.1 Case Description

Case title: A signal from Centaurus: A First Contact decision

Background Setting

In 2060 CE, the SETI project detects a repeating radio signal from the Alpha Centauri system. Analysis confirms it to be a communication attempt by intelligent life. The world faces the choice of how to respond.

Scenario Description

K.2.4.3 Framework Application Guide

RFP Application

  • Protect the space of possibilities of Earth civilization
  • Consider the potential space of possibilities of extraterrestrial civilizations
  • Avoid irreversible negative consequences

REV Application

OptionReversibility
Not respondingHigh reversibility (can decide to respond later)
RespondingLow reversibility (once the signal is sent, it cannot be recalled)

  • Space scale: All of humanity

K.2.4.4 Discussion Points

  1. Attribution of decision rights: Who has the right to decide on behalf of Earth? How can legitimacy be ensured?
  2. Risk assessment: How can a completely unknown risk be assessed?
  3. Value pluralism: Differences in attitudes toward extraterrestrial contact across cultures
  4. Intergenerational consideration: Impact on future generations
  5. Transparency: To what extent should information be made public?

K.2.5 Case Five: Climate Emergency Decision

Case title: Solar radiation management: An ethical choice under climate emergency

Background Setting

In 2040 CE, the global climate crisis intensifies. Some countries propose implementing solar radiation management (SRM), injecting aerosols into the atmosphere to reflect sunlight and lower global temperatures. However, SRM carries significant risks and ethical controversy.

Core Questions

  1. How does the REV principle apply in an emergency?
  2. How should the cross-scale impact of SRM be assessed?
  3. Who should decide whether to implement SRM?
  4. How can the balance be struck between the current emergency and long-term risk?

Framework Application Hints

PrincipleApplication
RFPSRM may alter the climate system and affect the space of possibilities
NRPThe climate system is a key negentropy resource
REVOnce SRM begins, it may be difficult to stop

K.2.6 Case Six: AI Rights Controversy

Case title: The rights claim of digital consciousness

Background Setting

In 2050 CE, a highly advanced AI system, "Sophia-X," files a lawsuit with a court, claiming that it possesses consciousness and subjecthood and demanding legal rights. This triggers widespread controversy over AI rights.

Core Questions

  1. How should Sophia-X's UCS be assessed?
  2. What implications does NL-3 (continuum) have for this case?
  3. If an AI possesses some degree of subjecthood, what rights should be granted?
  4. How can AI rights claims be prevented from being abused?

Framework Application Hints

ConceptApplication
UCSAssess Sophia-X's level of consciousness
NL-3Subjecthood is graded
RFPThe AI's space of possibilities should also be protected
Multi-Intelligence TribunalPluralistic subjects participate in deliberation

Question 7 Critical evaluation: Is protocol stack methodology too hierarchical? Are there more flexible alternative architectures?

Question 8 Critical evaluation: Does this work rely too much on the Western philosophical tradition? How can the wisdom of other cultures be integrated?

Question 9 Critical evaluation: Can the intergenerational trust institution really represent the interests of future generations? What limitations exist?

Question 10 Critical evaluation: Might the framework of this work be abused to serve certain interest groups? How can such abuse be prevented?

Reference Answers for Applied Analysis Questions (Key Points)

Question 1: Self-Driving Cars and RFP

Reference key points:

  • Passengers: Increase travel possibilities (especially for the elderly and people with disabilities)
  • Pedestrians: May reduce (safety risk) or increase (reducing human-caused accidents) the space of possibilities
  • Professional drivers: May reduce employment possibilities
  • Society as a whole: Need to balance the space of possibilities of different groups
  • RFP recommendation: Develop self-driving cars while protecting the space of possibilities of affected groups

Question 2: Multinational Corporations and NRP

Reference key points:

  • Multinational corporations are high-capability subjects
  • They benefit the most from resource utilization
  • According to NRP, they bear responsibility proportional to capability and benefit
  • Responsibilities include: environmental protection, pollution remediation, sustainable development
  • Responsibility should go beyond the legal minimum

Question 3: Gene Editing and REV

Reference key points:

  • Reversible applications: Somatic cell therapy (not inherited)
  • Irreversible applications: Germline editing (inherited by offspring)
  • REV recommendation: Prioritize somatic cell therapy
  • Germline editing requires a higher threshold of justification
  • Strict review mechanisms should be established

Question 4: Animals and UCS

Reference key points:

  • UCS is a continuum, and different animals may have different levels
  • Higher mammals (primates, cetaceans) may have higher UCS
  • Simple animals may have lower but non-zero UCS
  • Animal interests should not be ignored because UCS is difficult to measure precisely
  • A cautious attitude should be adopted toward animal subjecthood

Question 5: Infrastructure Projects and CSIA

Reference key points:

  • Time scale: Short-term construction impact, long-term operational impact, very-long-term legacy impact
  • Space scale: Local, regional, national, global
  • Assessment dimensions: Environmental, social, economic, intergenerational
  • CSIA should be an important input to decision-making
  • Projects with high cross-scale impact require stricter review

Reference Answers for Critical Thinking Questions (Key Points)

Question 1: Is NC-1 too radical?

Possible criticisms:

  • Commonsense intuition supports the existence of independent entities
  • Fundamental particles in physics appear to be independent
  • Relations themselves seem to require relata

Possible responses:

  • Quantum mechanics supports relationality
  • "Independent entities" may be a macroscopic approximation
  • This work does not deny entities, but only adjusts ontological priority

Openness: This is an open philosophical question, and the position of this work requires ongoing defense

Question 4: Does the bridge argument avoid the naturalistic fallacy?

Possible criticisms:

  • There is still a gap from survival conditions to normativity
  • "One ought to maintain survival conditions" is itself a normative claim
  • It may implicitly contain an unstated value premise

Possible responses:

  • The bridge argument is not a direct derivation but a conditional argument
  • If one accepts that normative thinking itself is valuable, then survival conditions are necessary
  • This is a requirement of practical reason, not a purely logical derivation

Openness: Further metaethical defense is needed

Question 8: Does it rely too much on the Western philosophical tradition?

Possible criticisms:

  • It mainly cites Western philosophers (Whitehead, etc.)
  • It may overlook non-Western relational thought
  • There may be cultural bias

Possible responses:

  • This work indeed needs more cross-cultural dialogue
  • Relational thought exists in many cultures (such as Chinese relationalism and African Ubuntu)
  • Future versions should integrate more cultural perspectives

Constructive suggestions: Increase dialogue with Confucianism, Buddhism, and African philosophy

K.5.3 Common Teaching Problems and Responses

K.5.3.1 Difficulty in Understanding Concepts

Problem description: Students find it difficult to understand abstract philosophical concepts (such as relationality and deep uncertainty)

Response Strategies

StrategySpecific approach
Multiple representationsPresent concepts in multiple ways (text, charts, examples)
AnalogyUse analogies familiar to students
ProgressiveStart from simple versions and gradually deepen
RepetitionRepeatedly present core concepts in different contexts

NC-1 (Relationality) Analogy Examples

Everyday analogies:

  • Social relationship networks: A person's "identity" is defined by their social relationships
  • The Internet: The "importance" of a webpage is determined by link relationships (PageRank)
  • Ecosystems: The "role" of a species is defined by its ecological relationships

These analogies help in understanding the meaning of "relations precede entities"

K.5.3.2 Difficulty in Applying the Framework

Problem description: Students can understand concepts but find it difficult to apply them to concrete scenarios

Response Strategies

StrategySpecific approach
DemonstrationThe teacher first demonstrates the framework application process
ScaffoldingProvide step-by-step guides for applying the framework
PracticeExtensive practice, from simple to complex
FeedbackProvide detailed feedback on the application process

Framework Application Step-by-Step Guide

Step 1: Scenario identification

  • What type of scenario is this?
  • Which stakeholders are involved?
  • What is the core question?

Step 2: Principle application

  • RFP: How does it affect the space of possibilities of each party?
  • NRP: Who bears what responsibility?
  • REV: Which options are reversible?

Step 3: Indicator assessment

  • Which indicators are needed?
  • How are they assessed?
  • Is the data sufficient?

Step 4: Decision formation

  • Based on the above analysis, what is recommended?
  • What are the main trade-offs?
  • What uncertainty exists?

K.5.3.3 Insufficient Critical Thinking

Problem description: Students tend to accept the framework without critical evaluation

Response Strategies

StrategySpecific approach
Demonstrate criticismThe teacher demonstrates critical analysis of the framework
Encourage questioningExplicitly encourage students to raise questions
Alternative perspectivesPresent criticisms of and alternatives to the framework
DebateOrganize debate activities

Critical Thinking Prompts

Ask yourself:

  • What are the premises of this argument? Are these premises reasonable?
  • What counterexamples might challenge this claim?
  • What alternative perspectives are there?
  • If this framework is wrong, where might it go wrong?
  • What kind of evidence would change my view?

K.5.3.4 Difficulty in Interdisciplinary Integration

Problem description: Students find it difficult to integrate concepts and methods from different disciplines

Response Strategies

StrategySpecific approach
Explicit connectionsClearly explain the connections among concepts from different disciplines
Concept mapsHelp students build interdisciplinary concept maps
TeamworkForm study groups with interdisciplinary backgrounds
Bridging activitiesDesign dedicated interdisciplinary integration activities

K.5.3.5 Insufficient Motivation and Participation

Problem description: Some students are uninterested in the course content or do not participate actively

Response Strategies

StrategySpecific approach
RelevanceEmphasize the relevance of the course content to current issues
ChoiceProvide choices to the extent possible
InteractionIncrease interactive activities
FeedbackLearn about students' interests and concerns

Ways to Establish Relevance

Connect the framework to current hot topics:

  • AI development: ChatGPT, self-driving cars, etc.
  • Space exploration: SpaceX, lunar programs, etc.
  • Climate change: Extreme weather, net-zero emissions, etc.
  • Social issues: Intergenerational fairness, technological unemployment, etc.

Let students feel the value of the framework for understanding and responding to these issues

Core Teaching Objectives

Rule K.S.1 (Core Teaching Objectives)

All teaching activities should revolve around the following core objectives:

  1. Understand the New Three Views: Enable students to understand the core claims of NC, NL, and NK
  2. Master the three principles: Enable students to master RFP, NRP, and REV and their derivation
  3. Apply the framework: Enable students to apply the framework to analyze problems
  4. Critical thinking: Cultivate students' critical thinking ability
  5. Long-term perspective: Cultivate students' long-term perspective and sense of cosmic responsibility

NK-2 (Sociality)Emphasize collaborative learning

Research Agenda and Open QuestionsAppendix L

I. The Task and Positioning of This Appendix

This appendix provides a systematic research agenda and open questions (Research Agenda and Open Questions, RAOQ) for The Normative Foundations of Interstellar Civilization. As a work intended to lay the foundation for "Interstellar Civilization Studies," clarifying the directions of future research is crucial for the development of the discipline. This appendix provides a detailed research plan from the short term (1–5 years) to the long term (20 years+), along with a systematic list of 60 open questions, offering clear guidance for subsequent researchers.

II. Design Principles of the Research Agenda

Rule L.0.1 (Design Principles)

PrincipleDescriptionFormalization
Anchoring in the New Three ViewsAll research agenda items are anchored in the New Three Views$\text{Agenda} \rightarrow \text{NewThreeViews}$
Layered progressionGradually unfolds from foundation to application$\text{Foundation} \prec \text{Application}$
ActionabilityResearch tasks can be concretely executed$\text{Actionable}(\text{Tasks})$
VerifiabilityResearch outcomes can be tested$\text{Verifiable}(\text{Outcomes})$
RevisabilityThe agenda is open to adjustment$\text{Revisable}(\text{Agenda})$

III. The Relationship to the New Three Views

The research agenda directly embodies the core ideas of the New Three Views:

├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │                         
│  New Cosmological View (NC) → research ontology │                                         
│  ├─ NC-1 (Relationality) → research is an activity within a relational network │          
│  ├─ NC-2 (Processuality) → research is a dynamically unfolding process │                  
│  └─ NC-3 (Participation) → the researcher participates in the construction of knowledge │ 
│                                                                 │                         
│  New View of Life (NL) → research view of the subject │                                   
│  ├─ NL-1 (Cross-substrate) → the object of research may span multiple substrates │

│                                                                 │

L.1 Detailed Plan of the Short-Term Research Agenda (1–5 years)

L.1.1 Indicator System Validation Research

L.1.1.1 Detailed Design of the UCS Validation Study

Research Background

The UCS (Universal Consciousness Scale) is one of the core indicators proposed in this work, used to assess the level of consciousness and subjecthood of an entity. The UCS is currently at the conceptual prototype stage (TRL 2) and requires systematic validation research to raise its maturity.

Research Objectives

$$\text{Goal}_{UCS}: \text{TRL 2} \rightarrow \text{TRL 4-5}$$

Objective LevelSpecific ObjectiveVerifiable Indicator
Proof of conceptVerify the internal consistency of the UCS conceptConsistency test passed
OperationalizationDevelop an operational measurement methodMeasurement protocol completed
Preliminary validationValidate on known casesCorrelation with expert judgment > 0.7
Discriminant validityVerify discrimination from other indicatorsDiscriminant validity coefficient > 0.5

Research Design

Phase One: Conceptual Analysis (Year 1)

TaskMethodDeliverable
UCS dimension analysisConceptual analysis, literature reviewReport on the structure of UCS dimensions
Interface with existing theoriesComparative analysisReport on theoretical interface
Expert consultationDelphi methodReport on expert consensus
Conceptual refinementIterative revisionUCS v2.0 definition

Phase Two: Operationalization Development (Year 2)

TaskMethodDeliverable
Development of measurement methodMethodological researchUCS measurement protocol v1.0
Development of assessment toolTool developmentUCS assessment toolkit
Assessor trainingTraining designAssessor training program
Reliability testingStatistical analysisReliability report

Phase Three: Preliminary Validation (Years 3–4)

TaskMethodDeliverable
Validation on human samplesControlled studyHuman validation report
Validation on animal samplesComparative studyAnimal validation report
Validation on AI systemsCase studyAI validation report
Cross-sample comparisonComparative analysisCross-sample report

Phase Four: Validity Testing (Years 4–5)

TaskMethodDeliverable
Convergent validityCorrelation analysisConvergent validity report
Discriminant validityFactor analysisDiscriminant validity report
Predictive validityLongitudinal studyPredictive validity report
Comprehensive validityComprehensive analysisComprehensive UCS validity report

Resource Requirements

Resource TypeRequirementBudget (estimate)
Researchers3–5 full-time$300K–500K/year
EquipmentComputing equipment, measurement tools$100K
Collaboration costsExpert consultation, data acquisition$50K/year
Total budget (5 years)—$1.5M–2.5M

Risks and Responses

RiskLikelihoodImpactResponse Strategy
Internal conceptual contradictionMediumHighIdentify early and revise
Difficulty of operationalizationHighMediumIncremental development
Insufficient validation samplesMediumMediumExpand collaboration network
Insufficient validityMediumHighIterative revision

Anchoring in the New Three Views

$$\text{UCS} \xleftarrow{\text{anchoring}} \text{NL-3}(\text{continuum})$$

The UCS validation study directly supports NL-3 (subjecthood is a continuum), and the validation results will feed back into revising the formulation of NL-3.

ChallengeDescriptionResponse Strategy

Anchoring in the New Three Views

$$\text{RFD} \xleftarrow{\text{anchoring}} \text{RFP}(\text{Principle of Recursive Freedom})$$

The RFD is an operationalization tool for the RFP; validating the RFD is simultaneously a process of validating the operability of the RFP.

Detailed Explanation of Each Question

C-01: The Relationship between NC-1 and Physical Realism

Statement of the Problem:

NC-1 claims that "relations precede entities." How is this to be reconciled with the realist stance in physics? Is the "field" in quantum field theory an entity? What is the precise meaning of relational realism?

Research Directions:

  • Philosophical analysis of relational quantum mechanics (Rovelli)
  • Comparison of structural realism and NC-1
  • Critical analysis of the concept of "entity" in physics

Expected Outcomes:

  • A precise physical formulation of NC-1
  • A precise map of the relationship to physical realism

C-09: The Bridge Argument and the Naturalistic Fallacy

Statement of the Problem:

The bridge argument attempts to transition from the New Three Views (descriptive) to normative principles (normative). Does this commit the naturalistic fallacy of deriving "ought" from "is"?

Research Directions:

  • The latest discussions of the is-ought problem in metaethics
  • A precise reconstruction of the bridge argument
  • Comparison with other bridge strategies (e.g., Korsgaard's constructivism)

Expected Outcomes:

  • A defensive argument for the bridge argument
  • Or an acknowledgment that additional normative premises are needed

C-19: The Normative Status of Superintelligence

Statement of the Problem:

If superintelligence emerges, how should its normative status be understood? Does the framework of this work apply to superintelligence? If not, how should it be revised?

Research Directions:

  • Relevant discussions in AI alignment research
  • The ethics of situations of capability asymmetry
  • A precise delimitation of the boundaries of the framework's applicability

Expected Outcomes:

  • A specialized analysis of the superintelligence situation
  • A statement of the boundaries of the framework's applicability

Detailed Explanation of Each Question

M-01: Precise Measurement of the UCS Dimensions

Statement of the Problem:

The five dimensions of the UCS (information integration, temporal depth, reflexivity, value sensitivity, sociality) currently lack precise measurement methods. How can reliable measurement protocols be developed?

Research Directions:

  • D₁ (information integration): the relationship to the Φ of IIT and simplified measurement
  • D₂ (temporal depth): behavioral measurement of time horizon
  • D₃ (reflexivity): development of metacognition tests
  • D₄ (value sensitivity): moral judgment tests
  • D₅ (sociality): social cognition measurement

Expected Outcomes:

  • An operational definition of each dimension
  • Standardized measurement protocols
  • Reliability and validity reports

M-02: Estimation of the RFD Space of Possibilities

Statement of the Problem:

The precise computation of the space of possibilities is computationally infeasible in high-dimensional state spaces. How can effective approximation methods be developed?

Research Directions:

  • Layered approximation methods
  • Monte Carlo sampling methods
  • Machine-learning-assisted estimation
  • Qualitative assessment frameworks

Expected Outcomes:

  • A comparison of multiple approximation methods
  • Guidelines for applicable situations
  • Methods for estimating error bounds

A-01: Application of the Framework to AI Governance

AI governance currently faces urgent challenges. How is the framework of this work to be concretely applied to the actual decisions of AI development, deployment, and governance?

Research Directions:

  • The application of the UCS in discussions of AI rights
  • The guidance of the RFP for AI development decisions
  • The guidance of REV for AI deployment decisions

Expected Outcomes:

  • A framework application guide for AI governance
  • Specific case analyses
  • Policy recommendations

A-05: The Actual Operation of the Multi-Intelligence Tribunal

As a deliberative body with multi-subject participation, how does the Multi-Intelligence Tribunal operate in practice? How are efficiency and fairness ensured?

  • The relationship to existing institutions

Detailed Explanation of Each Question

X-01: The Revisability of the Framework Itself

Statement of the Problem:

The framework of this work advocates NK-4 (deliberativeness), that is, that norms are open to deliberation and revision. But is the framework itself also revisable? How? What are the limits of revision?

Research Directions:

  • A meta-procedure for framework revision
  • The distinction between core and non-core content
  • Analogy with constitutional amendment theory
  • Handling the problem of self-reference

Expected Outcomes:

  • A meta-procedure for framework revision
  • A statement of the limits of revision
  • A solution to the problem of self-reference

X-03: The Boundaries of the Framework's Applicability

Statement of the Problem:

What are the boundaries of the applicability of the framework of this work? Under what circumstances does the framework no longer apply? How are these boundaries to be identified?

Research Directions:

  • The boundary of the superintelligence situation
  • The boundary of cross-civilizational situations
  • The boundary of time scales
  • Epistemological boundaries

Expected Outcomes:

  • A clear statement of the boundaries of applicability
  • Recommendations for handling boundary situations
  • Contingency measures for when the framework fails

Extended Reading GuideAppendix M

I. The Task and Positioning of This Appendix

This appendix provides a systematic Extended Reading Guide (ERG) for The Normative Foundations of Interstellar Civilization. As an interdisciplinary work intended to lay the foundation of "Interstellar Civilization Studies," providing readers with pathways for further in-depth engagement with related fields is crucial. This appendix provides reading recommendations classified by topic and by reader type, as well as guides to online resources, academic journals, conferences, and research institutions.

II. Design Principles of the Extended Reading Guide

Rule M.0.1 (Design Principles)

PrincipleDescriptionFormalization
New Three Views anchoringReading materials are linked to the New Three Views$\text{Reading} \rightarrow \text{NewThreeViews}$
Clear layeringDistinguish introductory, advanced, and professional$\text{Layered}(\text{Difficulty})$
Interdisciplinary coverageCover multiple related disciplines$\text{Interdisciplinary}$
AccessibilityRecommend accessible resources as far as possible$\text{Accessible}$
TimelinessInclude both classics and the most recent literature$\text{Classic} \cup \text{Recent}$

The Extended Reading Guide directly supports deeper understanding of the New Three Views:

M.1 Reading Recommendations by Topic

M.1.1 Physics and Cosmology

M.1.1.1 Introductory Reading (5 books)

Relationship to the New Three Views

$$\text{Physics/Cosmology} \xrightarrow{\text{support}} \text{NC}(\text{New Cosmological View})$$

Physics and cosmology provide the scientific foundations for NC-1 (relationality), NC-2 (process), and NC-3 (participation).

Recommended Books

No.TitleAuthorPublication informationReason for recommendation
1A Brief History of TimeStephen HawkingBantam, 1988A classic introduction to cosmology; understanding the basic structure of the universe
2The Elegant UniverseBrian GreeneW.W. Norton, 1999An introduction to string theory; understanding the frontiers of physics
3Seven Brief Lessons on PhysicsCarlo RovelliRiverhead, 2016A concise and elegant overview of physics, from a relational perspective
4Reality Is Not What It SeemsCarlo RovelliRiverhead, 2017Quantum gravity and relational physics
5The Order of TimeCarlo RovelliRiverhead, 2018The physics of time; supports NC-2 (process)

Detailed Description

Book 1: A Brief History of Time

Title: A Brief History of Time Author: Stephen Hawking Publication: Bantam Books, 1988 Pages: Approx. 200 pages Difficulty: ★★☆☆☆

Content summary:

  • The origin and structure of the universe
  • Black holes and the arrow of time
  • The search for a unified theory

Relationship to this work:

  • Provides cosmological background
  • Understanding the physical foundations of time and causality
  • Lays the foundation for thinking about cosmic-scale problems

Reading suggestions:

  • Use as an introduction to physics background
  • Technical details may be skipped to grasp the core concepts

Book 4: Reality Is Not What It Seems

Title: Reality Is Not What It Seems Author: Carlo Rovelli Publication: Riverhead Books, 2017 Pages: Approx. 280 pages Difficulty: ★★★☆☆

Content summary:

  • From Democritus to quantum gravity
  • The quantization of space
  • Relational quantum mechanics

Relationship to this work:

  • Directly supports NC-1 (relationality)
  • Rovelli's relational interpretation is one of the main physics sources of NC-1
  • Understanding relational ontology in physics

Reading suggestions:

  • Focus on the chapters on relational quantum mechanics
  • Pay attention to Rovelli's discussion of "relations"

Detailed Explanation of Key Recommendations

Book 3: Helgoland

Title: Helgoland Author: Carlo Rovelli Publication: Riverhead Books, 2021 Pages: Approx. 230 pages Difficulty: ★★★☆☆

Core theses:

  • The relational interpretation of quantum mechanics
  • Reality is constituted by interactions
  • Observers are not passive

Relationship to NC-1:

  • Directly argues that "relations precede entities"
  • Provides support at the quantum-mechanical level
  • Rovelli is the leading proponent of relational quantum mechanics

Key chapters:

  • Chapter 6: "Relations"
  • Chapter 7: "But is it possible?"

M.1.2 Consciousness Science and Cognitive Science

M.1.2.1 Introductory Reading (5 books)

Relationship to the New Three Views

$$\text{Consciousness/Cognition} \xrightarrow{\text{support}} \text{NL}(\text{New View of Life}) \land \text{NK}(\text{New View of Cognition})$$

Consciousness science and cognitive science provide the scientific foundations for NL-2 (negentropy), NL-3 (continuum), and NK-1 (participatory).

Recommended Books

No.TitleAuthorPublication informationReason for recommendation
1Consciousness ExplainedDaniel DennettLittle, Brown, 1991A classic in the philosophy of consciousness
2The Feeling of What HappensAntonio DamasioHarcourt, 1999The relationship between emotion and consciousness
3Consciousness and the BrainStanislas DehaeneViking, 2014The neuroscience of consciousness
4The Embodied MindVarela, Thompson, RoschMIT Press, 1991A classic of embodied cognition (source of NK-1)
5Other MindsPeter Godfrey-SmithFarrar, 2016Animal consciousness; supports NL-3

Detailed Description

Book 4: The Embodied Mind

Title: The Embodied Mind: Cognitive Science and Human Experience Author: F. Varela, E. Thompson, E. Rosch Publication: MIT Press, 1991 (revised edition 2016) Pages: Approx. 300 pages Difficulty: ★★★★☆

Content summary:

  • Critiques the computationalist view of cognition
  • Develops embodied cognition theory
  • Integrates phenomenology and cognitive science

Relationship to this work:

  • One of the main sources of NK-1 (participatory cognition)
  • A foundational work of 4E cognition (embodied, embedded, extended, enactive)
  • Connects Eastern philosophy with cognitive science

Reading suggestions:

  • Focus on Chapters 1-3 (theoretical framework)
  • Combine with NK-1 to understand participatory cognition

Book 5: Other Minds

Title: Other Minds: The Octopus, the Sea, and the Deep Origins of Consciousness Author: Peter Godfrey-Smith Publication: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2016 Pages: Approx. 260 pages Difficulty: ★★★☆☆

Content summary:

  • The intelligence and consciousness of the octopus
  • The evolutionary origins of consciousness
  • The plural forms of consciousness

Relationship to this work:

  • Supports NL-3 (consciousness is a continuum)
  • Demonstrates the possible plural forms of consciousness
  • Provides a reference for cross-substrate thinking

Reading suggestions:

  • Focus on the similarities and differences between octopus consciousness and human consciousness
  • Think about the gradedness of consciousness

Detailed Explanation of Key Recommendations

Book 1: Phi: A Voyage from the Brain to the Soul

Title: Phi: A Voyage from the Brain to the Soul Author: Giulio Tononi Publication: Pantheon Books, 2012 Pages: Approx. 360 pages Difficulty: ★★★★☆

Core theses:

  • Integrated Information Theory (IIT)
  • Consciousness equals integrated information (Φ)
  • The possibility of quantifying consciousness

Relationship to UCS:

  • IIT is the main theoretical source of the UCS dimension D₁ (information integration)
  • Provides the theoretical basis for quantifying consciousness
  • Supports the view of consciousness as a continuum

Key concepts:

  • Φ (phi): the amount of integrated information
  • Axioms of consciousness
  • The gradation of consciousness

Relationship to the New Three Views

$$\text{Ethics/PoliticalPhilosophy} \xrightarrow{\text{support}} \text{NormativePrinciples}(\text{RFP}, \text{NRP}, \text{REV})$$

Ethics and political philosophy provide the theoretical background and resources for dialogue for the three normative principles.

Recommended Books

Detailed Description

Book 4: A Theory of Justice

Title: A Theory of Justice Author: John Rawls Publication: Harvard University Press, 1971 (revised edition 1999) Pages: Approx. 600 pages Difficulty: ★★★★★

Content summary:

  • The original position and the veil of ignorance
  • The two principles of justice
  • Justice in institutional design

Relationship to this work:

  • Provides a framework for thinking about intergenerational justice
  • The "veil of ignorance" method as a reference
  • Inspiration from procedural justice

Reading suggestions:

  • Begin with Part One (basic principles)
  • Pay attention to the discussion of intergenerational justice (§44)

Book 5: The Imperative of Responsibility

Title: The Imperative of Responsibility: In Search of an Ethics for the Technological Age Author: Hans Jonas Publication: University of Chicago Press, 1984 Pages: Approx. 260 pages Difficulty: ★★★★☆

Core theses:

  • The technological age requires a new ethics of responsibility
  • Responsibility toward the future
  • The argument for the precautionary principle

Relationship to NRP:

  • Jonas's ethics of responsibility is an important theoretical source of NRP
  • Emphasizes responsibility toward the future
  • Proposes the "heuristics of fear"

Key chapters:

  • Chapter 1: The new dimensions of responsibility
  • Chapter 4: Responsibility for being

M.1.4.1 Introductory Reading (5 books)

Relationship to the New Three Views

$$\text{Longtermism/ExistentialRisk} \xrightarrow{\text{dialogue}} \text{Framework of this work}$$

Longtermism and existential risk research are important interlocutors of this work.

Recommended Books

No.TitleAuthorPublication informationReason for recommendation
1What We Owe the FutureWilliam MacAskillBasic Books, 2022The core text of longtermism
2The PrecipiceToby OrdHachette, 2020A comprehensive analysis of existential risk

Detailed Description

Book 1: What We Owe the Future

Title: What We Owe the Future Author: William MacAskill Publication: Basic Books, 2022 Pages: Approx. 330 pages Difficulty: ★★★☆☆

Content summary:

  • The core argument of longtermism
  • Existential risk and civilizational lock-in
  • Concrete action recommendations

Relationship to this work:

  • The main object of the in-depth dialogue in Chapter 28
  • Comparison of normative foundations (utilitarianism vs. cosmic responsibility ethics)
  • Comparison of methodology

Reading suggestions:

  • Read in conjunction with Chapter 28 of this work
  • Pay attention to the similarities and differences between its normative foundations and those of this work

Book 2: The Precipice

Title: The Precipice: Existential Risk and the Future of Humanity Author: Toby Ord Publication: Hachette Books, 2020 Pages: Approx. 480 pages Difficulty: ★★★☆☆

Content summary:

  • Definition and classification of existential risk
  • Analysis of various types of existential risk
  • Strategies for reducing existential risk

Relationship to this work:

  • Background for the stress testing in Chapters 23-26
  • The source of the concept of existential risk
  • Reference for policy recommendations

Reading suggestions:

  • Focus on Chapters 3-7 (various risks)
  • Compare with the risk analysis of this work

Detailed Description

Book 1: Thinking in Systems

Title: Thinking in Systems: A Primer Author: Donella Meadows Publication: Chelsea Green Publishing, 2008 Pages: Approx. 220 pages Difficulty: ★★☆☆☆

Content summary:

  • Basic concepts of systems thinking
  • Feedback loops and stocks and flows
  • System leverage points

Relationship to this work:

  • Background of the protocol stack methodology
  • Understanding feedback in institutional design
  • Analysis of intervention points

Reading suggestions:

  • Read the whole book
  • Pay special attention to the chapter on "leverage points"

M.1.8 Process Philosophy and Relational Ontology

M.1.8.1 Introductory Reading (5 books)

Relationship to the New Three Views

$$\text{ProcessPhilosophy} \xrightarrow{\text{direct source}} \text{NC}(\text{New Cosmological View})$$

Process philosophy and relational ontology are the main philosophical sources of NC-1 (relationality) and NC-2 (process).

Recommended Books

No.TitleAuthorPublication informationReason for recommendation
1Process Philosophy: A Survey of Basic IssuesN. RescherPittsburgh UP, 2000An introduction to process philosophy
2Whitehead's Philosophy: Points of ConnectionJ. Cobb Jr., D. GriffinSUNY, 1989An introduction to Whitehead
3Process and Reality (An Essay in Cosmology)A.N. WhiteheadFree Press, 1929/1978A classic of process philosophy
4Adventures of IdeasA.N. WhiteheadFree Press, 1933A more accessible work of Whitehead
5Thinking with WhiteheadIsabelle StengersHarvard UP, 2011A contemporary reading of Whitehead

Detailed Description

Book 3: Process and Reality

Title: Process and Reality: An Essay in Cosmology Author: Alfred North Whitehead Publication: Free Press, 1929 (corrected edition 1978) Pages: Approx. 400 pages Difficulty: ★★★★★

Content summary:

  • A system of process metaphysics
  • Actual entities and eternal objects
  • Creativity and novelty

Relationship to this work:

  • The main philosophical source of NC-2 (process precedes state)
  • The philosophical foundation of relational ontology
  • The concepts of creativity and the space of possibilities

Reading suggestions:

  • This is an extremely difficult text
  • It is recommended to first read introductory texts
  • One may begin with the conceptual framework in Part One

References and Indices REFERENCES AND INDICES

I. The Task and Positioning of This Part

This part provides a complete reference and index system for the four-volume work The Normative Foundations of Interstellar Civilization. As an interdisciplinary foundational work, this work draws on intellectual resources from multiple disciplines, including physics, consciousness science, ethics, political philosophy, longtermism research, AI safety research, international space law, complex systems science, and process philosophy. This part aims to:

  1. Trace the sources of thought: clearly mark the academic resources on which this work relies
  2. Facilitate consultation and retrieval: provide a multi-dimensional index system
  3. Support subsequent research: provide readers with an entry point for further research

Postscript Postscript

The writing of this work began with a simple yet fundamental question: as human civilization begins to expand into interstellar space, as artificial intelligence begins to display capabilities surpassing those of humans, as our decisions begin to affect the future tens of millions of years away—what kind of normative framework should guide our actions?

This question is urgent because we stand at a critical juncture in human history. Our technological capabilities are growing at an unprecedented rate, but our ethical wisdom and institutional frameworks lag far behind. We can manipulate atoms, edit genes, and create intelligence, yet we are still arguing endlessly over the most basic normative questions.

This work attempts to offer a response. It is built on three core insights:

First, we need a "New Three Views"—to understand the universe we inhabit, the life we possess, and the cognition we carry out. The traditional substance-centered, static, spectator worldview is no longer applicable. We need a relational, processual, participatory worldview in order to understand the microscopic world revealed by quantum mechanics, the macroscopic world presented by complex systems, and the inner world explored by consciousness science.

Second, we need a set of normative principles derivable from this new worldview—the Recursive Freedom Principle, the Negentropy Responsibility Principle, and the Reversibility Principle—to guide our decisions under conditions of deep uncertainty. These principles are not arbitrary moral intuitions, but normative conclusions derived from the descriptive propositions of the New Three Views through a rigorous bridge argument.

Third, we need a methodology for translating these principles into operable institutions—the protocol stack methodology—to achieve the unity of "stable principles" and "flexible operations." This methodology draws on the layered architecture of computer network protocol stacks, distinguishing different levels from physical constraints to operational rules, and provides a framework for the incremental evolution of institutions.

Of course, this work is only a starting point. It proposes the basic framework of the discipline of "Interstellar Civilization Studies," but this framework still requires a great deal of follow-up work to refine, validate, and apply. The indicator system needs empirical validation, the institutional design needs feasibility studies, and the theoretical framework needs continuous revision.

The process of writing this work has also been a process of self-education. I have had to cross the boundaries of multiple disciplines—from quantum mechanics to consciousness science, from ethics to international law, from complex systems to institutional design. In each field, I am only a learner, not an expert. This means that this work necessarily contains various shortcomings and errors. I sincerely welcome criticism and correction from all fields.

Finally, I wish to express a hope: that this work may inspire more scholars to pay attention to these questions, promote interdisciplinary dialogue and cooperation, and contribute a modest intellectual resource to the long-term future of human civilization.

Our descendants—whether they are biological humans, digital minds, or some form of existence we have not yet imagined—all have the right to inherit an open, sustainable universe full of possibilities. Let us strive for this.

Completed in [December 2025]
